subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define nutrition and nutrient. Explain the role of nutrition in maintaining health and the factors affecting nutritional status. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
Introduction Food is one of the basic needs of life. What we eat, and how the body uses it, decides our growth, our capacity to work, our resistance to disease and even how long we live. For a nurse, nutrition is part of every patient's care – from the antenatal mother to the post-operative patient and the elderly.

A. Definitions (2 marks)

1. Nutrition

  • Nutrition is the science of food, the nutrients and other substances in it, their action, interaction and balance in relation to health and disease, and the processes by which the body ingests, digests, absorbs, transports, uses and excretes food substances
  • WHO: nutrition is the intake of food considered in relation to the body's dietary needs; good nutrition – an adequate, well-balanced diet with regular physical activity – is a cornerstone of good health

2. Nutrient

  • A nutrient is a chemical substance present in food that the body needs for energy, growth, repair and regulation of body processes
  • Six groups – carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water; dietary fibre is also important

3. Related terms

  • Food – anything eaten or drunk that nourishes the body
  • Nutritional status – the condition of health of a person as influenced by the intake and utilisation of nutrients
  • Malnutrition – deficiencies, excesses or imbalances in the intake of energy and/or nutrients (includes both under-nutrition and over-nutrition)
  • Health (WHO) – a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity

B. Role of nutrition in maintaining health (4 marks)

  1. Growth and development
    • Adequate protein, energy, calcium and vitamins are needed for normal growth of the fetus, infant, child and adolescent
    • Under-nutrition leads to stunting, wasting and low birth weight
  2. Energy for body functions and work
    • Carbohydrates and fats provide energy for the heart, brain, breathing and physical work
    • Well-nourished people have better work capacity and productivity
  3. Maintenance and repair of tissues
    • Proteins, zinc and vitamin C help wound healing and recovery after illness and surgery
  4. Immunity and resistance to infection
    • Malnutrition lowers immunity; infections in turn worsen malnutrition – the malnutrition–infection cycle
    • Vitamin A, zinc, iron and protein are essential for immunity
  5. Mental development and function
    • Iodine, iron, protein and DHA are needed for brain development and learning; deficiency lowers IQ and school performance
  6. Reproductive health
    • Good maternal nutrition gives healthy pregnancy, normal birth weight and adequate breast milk
    • Anaemia and under-nutrition increase maternal and infant deaths
  7. Prevention of deficiency diseases
    • Kwashiorkor, marasmus, anaemia, goitre, rickets, night blindness and scurvy are all preventable by proper diet
  8. Prevention of non-communicable diseases
    • A diet low in salt, sugar and saturated fat and rich in fibre, fruits and vegetables reduces obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and some cancers
  9. Regulation of body processes
    • Vitamins and minerals act as coenzymes and cofactors; water regulates temperature and transport
  10. Healthy ageing and longevity
    • Good nutrition maintains bone, muscle and mental health in old age

C. Factors affecting food intake and nutritional status (4 marks)

1. Food availability (food security)

  • Agricultural production, seasons, storage, transport and distribution (Public Distribution System)
  • Natural disasters – floods, drought – cause food shortage

2. Economic factors

  • Income and purchasing power – poverty is the main cause of under-nutrition
  • Food prices, unemployment and family size – more members means less food per person

3. Socio-cultural factors

  • Food habits and customs – traditional diets, regional preferences (rice in the south and east, wheat in the north)
  • Religion – vegetarianism, fasting days, avoidance of certain foods
  • Food taboos and beliefs – e.g. avoiding papaya, eggs or green vegetables in pregnancy; withholding colostrum
  • Food fads – unscientific beliefs about "hot" and "cold" foods
  • Gender discrimination – women and girls often eat last and least
  • Joint family customs and cooking practices

4. Education and knowledge

  • Mother's literacy and nutrition knowledge strongly influence child nutrition
  • Media and advertisements promote junk food and soft drinks

5. Physiological and individual factors

  • Age, sex, body size and physiological state (pregnancy, lactation, growth)
  • Physical activity level
  • Appetite, taste preferences, chewing and swallowing ability, dental health
  • Psychological state – stress, depression, anxiety, loneliness

6. Health status and disease

  • Infections – diarrhoea, worm infestation, tuberculosis – reduce appetite and absorption and increase needs
  • Chronic illness, malabsorption, surgery, cancer
  • Drugs – some reduce appetite or interfere with absorption; alcohol and tobacco

7. Environmental factors

  • Safe drinking water and sanitation – poor sanitation causes repeated infections
  • Climate and housing conditions

8. Lifestyle and urbanisation

  • Working parents, eating out, fast and processed foods, sedentary life – leading to obesity

9. Government policies and programmes

  • ICDS, PM POSHAN (mid-day meal), PDS, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, food fortification improve nutritional status

D. Role of the nurse

  • Assess nutritional status of every patient on admission
  • Educate families about balanced diet, breastfeeding and complementary feeding
  • Identify and correct food taboos sensitively
  • Link vulnerable families to government nutrition programmes

Conclusion Nutrition is the science of food and its relation to health, and nutrients are the substances in food that the body needs; good nutrition supports growth, immunity, work capacity and prevention of disease, while income, culture, education, illness and environment decide a person's nutritional status.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on nutrients – classification and functions.
answer_html:
Introduction Nutrients are chemical substances in food that the body needs for energy, growth, repair and regulation of life processes. Most foods contain several nutrients in different amounts.

A. Classification of nutrients

1. Based on chemical nature (six groups)

  • Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water; dietary fibre is also important

2. Based on quantity required

  • Macronutrients – needed in grams: carbohydrates, proteins, fats (and water)
  • Micronutrients – needed in milligrams or micrograms: vitamins and minerals

3. Based on chemical composition

  • Organic – contain carbon: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins
  • Inorganic – no carbon: minerals and water

4. Based on energy value

  • Energy-yielding – carbohydrates (4 kcal/g), proteins (4 kcal/g), fats (9 kcal/g)
  • Non-energy-yielding – vitamins, minerals, water

5. Based on function

  • Energy-giving – carbohydrates, fats
  • Body-building – proteins, minerals (calcium, phosphorus)
  • Protective / regulatory – vitamins, minerals, water, fibre

6. Based on essentiality

  • Essential – must be supplied by food (essential amino acids and fatty acids, most vitamins, minerals)
  • Non-essential – can be made in the body

B. Functions of each nutrient

Nutrient Main functions Good sources
Carbohydrates main source of energy; spare protein; fuel for the brain cereals, millets, roots, sugar
Proteins growth, repair, enzymes, hormones, antibodies pulses, milk, egg, meat, fish
Fats concentrated energy; fat-soluble vitamins; essential fatty acids; insulation oils, ghee, nuts, oilseeds
Vitamins regulate metabolism (coenzymes); vision, immunity, blood formation fruits, vegetables, milk, liver
Minerals bones and teeth, blood formation, fluid balance, nerve and muscle function milk, green leafy vegetables, salt, meat
Water medium for all reactions; transport; temperature regulation; excretion drinking water, beverages, foods
Dietary fibre prevents constipation; lowers cholesterol and blood sugar whole grains, vegetables, fruits

C. Interrelationship of nutrients

  • Nutrients work together – e.g. vitamin C improves iron absorption; vitamin D is needed for calcium absorption; B-vitamins are needed to release energy from carbohydrates
  • Adequate carbohydrate spares protein for body-building

D. Nursing relevance

  • Assess whether the patient's diet supplies all nutrient groups
  • Choose foods from all food groups while planning diets
  • Identify patients at risk of deficiency – pregnant women, children, elderly, chronically ill

Conclusion Nutrients are classified by chemical nature, quantity required, composition, energy value, function and essentiality; each has specific functions, and all must be present in the right proportion in a balanced diet.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Classify foods with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Foods can be grouped in several ways. Classification helps in planning balanced diets, menus and nutrition education, and in storage of food.

1. Classification by origin

  • Plant (vegetable) foods – cereals, millets, pulses, vegetables, fruits, nuts, oilseeds, sugar
  • Animal foods – milk and milk products, eggs, meat, fish, poultry, organ meats

2. Classification by chemical composition (predominant nutrient)

  • Carbohydrate-rich – rice, wheat, millets, potato, sugar, jaggery
  • Protein-rich – pulses, soybean, milk, egg, meat, fish, groundnut
  • Fat-rich – oils, ghee, butter, nuts, oilseeds
  • Vitamin- and mineral-rich – fruits, vegetables, green leafy vegetables

3. Classification by function

  • Energy-yielding foods – cereals, millets, roots and tubers, sugars, fats and oils, nuts
  • Body-building foods – milk, egg, meat, fish, pulses, nuts and oilseeds
  • Protective (regulatory) foods – fruits, vegetables, green leafy vegetables, milk, eggs, liver

4. Classification by nutritive value – ICMR basic five food groups

Food group Examples Main nutrients
1. Cereals, millets and products rice, wheat, jowar, bajra, ragi, maize, poha energy, protein, B-vitamins, fibre, iron (millets), calcium (ragi)
2. Pulses and legumes Bengal gram, red gram, green gram, black gram, rajma, soybean protein, energy, B-vitamins, fibre, iron
3. Milk and meat products milk, curd, paneer, egg, meat, fish, chicken protein, fat, calcium (milk), iron (meat), vitamin B₁₂
4. Fruits and vegetables green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, roots, fruits vitamins (A, C, folate), minerals, fibre, antioxidants
5. Fats and sugars oil, ghee, butter, sugar, jaggery energy; essential fatty acids (oils)

5. Classification by perishability

  • Perishable – spoil within a day or two: milk, meat, fish, leafy vegetables, cooked food → refrigerate
  • Semi-perishable – keep for weeks to months if stored well: potatoes, onions, flour, nuts, eggs (under refrigeration)
  • Non-perishable – keep for long periods: cereals, pulses, sugar, salt, dried and canned foods

6. Other classifications

  • Fresh and processed foods; ultra-processed foods (chips, soft drinks, instant noodles) – to be limited
  • Fortified foods – iodised salt, double-fortified salt, fortified rice and oil

Uses of food classification

  • Planning a balanced diet – include foods from every group each day
  • Nutrition education – simple messages using food groups
  • Food exchange lists for therapeutic diets
  • Proper storage to prevent spoilage

Conclusion Foods are classified by origin, predominant nutrient, function, nutritive value (the ICMR five food groups) and perishability; choosing foods from all groups every day is the basis of a balanced diet.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Differentiate between macronutrients and micronutrients.
answer_html:
Point Macronutrients Micronutrients
Amount needed large amounts – grams per day small amounts – milligrams or micrograms per day
Examples carbohydrates, proteins, fats (and water) vitamins (A, D, B-complex, C) and minerals (iron, iodine, zinc, calcium)
Energy provide energy (except water) – 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g do not provide energy
Main role energy, growth, body structure regulate body processes – enzymes, immunity, blood formation
Deficiency protein-energy malnutrition – marasmus, kwashiorkor "hidden hunger" – anaemia, goitre, night blindness, rickets
Sources cereals, pulses, oils, milk, meat fruits, vegetables, milk, eggs, meat, iodised salt

Note: both are equally essential; a diet adequate in calories may still lack micronutrients.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Differentiate between under-nutrition and over-nutrition.
answer_html:
Introduction Both are forms of malnutrition.

Point Under-nutrition Over-nutrition
Meaning intake of energy and/or nutrients less than the body's needs intake of energy and/or nutrients more than the body's needs
Forms wasting, stunting, underweight, micronutrient deficiencies overweight, obesity, hypervitaminosis
Main causes poverty, food shortage, infections, poor feeding practices excess calories, fast food, sugar, fat, physical inactivity
Indicators BMI below 18.5; low weight-for-age or height-for-age in children BMI 23 or more (Asian cut-off for overweight; 25 or more for obesity)
Consequences PEM, anaemia, repeated infections, poor growth, death in children diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, joint problems, some cancers
More common in poor and rural populations, children, pregnant women urban, affluent and sedentary people (now spreading to all groups)

Note: India faces both at the same time – the double burden of malnutrition.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Differentiate between organic and inorganic nutrients.
answer_html:
Point Organic nutrients Inorganic nutrients
Chemical nature contain carbon (with hydrogen and oxygen) do not contain carbon
Examples carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins minerals and water
Origin made by living organisms (plants and animals) come from soil, water and rocks; plants absorb minerals from soil
Effect of heat, light, air many are destroyed – especially vitamins B₁ and C not destroyed by cooking, but may be lost in cooking water
Energy carbohydrates, proteins and fats provide energy no energy
Amount needed macronutrients in grams; vitamins in mg/µg water in litres; minerals in mg or µg
Main role energy, growth, regulation (vitamins) bones and teeth, fluid balance, enzymes, blood formation

Practical point: use cooking water and avoid overcooking to save both water-soluble vitamins and minerals.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is naturopathy?
answer_html:
Definition Naturopathy (nature cure) is a drugless system of healing based on the belief that the body has the power to heal itself when it is helped by natural means and a healthy way of living.

Principles

  1. Disease is caused by accumulation of waste (morbid matter) and unhealthy living
  2. Nature is the healer; treat the whole person – body, mind and lifestyle
  3. Emphasis on prevention and health promotion

Methods (therapies)

  • Diet therapy and fasting – fresh fruits, raw vegetables, juices, whole grains
  • Hydrotherapy (water), mud therapy, heliotherapy (sunlight), fresh air
  • Massage, yoga, exercise and relaxation

In India

  • Part of AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy)
  • National Institute of Naturopathy, Pune; Naturopathy Day – 18 November

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What are functional foods and nutraceuticals?
answer_html:
Functional foods

  • Foods that give health benefits beyond basic nutrition and may reduce the risk of disease
  • Examples:
    • curd / yoghurt – probiotics (good bacteria) for gut health
    • oats and barley – beta-glucan lowers cholesterol
    • flaxseed, walnuts – omega-3 fatty acids
    • turmeric, garlic, green tea – antioxidants
    • fortified foods – iodised salt, fortified rice

Nutraceuticals

  • Products derived from foods but sold in medicinal forms (capsules, tablets, powders) for health benefit
  • Examples – omega-3 capsules, probiotic sachets, antioxidant supplements, glucosamine
  • Regulated in India by FSSAI (Nutraceutical Regulations, 2016)

Related terms: probiotics – live beneficial microbes; prebiotics – fibres that feed them (onion, banana, garlic).

Caution: they support but do not replace a balanced diet or prescribed medicines.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is the triple burden of malnutrition?
answer_html:
Definition The triple burden of malnutrition is the coexistence of three forms of malnutrition in the same country, community, household or even the same person:

  1. Under-nutrition – stunting, wasting, underweight
  2. Micronutrient deficiencies ("hidden hunger") – iron, iodine, vitamin A, zinc, folate
  3. Over-nutrition – overweight, obesity and diet-related diseases (diabetes, hypertension)

Indian situation (NFHS-5, 2019–21)

  • Children under 5: stunting 35.5%, wasting 19.3%, underweight 32.1%
  • Anaemia – 67% of children (6–59 months) and 57% of women (15–49 years)
  • Overweight/obesity – about 24% of women and 23% of men

Causes: poverty with nutrition transition – shift to refined, processed, high-fat and high-sugar foods with less physical activity.

Action: dietary diversity, fortification, programmes like POSHAN Abhiyaan and Anaemia Mukt Bharat, and promotion of healthy lifestyles.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on carbohydrates.
answer_html:
Introduction Carbohydrates are organic compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, usually in the ratio 1:2:1 [general formula Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ]. They are the cheapest and most important source of energy in the Indian diet, supplying about 60–70% of total calories in most Indian homes.

A. Composition – types

  1. Sugars
    • Monosaccharides – glucose, fructose (fruits, honey), galactose
    • Disaccharides – sucrose (cane sugar), lactose (milk sugar), maltose (malt)
  2. Starches – complex carbohydrates in cereals, millets, roots and tubers, pulses; glycogen is the animal starch stored in liver and muscle
  3. Cellulose and other fibres – cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, gums; not digested by humans – form dietary fibre

B. Dietary sources

  • Cereals – rice, wheat, maize; millets – jowar, bajra, ragi
  • Roots and tubers – potato, sweet potato, tapioca, yam
  • Sugars – sugar, jaggery, honey, sweets
  • Pulses, dried fruits (dates, raisins), fruits (banana, mango, chikoo), milk (lactose)
  • Fibre – whole grains, vegetables, fruits, pulses

C. Functions

  1. Main source of energy – 4 kcal per gram
  2. Protein sparing – adequate carbohydrate allows protein to be used for body-building
  3. Prevents ketosis – needed for complete oxidation of fats
  4. Essential fuel for the brain, nervous system and red blood cells
  5. Glycogen in liver and muscle is a quick energy reserve
  6. Dietary fibre – prevents constipation, lowers cholesterol and blood sugar, gives satiety
  7. Lactose – helps absorption of calcium and growth of useful gut bacteria
  8. Forms parts of important compounds – ribose in nucleic acids, glycoproteins, glucuronic acid (detoxification)
  9. Gives flavour and sweetness to food

D. Requirement

  • Should provide about 50–60% of total energy, mainly as complex carbohydrates (whole grains, millets, pulses)
  • Minimum about 130 g/day for adults (based on the brain's glucose needs)
  • Added sugar should be less than 5–10% of energy (about 25 g or 5–6 teaspoons a day)
  • Dietary fibre about 25–40 g/day

E. Effects of deficiency and excess

  • Deficiency – weight loss, fatigue, ketosis, breakdown of body protein; part of PEM
  • Excess – obesity, raised triglycerides, dental caries (sugar), raised blood sugar in diabetics

F. Nursing points

  • Encourage whole grains and millets over refined flour and polished rice
  • Limit sweets, soft drinks and packaged juices, especially in children and diabetics
  • Ensure enough carbohydrate in fever, surgery and burns to spare protein

Conclusion Carbohydrates – sugars, starches and fibres – are the main and cheapest source of energy, spare protein, prevent ketosis and keep the bowel healthy; they should come mainly from whole grains, millets and pulses, with limited added sugar.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Classify carbohydrates with examples.
answer_html:
Classification (based on number of sugar units)

  1. Monosaccharides – single sugar units; cannot be further broken down
    • Glucose (grape sugar, blood sugar), fructose (fruit sugar, honey), galactose (from milk sugar)
  2. Disaccharides – two sugar units
    • Sucrose = glucose + fructose (cane sugar)
    • Lactose = glucose + galactose (milk)
    • Maltose = glucose + glucose (malt, germinating grains)
  3. Oligosaccharides – 3–10 sugar units
    • Raffinose, stachyose in pulses and beans – cause flatulence as they are not digested
  4. Polysaccharides – many sugar units
    • Digestible – starch (cereals, potato), glycogen (liver, muscle), dextrins
    • Non-digestible (dietary fibre) – cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin (fruits), gums

Other classification: simple carbohydrates (sugars) and complex carbohydrates (starch and fibre) – complex ones are healthier.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the dietary sources of carbohydrates.
answer_html:
Introduction Carbohydrates are found mainly in plant foods; milk is the only important animal source.

Sources

  1. Cereals (70–78% carbohydrate) – rice, wheat, maize, oats, barley; products – poha, rava, bread, pasta
  2. Millets – jowar, bajra, ragi, kodo, foxtail millet – also rich in fibre and minerals
  3. Pulses and legumes (about 55–60%) – chana, moong, masoor, rajma
  4. Roots and tubers – potato, sweet potato, tapioca, yam, colocasia
  5. Sugars – sugar, jaggery, honey, sweets, jams, soft drinks
  6. Fruits – banana, mango, chikoo, grapes; dried fruits – dates, raisins
  7. Milk – lactose (about 4.5–5 g per 100 ml)
  8. Fibre-rich sources – whole grains, vegetables, fruits, pulses

Healthy choice: prefer whole grains, millets and pulses (complex carbohydrates with fibre) over sugar and refined flour (maida).

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR).
answer_html:
Definition Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the minimum amount of energy required to maintain the vital functions of the body – heartbeat, breathing, circulation, body temperature and cell activity – when the person is at complete physical and mental rest.

Conditions for measurement

  • Post-absorptive state – 12–14 hours after the last meal
  • Awake, lying down, relaxed
  • At a comfortable room temperature, after a good night's sleep

Values

  • About 1 kcal per kg body weight per hour in adults (roughly 1,200–1,700 kcal/day)
  • Expressed as kcal/m² body surface area/hour or kcal/day

Significance

  • BMR forms 60–70% of total daily energy expenditure
  • Used to calculate energy requirements
  • Raised in hyperthyroidism, fever, growth and pregnancy; lowered in hypothyroidism and starvation

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define energy. Give its unit and the energy values of nutrients.
answer_html:
Definition Energy is the capacity to do work. The body obtains energy from the oxidation of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in food, and uses it for vital functions, physical activity, growth and maintenance of body temperature.

Unit

  • Kilocalorie (kcal) – the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C (from 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C)
  • SI unit – kilojoule (kJ); 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ

Measurement: energy value of food is measured in a bomb calorimeter.

Physiological fuel values (Atwater factors)

Nutrient Energy
Carbohydrate 4 kcal/g
Protein 4 kcal/g
Fat 9 kcal/g
Alcohol 7 kcal/g (no nutritive value)

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is specific dynamic action (thermic effect) of food?
answer_html:
Definition Specific dynamic action (SDA) – also called the thermic effect of food or diet-induced thermogenesis – is the increase in heat production (energy expenditure) above the BMR after taking food.

Cause

  • Energy is used for digestion, absorption, transport, metabolism and storage of nutrients

Values

  • Proteins – highest, about 20–30% of their energy value
  • Carbohydrates – about 5–10%
  • Fats – about 0–5%
  • Mixed diet – about 10% of total energy intake

Significance

  • An allowance of about 10% for SDA is added when calculating energy requirements
  • High-protein meals produce more body heat – people in hot climates feel warmer after them
  • Explains the feeling of warmth after a meal

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is glycaemic index? Give examples of high and low GI foods.
answer_html:
Definition Glycaemic index (GI) is a ranking of carbohydrate-containing foods according to how quickly they raise blood glucose after eating, compared with glucose (GI = 100).

Categories and examples

  • Low GI (55 or less) – whole pulses (rajma, chana), barley, oats, most fruits (apple, orange, guava), milk, curd, nuts
  • Medium GI (56–69) – whole-wheat roti, brown rice, banana, sweet potato
  • High GI (70 or more) – glucose, white bread, polished white rice, potato, cornflakes, sugary drinks

Factors lowering GI: fibre, fat and protein in the meal, less processing, less cooking, cooling cooked rice.

Glycaemic load = GI × grams of carbohydrate per serving ÷ 100 – also considers portion size.

Uses: planning diets in diabetes, obesity and heart disease; low-GI foods give longer satiety.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: State the recommended intake of carbohydrates and the limits for added sugar.
answer_html:
Recommended intake

  1. Total carbohydrates – about 50–60% of total daily energy for adults
  2. Minimum requirement – about 130 g/day for adults, based on the glucose needs of the brain
  3. Most should be complex carbohydrates – whole grains, millets, pulses, vegetables
  4. Dietary fibre – about 25–40 g/day (ICMR suggests about 40 g per 2,000 kcal)

Limits for added (free) sugar

  • WHO – free sugars less than 10% of total energy, preferably less than 5% (about 25 g or 6 teaspoons a day)
  • ICMR-NIN – limit added sugar to about 5% of energy (25 g a day); children should get even less
  • Hidden sugar in soft drinks, packaged juices, biscuits, sweets counts too

Why: excess sugar causes dental caries, obesity, diabetes and high triglycerides.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the factors affecting basal metabolic rate.
answer_html:
Introduction Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy needed for vital functions at complete rest. It forms 60–70% of daily energy expenditure and varies from person to person due to many factors.

1. Body size and surface area

  • BMR is proportional to body surface area – taller and larger persons have higher BMR
  • Heat loss is greater with a larger surface area

2. Body composition

  • Lean body mass (muscle) is metabolically active; fat tissue is less active
  • Athletes and muscular persons have higher BMR; obese persons have lower BMR per kg

3. Age

  • Highest in infancy and early childhood (rapid growth)
  • Falls gradually after about 20–30 years (about 2% per decade) due to loss of muscle

4. Sex

  • Men have about 5–10% higher BMR than women – more muscle, less fat

5. Growth, pregnancy and lactation

  • Growth raises BMR in children and adolescents
  • Pregnancy raises BMR (by about 15–20% in the last trimester) – fetus, placenta and maternal tissues
  • Lactation increases energy needs

6. Hormones

  • Thyroxine – the most important; hyperthyroidism raises BMR (up to 50–100%), hypothyroidism lowers it
  • Adrenaline (stress, fear), growth hormone and male sex hormones raise BMR

7. Body temperature (fever)

  • BMR rises by about 13% for every 1 °C rise in body temperature
  • So febrile patients need more calories and fluids

8. Climate

  • BMR is slightly higher in cold climates (to produce heat) and lower in hot climates

9. Nutritional state

  • Starvation and under-nutrition lower BMR (body adapts to save energy)
  • Over-feeding slightly raises it

10. Sleep – BMR falls by about 10% during sleep

11. Disease and injury

  • Raised in burns, major surgery, trauma, sepsis, cancer, hyperthyroidism
  • Lowered in hypothyroidism, Addison's disease

12. Drugs and stimulants

  • Caffeine, nicotine and amphetamines raise BMR; sedatives and beta-blockers lower it

13. Physical training and race – regular exercise increases muscle mass and BMR; small racial differences exist

Nursing relevance

  • Increase calories and fluids in fever, burns, surgery and hyperthyroidism
  • Elderly persons need fewer calories but the same or more protein and micronutrients
  • Weight reduction diets should be combined with exercise to preserve muscle and BMR

Conclusion BMR depends on body size and composition, age, sex, growth, hormones (especially thyroxine), body temperature, climate, nutritional state, disease and drugs; these factors explain why energy needs differ between individuals and conditions.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the energy requirements of the body and the factors influencing them.
answer_html:
Introduction Energy requirement is the amount of food energy needed to balance energy expenditure so as to maintain body weight, body composition and physical activity, and to allow growth, pregnancy and lactation. It is expressed in kcal/day.

A. Components of energy expenditure

  1. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) – 60–70% of daily expenditure; energy for vital functions at rest
  2. Thermic effect of food (SDA) – about 10%; energy used to digest and metabolise food
  3. Physical activity – 20–30% or more; the most variable component – depends on occupation and exercise
  4. Additional needs – growth (children, adolescents), pregnancy and lactation, recovery from illness

B. Assessment of energy requirement

  • Factorial method: energy requirement = BMR × physical activity level (PAL)
    • sedentary PAL about 1.53
    • moderate about 1.8
    • heavy about 2.3
  • Expressed for a reference man and woman of healthy body weight

C. Energy requirements of Indian adults (ICMR-NIN 2020)

Group Sedentary Moderate Heavy
Man (65 kg) 2,110 kcal 2,710 kcal 3,470 kcal
Woman (55 kg) 1,660 kcal 2,130 kcal 2,720 kcal
Pregnant woman +350 kcal/day (2nd and 3rd trimesters)
Lactating woman +600 kcal/day (0–6 months); +520 kcal/day (7–12 months)
  • Sedentary – office workers, teachers, housewives with help
  • Moderate – drivers, nurses, farm workers with machines, housewives without help
  • Heavy – manual labourers, stone cutters, miners, agricultural labourers

D. Factors influencing energy requirement

  1. Age – high per kg in infants and children; falls in the elderly
  2. Sex – men need more than women
  3. Body size and composition
  4. Physical activity and occupation – the largest variable
  5. Physiological state – pregnancy, lactation, growth
  6. Climate – slightly more in cold weather
  7. Illness – fever, infections, burns, trauma, surgery and cancer increase needs; immobility decreases them
  8. Hormonal status – thyroid disorders

E. Energy balance

  • Intake = expenditure → weight stable
  • Intake > expenditure → weight gain, obesity
  • Intake < expenditure → weight loss, under-nutrition
  • About 7,700 kcal of excess or deficit roughly equals 1 kg of body fat

F. Sources of energy in the diet

  • Carbohydrates 50–60%, fats 20–30% (not more than 30%), proteins 10–15% of total energy

G. Nursing relevance

  • Calculate patients' needs using weight and activity; increase in fever and burns
  • Monitor weight regularly to judge energy balance
  • Counsel pregnant and lactating women about extra energy needs

Conclusion Daily energy requirement is the sum of BMR, thermic effect of food and physical activity, with extra allowances for growth, pregnancy and lactation; ICMR-NIN 2020 values range from about 1,660 kcal for a sedentary woman to 3,470 kcal for a man doing heavy work.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the measurement of energy – the energy value of foods and the energy expenditure of the body. Add a note on respiratory quotient. (4 + 4 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction The body needs a continuous supply of energy for vital functions, activity and growth. To plan diets we must know how much energy foods provide and how much energy the body spends. Energy is expressed in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ) – 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ; 1 megajoule (MJ) = 239 kcal.

A. Measurement of the energy value of foods (4 marks)

1. Bomb calorimeter

  • Principle: a known weight of dried food is burnt completely in oxygen inside a sealed steel container (the "bomb") placed in a known volume of water; the rise in water temperature gives the heat produced
  • This is the gross energy (heat of combustion) of the food
  • Gross values – carbohydrate about 4.1, fat about 9.45 and protein about 5.65 kcal/g

2. Physiological fuel values (Atwater factors)

  • The body does not obtain all the gross energy because:
    • digestion is incomplete (about 98% of carbohydrate, 95% of fat and 92% of protein is absorbed)
    • protein is not completely oxidised – its nitrogen leaves the body as urea, which still contains energy
  • After these corrections, the physiological fuel values are:
    • carbohydrate – 4 kcal/g
    • protein – 4 kcal/g
    • fat – 9 kcal/g
    • alcohol – 7 kcal/g; dietary fibre about 2 kcal/g

3. Calculation from food composition tables

  • Energy = (4 × carbohydrate g) + (4 × protein g) + (9 × fat g)
  • Example – 100 g of whole-wheat flour (protein 12 g, fat 1.7 g, carbohydrate 69 g): 48 + 15 + 276 = about 339 kcal

4. Food labels

  • Packaged foods show energy per 100 g and per serving – useful for consumers and patients

B. Measurement of energy expenditure of the body (4 marks)

1. Direct calorimetry

  • The person stays in an insulated chamber (respiration calorimeter); the heat given off by the body is measured by the rise in temperature of water circulating through the chamber
  • Very accurate, but expensive and impractical – used only in research

2. Indirect calorimetry

  • Measures oxygen consumed (and carbon dioxide produced); about 4.8 kcal of energy is released for each litre of oxygen used on a mixed diet
  • Closed-circuit method – Benedict–Roth spirometer – used to measure BMR
  • Open-circuit method – Douglas bag collects expired air during activity for analysis
  • Modern metabolic carts and ventilated hoods are used in ICUs to measure patients' energy needs

3. Doubly labelled water method

  • The person drinks water labelled with stable isotopes of hydrogen (²H) and oxygen (¹⁸O); their elimination rates in urine give CO₂ production and hence total energy expenditure over 1–2 weeks
  • Accurate in free-living people; non-invasive but expensive

4. Factorial method

  • Time spent on each activity (from a 24-hour activity diary) × energy cost of the activity (expressed as multiples of BMR)
  • Gives the physical activity level (PAL); used by ICMR-NIN to set energy requirements

5. Field methods

  • Heart-rate monitoring, pedometers, accelerometers and wearable fitness devices
  • Prediction equations for BMR from weight, height, age and sex (e.g. Harris–Benedict, Schofield, FAO/WHO)

C. Respiratory quotient (2 marks)

  • Definition: RQ = volume of CO₂ produced ÷ volume of O₂ consumed in the same time
  • Values:
    • carbohydrate – 1.0
    • protein – about 0.8
    • fat – about 0.7
    • mixed diet – about 0.82–0.85
  • Significance
    • shows which fuel is being oxidised
    • above 1 – fat being made from excess carbohydrate (over-feeding)
    • near 0.7 or below – fat breakdown, starvation, ketosis, uncontrolled diabetes
    • used to calculate energy expenditure in indirect calorimetry
    • in ventilated ICU patients, excess glucose in feeds raises CO₂ production and may delay weaning from the ventilator

D. Nursing relevance

  • Estimate patients' energy needs (often 25–35 kcal/kg/day) and adjust in fever, burns and sepsis
  • Teach patients to read calorie information on labels
  • Monitor weight to judge energy balance

E. Practical estimation of patients' energy needs

  • Healthy adults – ICMR-NIN tables based on BMR × physical activity level
  • Quick bedside rule – about 25–30 kcal per kg body weight per day for maintenance, 30–35 kcal/kg during illness and recovery, more in burns and sepsis (as advised by the dietitian)
  • Obese patients – calculated on adjusted or ideal body weight
  • Critically ill patients – indirect calorimetry where available; otherwise predictive equations, with gradual increase of feeds to avoid over-feeding

Conclusion The energy value of foods is measured by bomb calorimetry and expressed as physiological fuel values of 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g; energy expenditure is measured by direct and indirect calorimetry, doubly labelled water and factorial methods, and the respiratory quotient shows which fuel the body is using.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define proteins. Classify them. Explain their functions and digestion. (1 + 3 + 3 + 3)
answer_html:
A. Definition (1 mark) Proteins are complex nitrogen-containing organic compounds made up of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. They contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (about 16% nitrogen), and usually sulphur and sometimes phosphorus. The word protein comes from the Greek proteios – "of first importance".

B. Classification (3 marks)

1. Based on composition (chemical)

  • Simple proteins – give only amino acids on hydrolysis
    • albumins (egg albumin, serum albumin), globulins (serum globulins)
    • glutelins (glutenin of wheat), prolamins (gliadin of wheat, zein of maize)
    • scleroproteins – collagen, keratin, elastin
  • Conjugated proteins – protein + non-protein (prosthetic) group
    • phosphoproteins – casein of milk
    • glycoproteins – mucin
    • lipoproteins – LDL, HDL
    • chromoproteins – haemoglobin
    • nucleoproteins – in chromosomes; metalloproteins – ferritin
  • Derived proteins – formed by partial breakdown – proteoses, peptones, peptides; coagulated proteins

2. Based on shape

  • Fibrous – long, insoluble – collagen, keratin
  • Globular – round, soluble – albumin, haemoglobin, enzymes

3. Based on nutritional quality

  • Complete proteins – contain all essential amino acids in adequate amounts; support growth and maintenance – egg, milk, meat, fish; egg protein is the reference protein
  • Partially complete proteins – low in one or more essential amino acids; maintain life but do not support good growth – cereals (low lysine), pulses (low methionine)
  • Incomplete proteins – lack one or more essential amino acids; cannot support life or growth – gelatin (no tryptophan), zein of maize (low lysine and tryptophan)

4. Based on source

  • Animal proteins – high quality, more expensive
  • Plant proteins – cheaper; quality improved by combining foods

C. Functions (3 marks)

  1. Body-building and growth – formation of new tissues in infancy, childhood, adolescence and pregnancy
  2. Repair and maintenance – replacement of worn-out cells; wound healing after injury, burns and surgery
  3. Enzymes – all enzymes are proteins (amylase, pepsin, trypsin)
  4. Hormones – insulin, growth hormone, parathormone, thyroxine (from tyrosine)
  5. Defence – antibodies (immunoglobulins); complement proteins
  6. Transport – haemoglobin (oxygen), transferrin (iron), lipoproteins (fats), albumin (drugs, bilirubin)
  7. Oncotic pressure and fluid balance – plasma albumin prevents oedema
  8. Blood clotting – fibrinogen, prothrombin
  9. Structural – collagen (bone, skin, tendons), keratin (hair, nails)
  10. Muscle contraction – actin and myosin
  11. Acid–base balance – proteins act as buffers
  12. Energy – 4 kcal/g when carbohydrate and fat are insufficient
  13. Precursors of neurotransmitters, niacin, melanin, creatine

D. Digestion (3 marks)

1. Mouth – no digestion of protein; only chewing

2. Stomach

  • Hydrochloric acid denatures proteins and converts pepsinogen to pepsin
  • Pepsin breaks proteins into proteoses, peptones and polypeptides
  • In infants, milk protein (casein) is curdled so that it stays longer in the stomach

3. Small intestine

  • Pancreatic juice:
    • trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by enterokinase
    • trypsin activates chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase
    • these break polypeptides into smaller peptides and some amino acids
  • Intestinal juice (brush border) – aminopeptidases and dipeptidases split peptides into amino acids

4. Absorption

  • Amino acids (and some di- and tripeptides) are absorbed by active transport in the small intestine → portal vein → liver
  • Used to make body proteins; excess is deaminated and its nitrogen excreted as urea

Summary of protein digestion

Site Enzyme Action
Stomach pepsin (with HCl) proteins → proteoses, peptones
Small intestine (pancreas) trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase polypeptides → peptides, amino acids
Small intestine (brush border) aminopeptidase, dipeptidase peptides → amino acids

E. Nursing relevance

  • Ensure adequate good-quality protein for children, pregnant and lactating women, surgical, burn and convalescent patients
  • Combine cereals and pulses in vegetarian diets
  • Restrict protein only when advised – e.g. in kidney failure or hepatic encephalopathy

F. Effects of deficiency and excess of protein

  • Deficiency:
    • children – poor growth, kwashiorkor and marasmus (protein-energy malnutrition)
    • adults – weight loss, muscle wasting, weakness, oedema (low albumin), anaemia
    • low immunity – repeated infections; delayed wound healing; pressure ulcers
    • fatty liver, hair and skin changes
  • Excess (usually from supplements or very high-meat diets):
    • extra load on the kidneys (more urea to excrete) – harmful in kidney disease
    • dehydration if fluid intake is low; possible loss of calcium in urine
    • excess calories are stored as fat
    • high red-meat diets are linked with heart disease and some cancers

G. Factors that impair protein digestion

  • Pancreatic disease (pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) – lack of trypsin and chymotrypsin
  • Achlorhydria and gastric surgery – less pepsin activity
  • Anti-nutrients in raw pulses and soybean (trypsin inhibitors) – destroyed by proper cooking
  • Diarrhoea and intestinal infections – food passes quickly, less absorption

Conclusion Proteins are nitrogenous compounds of amino acids, classified by composition, shape, nutritional quality and source; they build and repair tissues, form enzymes, hormones and antibodies and maintain fluid balance, and are digested by pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin and peptidases to amino acids for absorption.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the dietary sources of protein. Add a note on animal and plant sources.
answer_html:
Introduction Proteins are present in both animal and plant foods, but their quantity and quality differ. Most Indians depend on plant proteins, so the right combination of foods is important.

A. Animal sources (protein per 100 g, approximate)

  • Egg – about 13 g (one egg gives about 6 g) – the reference protein, highest biological value
  • Milk – 3.2–4.3 g per 100 ml; paneer about 18 g; cheese about 24 g; curd, buttermilk
  • Meat (mutton) – about 18–22 g; chicken about 25 g
  • Fish – about 15–20 g; dried fish much higher
  • Liver and organ meats – about 19–20 g

Features of animal proteins

  • Complete proteins – contain all essential amino acids
  • High biological value and digestibility
  • Also supply vitamin B₁₂, haem iron, zinc, calcium (milk)
  • More expensive; some (red meat, egg yolk) contain saturated fat and cholesterol

B. Plant sources (protein per 100 g, approximate)

  • Soybean – about 40–43 g (richest plant source)
  • Pulses and legumes – 20–25 g – Bengal gram (chana), red gram (tur), green gram (moong), black gram (urad), lentil (masoor), rajma, cowpea
  • Groundnut – about 25 g; other nuts and oilseeds (almond, cashew, sesame, flaxseed) – 18–25 g
  • Cereals – 6–12 g – wheat about 12 g, rice about 7 g; eaten in large amounts, so they supply much of the daily protein
  • Millets – bajra about 11 g, jowar about 10 g, ragi about 7 g
  • Green leafy vegetables – 2–5 g; mushrooms

Features of plant proteins

  • Mostly partially complete – cereals are low in lysine, pulses are low in methionine
  • Cheaper and widely available; also give fibre and no cholesterol
  • Contain anti-nutrients (phytates, trypsin inhibitors), reduced by soaking, sprouting and cooking

C. Comparison

Point Animal protein Plant protein
Quality complete, high biological value partially complete
Digestibility high (90–95%) lower (about 75–85%)
Cost high low
Other nutrients B₁₂, haem iron, zinc fibre, phytochemicals, no cholesterol

D. Improving protein intake – practical tips

  • Cereal + pulse combinations in a ratio of about 3:1 to 4:1 – dal-rice, khichdi, idli, roti-dal, rajma-chawal – give a protein as good as animal protein
  • Add milk, curd or an egg to meals where possible
  • Low-cost protein foods – pulses, groundnut, soybean, roasted chana, sprouts

Conclusion Animal foods such as egg, milk, meat and fish provide complete, high-quality protein, while soybean, pulses, nuts and cereals are cheaper plant sources whose quality is greatly improved when cereals and pulses are eaten together.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions of protein.
answer_html:
Functions

  1. Growth – builds new tissues in children, adolescents and in pregnancy
  2. Repair and maintenance – replaces worn-out cells; wound healing
  3. Enzymes – all enzymes are proteins (pepsin, amylase)
  4. Hormones – insulin, growth hormone
  5. Antibodies – defence against infection
  6. Transport – haemoglobin (oxygen), transferrin (iron), lipoproteins (fats)
  7. Fluid balance – albumin maintains oncotic pressure and prevents oedema
  8. Blood clotting – fibrinogen, prothrombin
  9. Structure – collagen (bone, skin), keratin (hair, nails); actin and myosin (muscle contraction)
  10. Acid–base balance – act as buffers
  11. Energy – 4 kcal/g when carbohydrates and fats are insufficient

Note: adequate carbohydrate and fat must be eaten so that protein is spared for these functions instead of being burnt for energy.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is nitrogen balance? Give examples of positive and negative nitrogen balance.
answer_html:
Definition Nitrogen balance is the difference between nitrogen intake (from dietary protein) and nitrogen output (in urine, faeces and sweat).

  • 1 g of nitrogen = 6.25 g of protein (protein contains 16% nitrogen)

Types

  1. Nitrogen equilibrium – intake = output – healthy adults
  2. Positive nitrogen balance – intake > output – protein is being retained to build tissues
    • growing children, adolescents
    • pregnancy and lactation
    • recovery from illness, surgery, malnutrition; body-building exercise
  3. Negative nitrogen balance – output > intake – body protein is being broken down
    • starvation, protein-energy malnutrition, lack of an essential amino acid
    • fever, infections, burns, trauma, major surgery
    • cancer, uncontrolled diabetes, prolonged immobilisation

Significance: used to assess protein needs and adequacy of nutritional support in seriously ill patients.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: How is the quality of protein measured? Name the indices.
answer_html:
Introduction Protein quality depends on its essential amino acid content and digestibility. Egg protein is used as the reference protein.

Indices of protein quality

  1. Biological value (BV) – percentage of absorbed nitrogen retained in the body
    • egg about 94–100, milk about 85–90, meat about 75, rice about 64–80, wheat about 55–65, pulses about 50–60
  2. Digestibility coefficient – percentage of eaten protein that is absorbed
  3. Net protein utilisation (NPU) – percentage of eaten protein retained = BV × digestibility ÷ 100
  4. Protein efficiency ratio (PER) – weight gain (g) per g of protein eaten by growing animals
  5. Amino acid (chemical) score – content of the limiting amino acid compared with the reference protein
  6. PDCAAS / DIAAS – newer scores corrected for digestibility

Use: comparing foods and planning diets of good protein quality.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the protein requirements for different groups and the factors affecting them.
answer_html:
Introduction Protein requirement is the amount of dietary protein needed to maintain nitrogen balance in adults and to allow growth, pregnancy and lactation. It is expressed as g/kg body weight/day or g/day.

A. Recommended dietary allowance (ICMR-NIN 2020, approximate)

Group Protein
Adult man (65 kg) 0.83 g/kg/day – about 54 g/day
Adult woman (55 kg) 0.83 g/kg/day – about 46 g/day
Pregnancy additional 9.5 g/day (2nd trimester) and 22 g/day (3rd trimester)
Lactation additional 17 g/day (0–6 months) and 13 g/day (7–12 months)
Infants and children higher per kg than adults for growth (above 1 g/kg in infants)
Adolescents high, due to the growth spurt
Elderly at least the adult level; about 1 g/kg is often advised to prevent muscle loss

B. Factors affecting protein requirement

  1. Age and growth – infants, children and adolescents need more per kg
  2. Body weight and lean body mass
  3. Physiological state – pregnancy and lactation
  4. Quality of dietary protein – more is needed when the diet is mainly plant protein of lower quality and digestibility
  5. Energy intake – if calories are insufficient, protein is burnt for energy; adequate energy spares protein
  6. Illness and stress – requirement rises in:
    • burns (1.5–2 g/kg or more), major surgery, trauma, fractures
    • fever, infections, tuberculosis, sepsis
    • wounds and pressure ulcers
    • recovery from malnutrition
  7. Physical activity – athletes and body-builders need slightly more
  8. Losses – proteinuria, protein-losing enteropathy, repeated paracentesis, dialysis

C. Conditions requiring protein restriction (as advised)

  • Chronic kidney disease (not on dialysis) – about 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day
  • Hepatic encephalopathy – temporary adjustment; long-term restriction is now avoided
  • Some inborn errors of amino acid metabolism (phenylketonuria)

D. Protein in the total diet

  • Proteins should provide about 10–15% of total energy
  • At least one-third of protein from pulses, milk, eggs or flesh foods for good quality

E. Nursing relevance

  • Encourage extra protein – milk, egg, dal, paneer, soya – for pregnant women, children, surgical and burn patients
  • Monitor weight, albumin and wound healing
  • Follow the dietitian's order for restricted-protein diets in kidney disease

Conclusion Healthy Indian adults need about 0.83 g of protein per kg per day (54 g for men and 46 g for women), with extra allowances for growth, pregnancy, lactation and illness; requirements depend on age, body size, protein quality, energy intake and stress.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain mutual supplementation of proteins and other methods of improving the quality of dietary protein.
answer_html:
Introduction Most Indian diets are based on cereals and pulses, whose proteins are of lower quality because each lacks some essential amino acid (limiting amino acid). Simple household methods can greatly improve protein quality at low cost.

A. Mutual (complementary) supplementation

  • Meaning: combining two or more foods so that the amino acid lacking in one is supplied by the other
  • Cereals are low in lysine but have enough methionine; pulses are rich in lysine but low in methionine
  • Eaten together, they give a complete protein with a quality close to animal protein
  • Best ratio – about 3–4 parts cereal to 1 part pulse
  • Examples: dal-rice, khichdi, roti with dal, idli and dosa (rice + urad dal), rajma-chawal, chole with roti, besan (chana) with wheat, sprouts with poha
  • Both foods should be eaten in the same meal

B. Supplementation with small amounts of animal protein

  • Adding milk, curd, egg or fish to cereal meals – kheer, curd rice, milk with porridge – improves quality markedly

C. Germination (sprouting)

  • Increases vitamin C and B-vitamins
  • Reduces anti-nutrients (phytates, trypsin inhibitors) and flatulence-causing sugars
  • Improves digestibility and availability of protein and iron
  • e.g. sprouted moong, chana, matki

D. Fermentation

  • Idli, dosa, dhokla, curd, khaman
  • Improves digestibility, increases B-vitamins, reduces phytates

E. Proper processing and cooking

  • Soaking and cooking destroy trypsin inhibitors in pulses and soybean
  • Avoid overheating and prolonged frying – reduces available lysine
  • Roasting (roasted chana) improves flavour and digestibility

F. Fortification and enrichment

  • High-protein food mixes made from cereals, pulses, groundnut and soybean are used in supplementary nutrition programmes (take-home rations)
  • Soy-fortified flour and protein-rich snacks

G. Improved varieties

  • Quality protein maize (higher lysine and tryptophan) and other bio-fortified crops

H. Adequate energy intake

  • When enough calories are eaten, protein is used for body-building rather than for energy (protein sparing)

I. Nursing and community relevance

  • Teach mothers to prepare low-cost, protein-rich complementary foods – khichdi with oil, dal-rice mash, sattu, sprouted flour
  • Encourage use of pulses, groundnut and soybean by vegetarian families
  • Promote traditional fermented foods in hospital and school diets

Conclusion Protein quality is improved by mutual supplementation of cereals and pulses, adding small amounts of milk or egg, germination, fermentation, proper cooking and fortification – simple, low-cost methods that are vital for vegetarian and poor families.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions and dietary sources of fat.
answer_html:
Functions

  1. Concentrated source of energy – 9 kcal per gram, more than twice that of carbohydrate or protein
  2. Carrier of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and helps their absorption
  3. Supplies essential fatty acids (linoleic and α-linolenic acids)
  4. Insulation – subcutaneous fat prevents heat loss
  5. Protection – cushions vital organs such as the kidneys and eyes
  6. Structure – part of cell membranes (phospholipids, cholesterol) and the myelin sheath
  7. Forms steroid hormones and prostaglandins
  8. Satiety and taste – slows stomach emptying and makes food tasty
  9. Spares protein for body-building

Sources

  • Visible fats – oils (groundnut, mustard, sunflower, rice bran, soybean, sesame, coconut), ghee, butter, vanaspati
  • Invisible fats – nuts and oilseeds, whole milk, cheese, egg yolk, meat, fish; small amounts in cereals and pulses

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated fats.
answer_html:
Point Saturated fats Unsaturated fats
Chemical structure fatty acids with no double bonds fatty acids with one (MUFA) or more (PUFA) double bonds
Physical state at room temperature usually solid usually liquid (oils)
Main sources animal fats – ghee, butter, cream, lard, red meat; also coconut and palm oil vegetable oils – groundnut, mustard, sunflower, safflower, soybean, rice bran, olive; fish oils, nuts
Effect on blood cholesterol raise LDL ("bad") cholesterol lower LDL; MUFA and ω-3 fats protect the heart
Heart disease risk increased when eaten in excess reduced
Stability stable – slow to become rancid easily oxidised – rancidity
Essential fatty acids none PUFA include essential fatty acids
Recommended less than 10% of total energy should form most of the fat in the diet

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What are visible and invisible fats?
answer_html:
Visible fats

  • Fats that are separated from their source and used as such in cooking or at the table
  • They can be seen and measured easily
  • Examples – cooking oils, ghee, butter, vanaspati, margarine
  • ICMR advises about 20–30 g of visible fat a day for most adults (up to about 40 g for heavy workers)

Invisible fats

  • Fats present naturally within foods, not seen separately
  • Examples – cereals and pulses (small amounts but eaten in large quantity), nuts and oilseeds, milk, cheese, egg yolk, meat, fish; also hidden fat in biscuits, bakery items, namkeen and fried snacks
  • They contribute a large share of total fat intake

Practical point: while limiting fat, remember hidden (invisible) fats in processed and fried foods, not just the oil used for cooking.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is rancidity of fats? How can it be prevented?
answer_html:
Definition Rancidity is the spoilage of fats and oils that produces an unpleasant smell and taste when they are exposed to air, light, heat, moisture or microbes.

Types

  1. Oxidative – oxygen attacks the double bonds of unsaturated fats → peroxides and aldehydes (commonest)
  2. Hydrolytic – moisture or enzymes (lipase) release free fatty acids (e.g. butter)
  3. Microbial (ketonic) – caused by moulds and bacteria

Effects: bad flavour, destruction of vitamins A and E and essential fatty acids, formation of harmful compounds, stomach upset.

Prevention

  • Store oils in airtight, opaque containers in a cool, dark place
  • Avoid moisture; buy in small quantities; do not mix old and new oil
  • Antioxidants – natural vitamin E; permitted additives (BHA, BHT)
  • Do not reuse frying oil repeatedly; refrigerate butter

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the fat requirements and the guidelines for healthy intake of fats and oils.
answer_html:
Introduction Fat is essential for energy, essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins, but excess or the wrong type of fat leads to obesity, heart disease and diabetes. Both the amount and the quality of fat matter.

A. Requirements

  1. Total fat – should provide about 20–30% of total energy (not more than 30%)
  2. Visible fat (ICMR) – about 20–30 g/day for sedentary and moderately active adults; up to about 40 g for heavy workers; about 30 g in pregnancy and lactation
  3. Saturated fat – less than 10% of total energy
  4. Trans fat – less than 1% of energy – practically avoid
  5. Essential fatty acids
    • linoleic acid (ω-6) – about 5–8% of energy
    • α-linolenic acid (ω-3) – about 0.5–1% of energy
    • ratio of ω-6 to ω-3 ideally 5–10 : 1 (most Indian diets have far more ω-6)
  6. Cholesterol – limit high-cholesterol foods (egg yolk, organ meats, ghee) especially in heart disease
  7. Special groups
    • Infants – fat supplies about half the energy in breast milk; fat must not be restricted in young children
    • Pregnancy and lactation – DHA (ω-3) for the baby's brain and eyes
    • Obese, diabetic and heart patients – lower fat, mainly unsaturated

B. Guidelines for healthy intake

  1. Use a combination or rotation of oils – e.g. groundnut, sesame or rice bran oil with mustard or soybean oil – to balance MUFA, ω-6 and ω-3
  2. Limit saturated fats – ghee, butter, cream, coconut and palm oil
  3. Avoid trans fats – vanaspati, partially hydrogenated fats, bakery items made with them; FSSAI limits trans fat to not more than 2% in oils and fats
  4. Do not reheat oil repeatedly – it forms trans fats and toxic compounds; discard dark, smoky or foamy oil
  5. Prefer low-fat cooking methods – boiling, steaming, pressure cooking, grilling, shallow frying instead of deep frying
  6. Limit fried snacks – samosa, pakoda, namkeen, chips, biscuits, fast foods
  7. Include ω-3 sources – flaxseed (alsi), walnuts, mustard and soybean oils, green leafy vegetables, fish twice a week
  8. Read food labels – check total fat, saturated fat, trans fat and "partially hydrogenated oil"
  9. Measure oil – use a spoon rather than pouring; about ½ litre of oil per person per month is a practical household guide
  10. Follow FSSAI's "Eat Right India" advice to cut salt, sugar and fat gradually

C. Effects of improper fat intake

  • Excess – obesity, high LDL cholesterol, atherosclerosis, heart attack, stroke, fatty liver, gallstones, some cancers
  • Deficiency – low energy intake, poor growth in children, deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids (rough, scaly skin – phrynoderma)

D. Nursing relevance

  • Advise families on choice and quantity of cooking oil
  • Teach patients with heart disease, diabetes and obesity to recognise hidden fats
  • Ensure adequate fat for children and underweight patients

Conclusion Fat should provide 20–30% of daily energy, with saturated fat below 10% and trans fat avoided; using a mix of oils, measuring oil, choosing low-fat cooking methods and including ω-3 sources keep fat intake healthy.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Describe the processing of edible fats and oils – extraction, refining, hydrogenation, blending and fortification. Add a note on smoke point and safe use of cooking oil. (6 + 4)
answer_html:
Introduction Edible oils come from oilseeds and fruits – groundnut, mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame, safflower, cottonseed, rice bran, coconut, palm and olive – and animal fats include ghee and butter. The way oils are processed, stored and used affects their nutritive value, safety and effect on health.

A. Processing of oils (6 marks)

1. Extraction

  • Mechanical pressing
    • ghani/kolhu (traditional, "kachi ghani" or cold-pressed) – little heat; keeps flavour, vitamin E and natural antioxidants
    • expellers (screw presses) – faster; some heat produced; oil is filtered and sold as "filtered oil"
  • Solvent extraction – the oil cake is treated with a solvent (hexane) to remove remaining oil; this crude oil must be refined
  • The oil cake (groundnut, soybean) is a protein-rich by-product used for cattle feed and, when hygienically processed, for protein-rich foods

2. Refining (of crude oil)

  • Degumming – removes gums and phospholipids (lecithin is a by-product)
  • Neutralisation – alkali removes free fatty acids
  • Bleaching – clay or charcoal removes colour pigments
  • Deodorisation – steam under vacuum removes odours and volatile substances
  • Winterisation – chilling removes waxes so that oil stays clear
  • Effects: longer shelf life, bland taste, higher smoke point; but loss of vitamin E, carotenoids, phytosterols and flavour; small amounts of trans fats may form

3. Hydrogenation

  • Hydrogen is added to unsaturated fatty acids in the presence of a nickel catalyst at high temperature and pressure
  • Liquid oils become semi-solid fats – vanaspati, margarine, bakery shortenings
  • Advantages to industry – stability, longer shelf life, ghee-like texture, low cost
  • Disadvantages – partial hydrogenation forms trans fatty acids, which raise LDL and lower HDL and increase heart disease; essential fatty acids are destroyed
  • FSSAI limits trans fat to not more than 2% in oils and fats; vanaspati must be fortified with vitamins A and D
  • Interesterification is now used as an alternative to reduce trans fats

4. Blending

  • Mixing two or more vegetable oils (e.g. rice bran + sunflower, groundnut + soybean)
  • Improves the balance of saturated, MUFA and PUFA and the ω-6 : ω-3 ratio, stability and cost
  • Blended ("multi-source") oils must declare their composition on the label as per FSSAI rules

5. Fortification

  • Edible oil and vanaspati fortified with vitamins A and D (FSSAI Fortification Regulations, 2018; "+F" logo)
  • Oil is a good vehicle because it is used daily by almost every family and the vitamins are fat-soluble

6. Packaging and labelling

  • Packed oils with label details (FSSAI licence, composition, nutrition information, batch, best-before date) reduce adulteration (e.g. argemone oil in loose mustard oil)
  • Opaque, airtight containers protect from light and air

7. Ghee and butter

  • Butter is made by churning cream; ghee is obtained by heating butter to remove water (almost pure milk fat)
  • AGMARK grading assures quality; adulteration with vanaspati or animal fat must be guarded against

B. Smoke point and safe use of cooking oil (4 marks)

1. Smoke point

  • The temperature at which an oil starts to smoke and break down, producing acrolein (an irritant) and free radicals
  • Refined oils and ghee have high smoke points – suitable for frying
  • Cold-pressed/unrefined oils and butter have lower smoke points – better for low-heat cooking, tempering or dressing

2. Safe use

  • Choose the oil for the cooking method – stable, high-smoke-point oils for deep frying
  • Do not overheat oil beyond its smoke point
  • Avoid reusing frying oil; if unavoidable, use it only a limited number of times for the same type of food, filter it and top up with fresh oil
  • Discard oil that is dark, thick, foamy, smoky or rancid-smelling
  • FSSAI limits total polar compounds in used cooking oil to 25% for food businesses; used oil can be sent for biodiesel (RUCO – Repurpose Used Cooking Oil)
  • Store oil in a cool, dark place, tightly closed; buy small packs
  • Measure oil – about 20–30 g per person per day (roughly ½ litre per person per month)
  • Use a combination or rotation of oils; limit vanaspati, palm oil and excess ghee

C. Nursing relevance

  • Educate families about choosing, storing and using oils, and dangers of reused oil and vanaspati
  • Advise heart, diabetic and obese patients on oil quantity and quality

Conclusion Edible oils are extracted by pressing or solvent extraction, refined, sometimes hydrogenated, blended and fortified; hydrogenation creates harmful trans fats, while correct choice of oil, avoiding overheating and reuse, proper storage and measured use keep cooking oils safe and healthy.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define vitamins. Classify them and write their functions.
answer_html:
Definition Vitamins are organic compounds required in very small amounts (milligrams or micrograms) for normal growth, metabolism and health. The body cannot make them (or not in enough quantity), so they must come from food. They do not give energy but help release energy from food.

A. Classification

1. Fat-soluble vitamins – A, D, E, K

  • Absorbed with fat; stored in liver and fat tissue
  • Not needed every day; deficiency develops slowly
  • Toxicity can occur with excess (A and D)
  • Fairly stable to ordinary cooking

2. Water-soluble vitamins – B-complex and vitamin C

  • B-complex: thiamine (B₁), riboflavin (B₂), niacin (B₃), pantothenic acid (B₅), pyridoxine (B₆), biotin (B₇), folic acid (B₉), cobalamin (B₁₂)
  • Not stored (except B₁₂) – needed daily; excess excreted in urine
  • Lost in cooking water, destroyed by heat and air (especially vitamin C and thiamine)
  • Toxicity is rare

B. Functions of individual vitamins

Vitamin Main functions Deficiency
A (retinol) vision in dim light, healthy skin and mucous membranes, growth, immunity night blindness, xerophthalmia
D (calciferol) calcium and phosphorus absorption, bone formation rickets, osteomalacia
E (tocopherol) antioxidant – protects cell membranes and red cells haemolysis in preterm babies
K formation of clotting factors (prothrombin) bleeding
B₁ (thiamine) carbohydrate metabolism, nerve function beriberi
B₂ (riboflavin) energy release (FAD, FMN); healthy skin, eyes angular stomatitis, glossitis
B₃ (niacin) energy release (NAD); skin, nerves, gut pellagra
B₆ (pyridoxine) amino acid metabolism; neurotransmitters; haemoglobin neuropathy, fits, anaemia
Folic acid DNA synthesis, red cell formation, fetal neural tube megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects
B₁₂ red cell maturation, nerve myelin megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy
C (ascorbic acid) collagen formation, wound healing, iron absorption, antioxidant, immunity scurvy

C. General functions of vitamins

  1. Act as coenzymes in metabolism (most B-vitamins)
  2. Help release energy from carbohydrates, fats and proteins
  3. Growth and development
  4. Immunity and resistance to infection (A, C, D)
  5. Blood formation (folic acid, B₁₂) and clotting (K)
  6. Antioxidant protection (A, C, E)
  7. Health of eyes, skin, nerves and bones

D. Nursing relevance

  • Encourage fresh fruits and vegetables daily; use correct cooking methods to save vitamins
  • Give supplements as prescribed – vitamin A prophylaxis, IFA, vitamin K at birth, vitamin D

Conclusion Vitamins are essential organic micronutrients, classified as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B-complex and C); they act mainly as coenzymes and are needed for vision, bones, blood, nerves, immunity and energy release.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Name the fat-soluble vitamins with their chief functions and sources.
answer_html:
Fat-soluble vitamins – A, D, E and K

Vitamin Chief functions Main sources
A (retinol; β-carotene from plants) vision in dim light, healthy skin and eyes, immunity, growth liver, fish liver oil, egg yolk, milk, ghee; green leafy vegetables, carrot, papaya, mango
D (cholecalciferol) absorption of calcium and phosphate, healthy bones and teeth sunlight on skin, fish liver oil, egg yolk, fortified milk and oil
E (tocopherol) antioxidant; protects cell membranes vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, whole grains
K (phylloquinone) blood clotting – prothrombin and factors VII, IX, X green leafy vegetables, cabbage; made by gut bacteria

Common features: absorbed with fat (need bile), stored in the body, excess can be toxic (A, D); deficiency occurs in fat malabsorption and obstructive jaundice.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on vitamin A.
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin. Its active forms are retinol, retinal and retinoic acid. Plants contain β-carotene (provitamin A), which is converted to vitamin A in the intestine and liver. It is often called the "anti-infective vitamin".

A. Sources

  • Animal (preformed vitamin A) – liver (richest), fish liver oils (cod liver oil), egg yolk, milk, butter, ghee, cheese
  • Plant (β-carotene)
    • green leafy vegetables – spinach, amaranth, drumstick leaves, fenugreek, coriander
    • yellow-orange vegetables and fruits – carrot, pumpkin, sweet potato, mango, papaya
    • red palm oil

B. Functions

  1. Vision – retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin (visual purple) in the rods, needed for vision in dim light
  2. Healthy epithelium – maintains the skin and the lining of the eyes (cornea, conjunctiva), respiratory, digestive and urinary tracts
  3. Immunity – keeps mucous membranes intact and supports immune cells; reduces severity of measles, diarrhoea and respiratory infections and child deaths
  4. Growth – normal development of bones and teeth
  5. Reproduction – sperm formation and fetal development
  6. Antioxidant – β-carotene protects against free radicals
  7. Gene expression and cell differentiation (retinoic acid)

C. Requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020, approximate)

  • Adults about 1,000 µg/day (men) and 840 µg/day (women); more in pregnancy and lactation
  • Children need less in absolute amounts, but are most at risk of deficiency

D. Absorption and storage

  • Needs fat and bile for absorption; stored in the liver (several months' supply)
  • Zinc and protein are needed for its transport (retinol-binding protein)

E. Deficiency (in brief)

  • Night blindness (earliest symptom), xerophthalmia – conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis, keratomalacia (can cause blindness)
  • Dry, rough skin (follicular hyperkeratosis); frequent infections; poor growth
  • Prevention – vitamin A-rich foods; biannual vitamin A prophylaxis for children 9 months–5 years

F. Toxicity – excess preformed vitamin A from supplements causes hypervitaminosis A; β-carotene does not

G. Nursing points

  • Encourage green leafy and yellow-orange vegetables – cheap, local sources
  • Give vitamin A solution with the marked spoon at the correct dose; record in the immunisation card
  • Add a little oil while cooking vegetables to improve carotene absorption

Conclusion Vitamin A, from liver, milk, eggs and β-carotene-rich vegetables and fruits, is essential for dim-light vision, healthy epithelium, immunity and growth; its deficiency causes night blindness and preventable childhood blindness.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is hypervitaminosis A?
answer_html:
Definition Hypervitaminosis A is the toxicity caused by excessive intake of preformed vitamin A (retinol), usually from high-dose supplements, or rarely from eating large amounts of liver (e.g. polar bear or fish liver).

Types and features

  1. Acute (one very large dose)
    • nausea, vomiting, severe headache, drowsiness, dizziness
    • bulging fontanelle in infants (raised intracranial pressure)
    • peeling of skin after a few days
  2. Chronic (high doses for weeks or months)
    • loss of appetite, weight loss, bone and joint pain
    • dry, itchy skin, hair loss, cracked lips
    • liver enlargement and damage; raised intracranial pressure
  3. In pregnancy – high doses are teratogenic (birth defects); so high-dose vitamin A is not given to pregnant women

Note: β-carotene from plant foods does not cause toxicity – only harmless yellowing of skin (carotenaemia).

Treatment: stop vitamin A; symptoms usually subside.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on vitamin D.
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin and also acts as a hormone. It is called the "sunshine vitamin" because the skin makes it when exposed to sunlight.

A. Forms

  • Vitamin D₂ (ergocalciferol) – from plants and fungi (mushrooms)
  • Vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) – formed in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol by ultraviolet-B rays; also in animal foods

B. Activation

  1. Liver → 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) – the form measured in blood to assess vitamin D status
  2. Kidney → 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) – the active hormone; stimulated by parathyroid hormone - So liver and kidney disease cause vitamin D deficiency

C. Sources

  • Sunlight – the main source; exposure of face, arms and legs for about 15–30 minutes around midday, a few times a week
  • Foods (few): fish liver oils (cod liver oil), fatty fish, egg yolk, liver, butter
  • Fortified foods – milk and edible oil fortified with vitamins A and D (+F logo)

D. Functions

  1. Increases absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the intestine
  2. Mineralisation of bones and teeth
  3. Maintains blood calcium levels (with parathyroid hormone) – needed for nerves, muscles and clotting
  4. Increases reabsorption of calcium in the kidneys
  5. Muscle strength; prevents falls in the elderly
  6. Supports immunity and normal cell growth

E. Requirement

  • Adults – about 600 IU (15 µg) per day (ICMR-NIN 2020), as sunlight exposure is often inadequate
  • Infants – 400 IU/day supplement is commonly advised for breastfed babies

F. Deficiency

  • Rickets in children – soft, deformed bones (bow legs, knock knees)
  • Osteomalacia in adults – bone pain, muscle weakness
  • Osteoporosis and fractures in the elderly; hypocalcaemic tetany
  • Very common in India because of indoor living, clothing, air pollution, dark skin and low intake
  • Blood 25(OH)D below 20 ng/ml indicates deficiency

G. Toxicity

  • From excess supplements – hypercalcaemia: nausea, vomiting, thirst, polyuria, kidney stones, calcification of soft tissues

H. Nursing points

  • Encourage outdoor play and sunlight exposure
  • Give supplements only as prescribed; teach correct dose (avoid repeated mega-doses)
  • Watch for vitamin D deficiency in elderly, bedridden, pregnant and dark-skinned persons and those with kidney or liver disease

Conclusion Vitamin D is formed in the skin by sunlight and activated in the liver and kidney; it controls calcium and phosphorus absorption and bone mineralisation, and its deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions and sources of vitamin K. Why is it given to newborns?
answer_html:
Forms: K₁ (phylloquinone) – plants; K₂ (menaquinone) – made by intestinal bacteria; K₃ – synthetic.

Functions

  • Needed by the liver to make clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X
  • Helps bone formation (osteocalcin)

Sources: green leafy vegetables (spinach, cabbage, fenugreek), cauliflower, soybean oil, liver, eggs; gut bacteria.

Why it is given to newborns

  • Newborns have low vitamin K – little crosses the placenta, breast milk contains little and the gut has no bacteria at birth
  • Risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn)
  • Therefore all newborns receive vitamin K₁ 1 mg IM at birth (0.5 mg for preterm/very low-birth-weight babies)

Other causes of deficiency: obstructive jaundice, fat malabsorption, long-term antibiotics; warfarin acts against vitamin K (vitamin K is its antidote).

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions and sources of vitamin E.
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a fat-soluble vitamin and the body's main fat-soluble antioxidant.

Functions

  1. Antioxidant – protects cell membranes (rich in PUFA) and red blood cells from damage by free radicals
  2. Protects vitamin A and essential fatty acids from oxidation
  3. Supports immunity and nerve function
  4. Helps maintain healthy skin and muscles

Sources

  • Vegetable oils – sunflower, safflower, wheat germ oil, rice bran oil
  • Nuts and seeds – almonds, sunflower seeds, groundnuts
  • Green leafy vegetables, whole grains, eggs

Requirement: about 8–10 mg/day for adults; needs rise with more PUFA intake.

Deficiency (rare)

  • Haemolytic anaemia in preterm babies
  • Nerve damage – ataxia, muscle weakness – in long-standing fat malabsorption

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the B-complex vitamins – their functions, sources and requirements.
answer_html:
Introduction The B-complex is a group of water-soluble vitamins that mainly act as coenzymes in energy metabolism. They are not stored (except B₁₂), are lost in cooking water and are reduced by milling and polishing of grains.

A. Individual B-vitamins

Vitamin (coenzyme) Functions Sources Adult requirement (approx.)
B₁ – thiamine (TPP) carbohydrate metabolism; nerve and heart function; appetite whole grains, unpolished or parboiled rice, wheat, pulses, groundnut, yeast, pork, eggs 1.2–1.4 mg/day
B₂ – riboflavin (FAD, FMN) oxidation–reduction reactions; healthy skin, eyes, lips and tongue milk and milk products, eggs, liver, green leafy vegetables, sprouted pulses 1.6–2.0 mg/day
B₃ – niacin (NAD, NADP) energy release; health of skin, nerves and gut groundnut, meat, fish, liver, whole grains, pulses; also made from tryptophan 12–16 mg/day
B₅ – pantothenic acid (coenzyme A) metabolism of fats, carbohydrates and proteins widely present in foods ("pantos" = everywhere) about 5 mg/day
