B₆ – pyridoxine (pyridoxal phosphate) amino acid metabolism; forms neurotransmitters (serotonin, GABA) and haem whole grains, pulses, nuts, meat, fish, banana about 2 mg/day
B₇ – biotin carboxylation reactions – fat and glucose metabolism egg yolk, liver, nuts; made by gut bacteria 30–40 µg/day

B. Folic acid (B₉) and B₁₂ – needed for DNA synthesis and red cell formation (dealt with separately)

C. Special points

  • Thiamine is lost when rice is polished and washed repeatedly and when cooking water is thrown away; parboiling preserves it; requirement rises with carbohydrate intake (about 0.5 mg per 1,000 kcal)
  • Riboflavin is destroyed by sunlight – milk should not be kept in sunlight
  • Niacin – diets based mainly on maize or jowar predispose to pellagra (bound niacin, low tryptophan or excess leucine)
  • Pyridoxine – patients on isoniazid (anti-TB) are given pyridoxine to prevent neuropathy
  • Biotin – large amounts of raw egg white (avidin) bind biotin

D. General functions of the B-complex

  1. Release of energy from food (coenzymes of the TCA cycle and other pathways)
  2. Health of nervous system, skin, mucous membranes and digestive tract
  3. Formation of blood (B₆, folate, B₁₂)
  4. Appetite and growth

E. Deficiency (in brief) – beriberi (B₁), angular stomatitis and glossitis (B₂), pellagra (B₃), neuropathy and fits (B₆); mixed B deficiency is common in alcoholics and poor diets

F. Nursing points

  • Promote whole grains, unpolished/parboiled rice, pulses, milk and sprouts
  • Do not discard rice water (kanji) or vegetable cooking water; avoid baking soda
  • Give B-complex supplements to alcoholics, TB patients on isoniazid, pregnant women and the malnourished as prescribed

Conclusion B-complex vitamins – thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine and biotin – act as coenzymes for energy release and are needed for healthy nerves, skin and blood; whole grains, pulses, milk and correct cooking methods ensure adequate intake.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the importance of folic acid in pregnancy. Give its sources.
answer_html:
Introduction Folic acid (folate, vitamin B₉) is needed for DNA synthesis and cell division and for the formation of red blood cells.

Importance in pregnancy

  1. Prevents neural tube defects – spina bifida, anencephaly – when taken before conception and in early pregnancy (the neural tube closes by about 28 days after conception)
  2. Supports rapid growth of the fetus and placenta
  3. Prevents megaloblastic anaemia of pregnancy
  4. Reduces risk of low birth weight and preterm birth

Dose and programme

  • 400 µg (0.4 mg) daily from before conception till 12 weeks of pregnancy
  • Then IFA tablets (60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid) daily from the second trimester under Anaemia Mukt Bharat
  • Higher dose (5 mg) when a previous baby had a neural tube defect or the mother is on anti-epileptic drugs

Sources: green leafy vegetables (spinach, methi), pulses, liver, eggs, citrus fruits, groundnuts; easily destroyed by prolonged cooking.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on vitamin B₁₂.
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) contains cobalt. It is absorbed in the terminal ileum only with intrinsic factor from the stomach, and is stored in the liver (2–5 years' supply).

Functions

  • DNA synthesis and maturation of red blood cells
  • Formation and maintenance of the myelin sheath of nerves
  • Works with folic acid; needed for metabolism of fats and amino acids

Sources – only animal foods: liver (richest), meat, fish, eggs, milk and curd

Requirement: about 2.2–2.5 µg/day for adults

People at risk of deficiency

  • Strict vegetarians and vegans, elderly
  • Pernicious anaemia (no intrinsic factor), gastrectomy, ileal disease or resection
  • Long-term metformin or antacid use

Deficiency: megaloblastic anaemia, glossitis, tingling and numbness, memory loss, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord; treated with B₁₂ injections.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on vitamin C.
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble vitamin and the most easily destroyed of all vitamins. Humans cannot make it, so it must come daily from fresh foods.

A. Sources

  • Amla (Indian gooseberry) – the richest (about 600 mg per 100 g)
  • Guava (about 200 mg/100 g), citrus fruits – orange, lemon, mosambi
  • Drumstick leaves, green leafy vegetables, cabbage, capsicum, tomato
  • Sprouted pulses – sprouting increases vitamin C
  • Papaya, mango, pineapple, cashew fruit
  • Animal foods contain very little; fresh milk has small amounts

B. Functions

  1. Collagen formation – needed for healthy gums, skin, blood vessels, bones and wound healing
  2. Increases absorption of iron from plant foods (converts ferric to ferrous iron)
  3. Antioxidant – protects cells; regenerates vitamin E
  4. Immunity – supports white cells; helps fight infections
  5. Formation of adrenaline and noradrenaline, carnitine and steroid hormones
  6. Converts folic acid to its active form
  7. Helps healing of fractures and burns

C. Requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020, approximate)

  • Adults about 80 mg/day (men) and 65 mg/day (women)
  • More in pregnancy, lactation, infections, burns, surgery, wound healing and for smokers

D. Stability and preservation

  • Destroyed by heat, air (oxidation), light, alkali (baking soda) and copper vessels; dissolves in cooking water
  • Ways to preserve it:
    • eat raw fruits and salads
    • cut vegetables just before cooking, in large pieces
    • cook covered, for a short time, in little water; use the water
    • do not add soda; add lemon juice after cooking
    • avoid reheating and keeping cooked food for long

E. Deficiency

  • Scurvy – bleeding, spongy gums, skin bleeds, poor wound healing, bone pain
  • Mild deficiency – tiredness, frequent infections, iron-deficiency anaemia

F. Excess

  • Very large doses (more than about 2 g/day) can cause diarrhoea and kidney stones (oxalate)

G. Nursing points

  • Encourage a seasonal fruit or amla daily; advise lemon or amla with iron-rich meals
  • Give extra vitamin C-rich foods to surgical, burn and pressure-ulcer patients
  • Teach correct cooking practices

Conclusion Vitamin C, richest in amla, guava and citrus fruits, is essential for collagen formation, wound healing, iron absorption and immunity; because it is easily destroyed by heat, air and alkali, fresh foods and careful cooking are needed.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What are antioxidant vitamins? Name them with sources.
answer_html:
Introduction Free radicals are unstable molecules formed during metabolism and by smoking, pollution and radiation. They damage cells and are linked to ageing, heart disease, cancer and cataract. Antioxidants neutralise free radicals.

Antioxidant vitamins ("ACE")

  1. β-carotene / vitamin A – carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango, green leafy vegetables
  2. Vitamin C – amla, guava, citrus fruits, tomato, capsicum
  3. Vitamin E – vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, wheat germ

Antioxidant minerals – selenium, zinc, copper, manganese (parts of antioxidant enzymes)

Other antioxidants – polyphenols in tea, turmeric (curcumin), lycopene (tomato)

Advice: get antioxidants from colourful fruits and vegetables; high-dose supplements are not proven to help and may harm (β-carotene supplements increased lung cancer in smokers).

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain vitamin supplementation – indications, toxicity of excess vitamins and drug–vitamin interactions. Add the nurse's responsibilities. (3 + 3 + 2 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamins are best obtained from a varied diet, but supplements are needed in certain physiological states, diseases and drug treatments. At the same time, excess intake – especially self-medication with high-dose tablets and injections – can be harmful. ICMR-NIN (2020) has therefore given Tolerable Upper Limits (TUL) along with RDAs.

A. Indications for supplementation (3 marks)

1. Physiological states

  • Pre-conception and early pregnancy – folic acid 400 µg daily (prevents neural tube defects)
  • Pregnancy and lactation – IFA (iron + folic acid), calcium, vitamin D as advised
  • Newborns – vitamin K₁ injection at birth; vitamin D 400 IU/day for breastfed infants
  • Preterm and low-birth-weight babies – vitamin D, iron, multivitamins
  • Children 9 months–5 years – vitamin A prophylaxis
  • Elderly – vitamin D, vitamin B₁₂

2. Dietary causes

  • Strict vegetarians and vegans – vitamin B₁₂
  • Chronic alcoholics – thiamine, folate
  • Very restricted diets, food insecurity, severe malnutrition

3. Diseases

  • Malabsorption – coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, obstructive jaundice, pancreatic disease, after bariatric surgery – fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and B₁₂
  • Pernicious anaemia – lifelong B₁₂ injections
  • Chronic kidney disease – active vitamin D (calcitriol); water-soluble vitamins in dialysis
  • Measles and severe acute malnutrition – vitamin A
  • Burns, wounds, pressure ulcers – vitamin C, zinc
  • Long-term parenteral nutrition, chronic diarrhoea

B. Toxicity of excess vitamins (3 marks)

Vitamin Effects of excess
A headache, vomiting, raised intracranial pressure, liver damage, bone pain; birth defects in pregnancy
D hypercalcaemia – nausea, thirst, polyuria, kidney stones, calcification of soft tissues, arrhythmia (often from repeated high-dose sachets/injections)
E bleeding tendency (opposes vitamin K), especially with anticoagulants
K reduces the effect of warfarin; synthetic menadione can cause haemolysis and jaundice in newborns
Niacin (large doses) flushing, itching, liver damage, raised blood sugar and uric acid
B₆ (long-term high doses) sensory neuropathy – numbness, unsteady gait
C (more than about 2 g/day) diarrhoea, kidney stones (oxalate); iron overload in susceptible persons
Folic acid (high doses) masks B₁₂ deficiency – anaemia improves but nerve damage progresses
β-carotene harmless yellow skin; supplements increased lung cancer in smokers

Tolerable upper limits – the highest daily intake unlikely to cause harm; examples of international adult values: vitamin A 3,000 µg (preformed), vitamin D 100 µg (4,000 IU), vitamin E 1,000 mg, vitamin C 2,000 mg, vitamin B₆ 100 mg, folic acid 1,000 µg (from supplements)

C. Drug–vitamin interactions (2 marks)

Drug Interaction
Isoniazid (anti-TB) B₆ deficiency → neuropathy; give pyridoxine
Warfarin effect reduced by vitamin K – keep green-leafy-vegetable intake consistent; increased by high-dose vitamin E
Phenytoin, phenobarbitone lower folate and vitamin D
Methotrexate folate antagonist – folinic acid rescue
Metformin, proton pump inhibitors B₁₂ deficiency with long-term use
Broad-spectrum antibiotics vitamin K deficiency (gut bacteria reduced)
Orlistat, liquid paraffin, cholestyramine reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
Levodopa high-dose B₆ reduces its effect (when given without carbidopa)
Alcohol thiamine, folate and B₆ deficiency

D. Nurse's responsibilities (2 marks)

  1. Assess diet, risk factors and drug history before supplements are started
  2. Give supplements only as prescribed – correct dose, route and timing (e.g. vitamin K IM at birth, B₁₂ IM, vitamin A with the marked spoon)
  3. Discourage self-medication and repeated mega-doses (especially vitamin D)
  4. Teach correct intake – fat-soluble vitamins with meals; IFA after food
  5. Watch for toxicity – vomiting, headache, thirst, numbness, bleeding
  6. Check interactions with the patient's medicines; inform the doctor
  7. Store supplements away from light and children; check expiry dates
  8. Promote a "food first" approach – vitamin-rich foods are safer and cheaper
  9. Document doses in charts and MCP cards

E. Special precautions

  • Children – keep vitamin and iron tablets out of reach; accidental overdose of iron-containing tablets can be fatal
  • Pregnancy – avoid high-dose vitamin A and retinoid drugs (isotretinoin)
  • Injections – vitamin injections (e.g. B-complex, vitamin D) are often overused; oral routes are safer when the gut works
  • "Natural" or herbal supplements may also contain high doses or contaminants – ask patients about all products they take

Conclusion Vitamin supplements are needed in pregnancy, infancy, old age, special diets, malabsorption and with certain drugs, but excess intake causes toxicity, especially of vitamins A and D; the nurse ensures correct use, watches for interactions and toxicity and encourages a food-based approach.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Classify minerals and write their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction Minerals are inorganic elements needed by the body in small amounts for structure and regulation of body processes. They form about 4% of body weight, are obtained from food and water, are not destroyed by cooking but may be lost in cooking water.

A. Classification

1. Macro (major) minerals – required more than 100 mg/day

  • Calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride, sulphur

2. Micro (trace) minerals – required less than 100 mg/day

  • Iron, zinc, iodine, copper, fluoride, selenium, manganese, chromium, cobalt, molybdenum

3. Ultra-trace / possibly essential – nickel, silicon, boron, vanadium

4. Toxic minerals (no known function) – lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium

B. General functions

  1. Structural – bones and teeth (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, fluoride)
  2. Fluid and electrolyte balance and osmotic pressure (sodium, potassium, chloride)
  3. Acid–base balance (phosphate, bicarbonate)
  4. Nerve conduction and muscle contraction, including heart rhythm (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium)
  5. Blood clotting (calcium)
  6. Oxygen transport (iron in haemoglobin)
  7. Enzyme cofactors (zinc, magnesium, copper, manganese, selenium)
  8. Hormone formation and action (iodine – thyroxine; zinc – insulin; chromium – glucose tolerance)
  9. Immunity (zinc, selenium, iron)
  10. Part of vitamins (cobalt in vitamin B₁₂)

C. Important minerals at a glance

Mineral Main functions Sources Deficiency
Calcium bones, teeth, clotting, muscles, nerves milk, curd, ragi, green leafy vegetables, sesame rickets, osteomalacia, osteoporosis, tetany
Phosphorus bones, ATP (energy), DNA, buffers milk, meat, pulses, cereals rare – weakness, bone pain
Magnesium enzymes, nerves and muscles, bones whole grains, nuts, pulses, green vegetables cramps, tremors, arrhythmia
Sodium fluid balance, BP, nerves salt, processed foods hyponatraemia
Potassium heart rhythm, muscle, intracellular fluid fruits, vegetables, coconut water weakness, arrhythmia
Iron haemoglobin, oxygen transport green leafy vegetables, millets, meat, jaggery anaemia
Iodine thyroid hormones iodised salt, seafood goitre, cretinism
Zinc growth, immunity, wound healing meat, seafood, pulses, nuts stunting, poor healing, diarrhoea
Fluoride hard tooth enamel drinking water, tea dental caries (excess – fluorosis)

D. Nursing relevance

  • Watch electrolytes in vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics and kidney disease
  • Promote iodised salt, iron-rich and calcium-rich foods
  • Give IFA, calcium and zinc supplements as per national guidelines

Conclusion Minerals are inorganic nutrients classified as macro minerals (calcium, phosphorus, sodium, potassium, magnesium, chloride, sulphur) and trace elements (iron, iodine, zinc, fluoride and others); they build bones, maintain fluid balance and nerve-muscle function, carry oxygen and activate enzymes.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions of calcium.
answer_html:
Introduction Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body (about 1–1.2 kg); 99% is in bones and teeth. Normal serum calcium is 8.5–10.5 mg/dl.

Functions

  1. Formation of bones and teeth (as hydroxyapatite) and their strength
  2. Blood clotting (clotting factor IV)
  3. Muscle contraction, including heart muscle – normal heart rhythm
  4. Transmission of nerve impulses; low calcium causes tetany
  5. Regulates cell membrane permeability
  6. Activates enzymes (lipase, ATPase)
  7. Acts as a second messenger for hormones; helps hormone secretion
  8. Needed for milk secretion during lactation

Sources: milk and milk products, ragi, green leafy vegetables, sesame seeds, small fish eaten with bones.

Requirement: 1,000 mg/day for adults (ICMR-NIN 2020); in pregnancy and lactation calcium tablets (500 mg twice daily) are given in addition, as per national guidelines.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on iron – sources, functions, absorption and requirements.
answer_html:
Introduction Iron is a trace element essential for oxygen transport. The body contains about 3–4 g of iron – about two-thirds in haemoglobin, about one-quarter in storage (ferritin, haemosiderin), and the rest in myoglobin and enzymes.

A. Functions

  1. Haemoglobin – carries oxygen from lungs to tissues
  2. Myoglobin – stores oxygen in muscles
  3. Cytochromes – energy production in mitochondria
  4. Enzymes – catalase, peroxidase
  5. Brain development, learning and behaviour
  6. Immunity and work capacity; temperature regulation

B. Sources

  1. Haem iron (well absorbed – 15–35%) – liver, red meat, fish, poultry
  2. Non-haem iron (poorly absorbed – 2–20%)
    • green leafy vegetables – amaranth, drumstick leaves, fenugreek, mint
    • garden cress seeds (halim) – very rich
    • millets – bajra, ragi; poha (flattened rice)
    • pulses, soybean; jaggery; dried fruits – dates, raisins
    • cooking in iron vessels adds iron

C. Absorption

  • Mainly in the duodenum and upper jejunum, in the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form
  • Only about 10% of dietary iron is absorbed; absorption increases in deficiency and pregnancy
  • Factors increasing absorption:
    • vitamin C (amla, guava, lemon, orange)
    • animal protein (meat, fish)
    • gastric acid; ferrous form
    • germination and fermentation of grains and pulses
  • Factors decreasing absorption:
    • tea and coffee (tannins) taken with meals
    • phytates (bran, whole grains) and oxalates (spinach)
    • calcium tablets and milk taken with iron
    • antacids, achlorhydria, gastrectomy
    • worm infestation, diarrhoea, malabsorption

D. Transport, storage and loss

  • Carried in blood by transferrin; stored as ferritin and haemosiderin in liver, spleen and bone marrow
  • Iron from old red cells is recycled
  • Lost mainly through menstruation, bleeding, hookworm infestation; men lose about 1 mg/day

E. Requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020)

  • Men – 19 mg/day; women – 29 mg/day
  • Pregnancy – 27 mg/day (plus IFA tablets); lactation – 23 mg/day
  • Higher needs in adolescent girls, pregnancy and after blood loss

F. Deficiency – iron-deficiency anaemia (pallor, fatigue, breathlessness, poor school performance, low work output)

G. Nursing points

  • Advise iron-rich foods with vitamin C; avoid tea or coffee for an hour before and after meals
  • Teach correct intake of IFA tablets (after meals, with lemon water; expect black stools)
  • Deworming and use of footwear to prevent hookworm

Conclusion Iron is essential for haemoglobin, myoglobin and energy production; haem iron from meat is better absorbed than non-haem iron from plants, and absorption is improved by vitamin C and reduced by tea, phytates and calcium.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write a note on iodine – functions, sources and requirements.
answer_html:
Introduction Iodine is a trace element essential for making thyroid hormones. The body contains about 15–20 mg, of which 70–80% is in the thyroid gland. Iodine content of foods depends on the iodine in the soil; soils of hilly and flood-prone areas are poor in iodine.

A. Functions

  1. Formation of thyroxine (T₄) and tri-iodothyronine (T₃)
  2. Through thyroid hormones it regulates:
    • basal metabolic rate and body temperature
    • growth and development
    • brain development of the fetus and infant – the most critical role
    • protein synthesis and metabolism of carbohydrates and fats

B. Sources

  • Iodised salt – the main and cheapest source
  • Seafood – sea fish, prawns, seaweed
  • Milk, eggs; vegetables and cereals grown in iodine-rich soil
  • Double-fortified salt (iodine + iron)

C. Requirement

Group Iodine per day
Adults 150 µg
Pregnancy 220–250 µg
Lactation about 250–290 µg
Infants and young children 90 µg

D. Iodised salt

  • Iodine content: 30 ppm at manufacture and at least 15 ppm at the consumer level
  • Sale of non-iodised salt for human consumption is banned in India
  • Storage: airtight, covered container, away from moisture, heat and sunlight; do not buy loose salt kept in the open
  • Add salt towards the end of cooking

E. Goitrogens

  • Substances that interfere with iodine uptake by the thyroid – found in cabbage, cauliflower, turnip, mustard, soybean and tapioca (cassava)
  • Important only when iodine intake is already low; cooking reduces their effect

F. Deficiency – iodine deficiency disorders (in brief)

  • Goitre, hypothyroidism, cretinism, mental retardation, deaf-mutism, stillbirths and abortions, low IQ in children

G. Excess – very high intakes can cause thyroid dysfunction (rare)

H. Nursing points

  • Promote use of iodised salt in every household; teach proper storage
  • Use salt testing kits in the community
  • Ensure adequate iodine in pregnancy and lactation

I. Assessment of iodine status

  • Urinary iodine excretion – the best indicator of recent iodine intake in a community (median of 100–199 µg/L in school children is adequate)
  • Goitre prevalence in school children (palpation, ultrasound)
  • Neonatal TSH levels
  • Salt iodine testing at household level with spot test kits

Conclusion Iodine is essential for thyroid hormones that regulate metabolism and brain development; adults need 150 µg per day and pregnant women more, and universal use of properly stored iodised salt is the key to preventing iodine deficiency disorders.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions of sodium and the recommended salt intake.
answer_html:
Introduction Sodium is the main cation of extracellular fluid. Normal serum sodium is 135–145 mEq/L.

Functions

  1. Maintains fluid balance and osmotic pressure of ECF
  2. Regulates blood pressure and blood volume
  3. Nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction
  4. Acid–base balance (as sodium bicarbonate)
  5. Helps absorption of glucose and amino acids in the intestine

Sources: common salt (about 40% sodium), pickles, papad, chutneys, sauces, chips, namkeen, processed and bakery foods, baking soda.

Recommended intake: less than 5 g of salt a day (less than 2 g sodium) – WHO and ICMR.

Imbalances

  • Excess – hypertension, stroke, kidney disease, fluid retention, stomach cancer
  • Deficiency (hyponatraemia) – in vomiting, diarrhoea, heavy sweating, diuretics – weakness, cramps, confusion

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions and sources of potassium.
answer_html:
Introduction Potassium is the main cation inside cells. Normal serum potassium is 3.5–5.0 mEq/L.

Functions

  1. Nerve conduction and muscle contraction, especially the heart rhythm
  2. Maintains intracellular fluid volume and osmotic pressure
  3. Acid–base balance
  4. Lowers blood pressure – counteracts sodium
  5. Needed for glycogen and protein synthesis

Sources: fruits – banana, orange, coconut water, dried fruits; vegetables – potato, tomato, green leafy vegetables; pulses, nuts, milk.

Requirement: about 3,500 mg/day for adults.

Imbalances

  • Hypokalaemia – vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics – muscle weakness, cramps, arrhythmia, paralytic ileus
  • Hyperkalaemia – kidney failure – dangerous arrhythmias and cardiac arrest; renal patients restrict high-potassium foods and leach vegetables (soak in water, discard water)

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the functions of zinc. Add a note on zinc in diarrhoea.
answer_html:
Functions

  1. Cofactor of more than 300 enzymes
  2. Growth and development; protein and DNA synthesis
  3. Immunity – resistance to infections
  4. Wound healing and healthy skin
  5. Taste and smell; appetite
  6. Storage of insulin; sexual maturation and sperm formation

Sources: meat, seafood, eggs, milk, whole grains, pulses, nuts and seeds.

Requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020): about 17 mg/day (men) and 13 mg/day (women).

Deficiency: stunting, delayed puberty, loss of appetite and taste, poor wound healing, diarrhoea, dermatitis, frequent infections.

Zinc in diarrhoea

  • Given to all children with diarrhoea along with ORS
  • 2–6 months – 10 mg/day; 6 months–5 years – 20 mg/day, for 14 days
  • Reduces duration and severity and prevents recurrence for 2–3 months

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is the role of fluoride in health? Add a note on fluorosis.
answer_html:
Role of fluoride

  • Forms fluorapatite in tooth enamel, making teeth resistant to dental caries
  • Helps bone strength
  • Sources – drinking water (main), tea, seafood, fluoridated toothpaste
  • Safe level in drinking water about 0.5–1.0 mg/L; below 0.5 mg/L → dental caries

Fluorosis – caused by excess fluoride (above 1.5 mg/L) in drinking water over many years

  1. Dental fluorosis – mottled, chalky white to brown stained teeth
  2. Skeletal fluorosis – joint stiffness, bone pain, bent spine and legs, crippling
  3. Non-skeletal – stomach upset, muscle weakness

Endemic areas: parts of Rajasthan, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh (Nalgonda), Gujarat, Punjab and others.

Prevention: safe alternative water source, defluoridation (Nalgonda technique – alum, lime and bleaching powder), diet rich in calcium and vitamin C; National Programme for Prevention and Control of Fluorosis.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the trace elements – copper, selenium, chromium, manganese, cobalt and molybdenum – their functions, sources and effects of deficiency and excess.
answer_html:
Introduction Trace elements are minerals needed in very small amounts (milligrams or micrograms per day). Besides iron, iodine, zinc and fluoride, several other trace elements act mainly as parts of enzymes. Deficiencies are uncommon with a varied diet but occur in malnutrition, long-term parenteral nutrition and some genetic disorders; excess from the environment or industry can be toxic.

1. Copper

  • Functions
    • part of enzymes – cytochrome oxidase (energy), superoxide dismutase (antioxidant), lysyl oxidase (cross-linking of collagen and elastin), tyrosinase (melanin)
    • ceruloplasmin – helps iron transport and haemoglobin formation
    • nerve function and immunity
  • Sources – liver, shellfish, nuts, seeds, whole grains, pulses, cocoa
  • Requirement – about 2 mg/day for adults
  • Deficiency – anaemia not responding to iron, low white cell count, bone changes, depigmented hair and skin; in malnourished infants and with prolonged TPN; Menkes disease (genetic)
  • Excess – Wilson's disease (genetic accumulation of copper) – liver cirrhosis, Kayser–Fleischer rings in the cornea, tremors and psychiatric changes; acute poisoning from contaminated water or containers

2. Selenium

  • Functions
    • part of glutathione peroxidase – an important antioxidant enzyme
    • deiodinase enzymes – activation of thyroid hormone
    • immunity and reproduction
  • Sources – seafood, organ meats, eggs, cereals (content depends on soil), nuts
  • Requirement – about 40 µg/day
  • Deficiency – Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy) and Kashin–Beck disease (joint disease) in selenium-poor regions; weak immunity; worsens hypothyroidism with iodine deficiency
  • Excess (selenosis) – hair and nail loss, garlic odour of breath, skin lesions, nerve damage – reported from seleniferous soils in parts of Punjab

3. Chromium

  • Function – enhances the action of insulin ("glucose tolerance factor"); carbohydrate and fat metabolism
  • Sources – whole grains, meat, broccoli, nuts, brewer's yeast
  • Deficiency – impaired glucose tolerance, weight loss, neuropathy – seen in long-term TPN
  • Excess – dietary chromium is safe; industrial hexavalent chromium is toxic – skin ulcers, lung cancer

4. Manganese

  • Functions – cofactor of enzymes (manganese superoxide dismutase, pyruvate carboxylase, arginase); bone formation; metabolism of carbohydrates and fats
  • Sources – whole grains, nuts, pulses, tea, green leafy vegetables
  • Deficiency – rare; poor bone growth, skin changes
  • Excess – inhalation by miners and welders causes manganism – a Parkinson-like syndrome with psychiatric symptoms

5. Cobalt

  • Function – a component of vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin); needed for red cell formation
  • Sources – animal foods (as vitamin B₁₂)
  • Deficiency – appears as B₁₂ deficiency – megaloblastic anaemia
  • Excess – cardiomyopathy, thyroid enlargement, polycythaemia (industrial or from additives)

6. Molybdenum

  • Functions – cofactor of xanthine oxidase (uric acid formation), sulphite oxidase and aldehyde oxidase
  • Sources – pulses, cereals, nuts, leafy vegetables, organ meats
  • Deficiency – very rare (long-term TPN, genetic cofactor deficiency) – neurological problems
  • Excess – gout-like symptoms; may cause copper deficiency

Summary table

Element Key function Deficiency Excess
Copper iron use, collagen, antioxidant enzymes anaemia, neutropenia Wilson's disease
Selenium glutathione peroxidase, thyroid hormone activation Keshan disease selenosis
Chromium insulin action glucose intolerance toxic in industry (Cr⁶⁺)
Manganese enzyme cofactor, bone rare manganism
Cobalt part of vitamin B₁₂ megaloblastic anaemia cardiomyopathy
Molybdenum xanthine and sulphite oxidase rare gout-like symptoms

General points

  • A varied diet of whole grains, pulses, nuts, vegetables and animal foods meets trace-element needs
  • Patients on long-term TPN need trace-element additions
  • Supplements should be used only when indicated – the margin between need and toxicity is narrow

Nursing relevance

  • Monitor patients on TPN for deficiency signs; ensure trace elements are added as prescribed
  • Recognise occupational exposure (welders, miners) and educate on safety
  • Promote dietary diversity rather than unnecessary supplements

Interactions among minerals

  • Zinc and copper compete for absorption – long-term high-dose zinc supplements can cause copper deficiency anaemia
  • Iron and zinc compete when given together in high doses
  • Calcium taken with meals reduces iron absorption
  • Phytates in bran and whole grains bind zinc, iron and calcium; fermentation and germination reduce phytates

Trace elements in special situations

  • Long-term total parenteral nutrition – trace-element solutions (zinc, copper, selenium, chromium, manganese) are added daily; copper and manganese are reduced in cholestatic liver disease because they are excreted in bile
  • Burns and large wounds – increased losses of zinc, copper and selenium

Assessment – serum copper and ceruloplasmin (Wilson's disease, deficiency), serum selenium, urinary copper; most others are measured only in specialised laboratories.

Conclusion Copper, selenium, chromium, manganese, cobalt and molybdenum are trace elements that work mainly as parts of enzymes or vitamins; their deficiency is uncommon but occurs in malnutrition and long-term TPN, while excess – as in Wilson's disease, selenosis and manganism – is also harmful.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the food exchange system. Describe the principles of menu planning. (5 + 5)
answer_html:
Introduction Planning meals that are nutritious, affordable and acceptable is a key skill for nurses and dietitians. The food exchange system makes diet planning simple and flexible, and menu planning turns nutrient requirements into actual meals.

PART A – FOOD EXCHANGE SYSTEM (5 marks)

1. Definition

  • The food exchange system groups foods into lists (exchange lists) so that one portion ("exchange") of any food in a list gives approximately the same amount of energy, carbohydrate, protein and fat as any other food in that list
  • Foods within a list can therefore be exchanged (substituted) for one another without changing the nutrient content of the diet
  • First developed for diabetic diets; now used for all diet planning

2. Indian exchange lists (approximate values for one exchange/portion – NIN)

Exchange list One exchange Energy Protein
Cereals and millets 30 g raw (1 medium chapati or about ½ cup cooked rice) 100 kcal 3 g
Pulses 30 g raw dal 100 kcal 6 g
Milk 100 ml about 70 kcal 3 g
Egg / meat / fish 1 egg (50 g) / 50 g flesh food 85–100 kcal 7–9 g
Roots and tubers 100 g about 80 kcal 1–2 g
Green leafy vegetables 100 g about 45 kcal 3–4 g
Other vegetables 100 g about 30 kcal 1–2 g
Fruits 100 g (one medium fruit) about 40 kcal –
Fats and oils 5 g (1 teaspoon) 45 kcal –
Sugar 5 g (1 teaspoon) 20 kcal –

3. Steps in using the exchange system

  1. Calculate the requirement – energy and protein for the person (age, sex, weight, activity, disease)
  2. Decide the number of exchanges from each list to meet the requirement
  3. Distribute exchanges among breakfast, lunch, tea and dinner
  4. Select foods from each list according to taste, season and cost

4. Example – 1,800 kcal diabetic diet

  • Cereals 8 exchanges (800 kcal) + pulses 2 (200) + milk 500 ml (350) + vegetables 300–400 g (about 150) + fruits 2 (about 80) + oil 4 teaspoons (180) ≈ 1,760–1,800 kcal

5. Advantages

  • Variety and flexibility – the patient can choose foods without upsetting the diet
  • Easy calorie and carbohydrate counting; good for diabetes, obesity, kidney and heart diets
  • Simple for patient education; no need to calculate every meal
  • Helps maintain consistency of carbohydrate in diabetics

6. Limitations

  • Values are approximate – foods within a list are not identical in vitamins, minerals and fibre
  • Needs education and some literacy; portion sizes must be learnt
  • Mixed dishes and restaurant foods are hard to fit into lists

PART B – PRINCIPLES OF MENU PLANNING (5 marks)

Menu planning is the process of deciding in advance what foods and dishes will be served at each meal for a day or a week, so that the nutritional needs of all members are met within the available resources.

Principles

  1. Meet nutritional requirements – plan to meet the RDA of each family member; include foods from all food groups every day
  2. Consider the family – number, age, sex, activity and special needs – pregnant or lactating women, infants, children, elderly, sick members
  3. Economy – plan within the budget; use seasonal, local and low-cost nutritious foods (pulses, groundnut, green leafy vegetables, millets)
  4. Food habits and preferences – respect customs, religion, regional patterns, likes and dislikes; introduce new foods gradually
  5. Variety – vary colour, texture, flavour, shape and cooking methods; avoid repeating the same dish
  6. Satiety value – include some protein and fat in each meal so that hunger does not return quickly
  7. Meal pattern – distribute food through the day, e.g. breakfast 20–25%, lunch 30–35%, evening snack 10–15%, dinner 25–30% of energy; do not skip breakfast
  8. Time, energy and equipment – consider the time available (working women), fuel and kitchen equipment; plan quick dishes for busy days
  9. Preservation of nutrients and safety – choose cooking methods that save nutrients; ensure food hygiene; plan use of leftovers safely
  10. Aesthetic appeal – attractive presentation and serving
  11. Flexibility – menus should allow substitution (exchange system) depending on availability
  12. Special needs – modify menus for illness, festivals, fasting and travel

Steps of menu planning

  1. Collect information about family members and resources
  2. Calculate requirements and decide quantities of each food group (balanced diet tables)
  3. Plan the meal pattern and dishes for each meal
  4. Prepare a weekly menu; make a market list
  5. Evaluate for nutritive value, cost and acceptability, and modify

Sample one-day menu (vegetarian adult)

  • Breakfast – vegetable poha with peanuts, a glass of milk
  • Mid-morning – a seasonal fruit (guava)
  • Lunch – 2–3 chapatis, rice, dal, green leafy vegetable sabzi, salad, curd
  • Evening – roasted chana or sprouts chaat, tea
  • Dinner – vegetable khichdi with ghee, mixed vegetable curry, buttermilk

Conclusion The food exchange system groups foods with similar nutrient content into lists so that they can be substituted easily, making diet planning flexible; menu planning applies principles of nutrition, economy, food habits, variety and practicality to provide balanced meals for every member of the family.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Describe the WHO/UNICEF recommendations on infant and young child feeding (IYCF).
answer_html:
Introduction Infant and young child feeding (IYCF) refers to the feeding practices – breastfeeding and complementary feeding – for children from birth to 2 years. The first 1,000 days (pregnancy to the second birthday) are a window of opportunity for growth and brain development. Optimal IYCF practices are among the most effective ways to reduce under-five deaths. WHO and UNICEF issued the Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding (2003).

A. Recommendations on breastfeeding

  1. Early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour of birth
    • Place the baby skin-to-skin on the mother's chest immediately after birth
    • Also applies after caesarean section as soon as the mother is responsive
  2. Give colostrum – the baby's "first immunisation"; no pre-lacteal feeds (honey, ghutti, sugar water, animal milk)
  3. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months
    • Only breast milk – no water, other milk, foods or drinks
    • Exceptions – ORS, drops or syrups of vitamins, minerals or medicines
  4. Breastfeed on demand, day and night – 8–12 times in 24 hours; allow the baby to empty one breast before offering the other (to get the fat-rich hindmilk)
  5. Correct positioning and attachment – baby's body close and straight, chin touching the breast, mouth wide open, lower lip turned out, more areola visible above than below
  6. Continue breastfeeding up to 2 years of age or beyond
  7. Avoid bottles, teats and pacifiers

B. Recommendations on complementary feeding Complementary feeding should be timely, adequate, safe and responsive and should be given while breastfeeding continues.

  1. Timely – start at 6 months (180 days), when breast milk alone no longer meets the needs for energy, iron and zinc
  2. Adequate
    • Frequency and amount
Age Meals per day Amount per meal
6–8 months 2–3 meals + 1–2 snacks start with 2–3 tablespoons, increase to ½ cup (125 ml)
9–11 months 3–4 meals + 1–2 snacks ½ cup
12–24 months 3–4 meals + 1–2 snacks ¾ to 1 cup (250 ml) 
- **Consistency** – start with **thick** mashed foods (not watery dal water); finger foods by 8 months; **family foods** by 12 months
- **Energy density** – add a teaspoon of **oil or ghee** to each meal
- **Variety (dietary diversity)** – foods from at least **5 of 8 food groups** daily: breast milk; grains, roots and tubers; pulses, nuts and seeds; dairy; flesh foods; eggs; vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables; other fruits and vegetables
- Include **animal foods** (egg, meat, fish, milk) where acceptable, and **iron-rich** foods
  1. Safe
    • Wash hands with soap before preparing food and feeding
    • Use clean utensils; feed with cup and spoon (katori-chammach), not bottles
    • Serve food fresh; do not keep cooked food for more than about 2 hours at room temperature
    • Use safe water
  2. Responsive feeding
    • Feed young children directly and help older children feed themselves
    • Feed slowly and patiently; encourage but do not force
    • Talk to the child and maintain eye contact; minimise distractions (no mobile phones or TV)
    • Try different combinations and textures if the child refuses

C. Feeding during and after illness

  • Breastfeed more often; give extra fluids
  • Offer soft, favourite foods in small, frequent amounts
  • After illness, give one extra meal a day for at least 2 weeks (catch-up growth)

D. Other recommendations

  • Vitamin and mineral supplements or fortified foods when needed (vitamin A, IFA syrup under Anaemia Mukt Bharat)
  • Avoid sugar, excess salt, biscuits, chips, soft drinks, tea and coffee
  • Special support in difficult circumstances – low-birth-weight and preterm babies, HIV-positive mothers, malnourished children, emergencies

E. Indian situation and programmes

  • NFHS-5 (2019–21): early initiation about 42%, exclusive breastfeeding about 64%, and only about 11% of children aged 6–23 months receive a minimum adequate diet
  • MAA (Mothers' Absolute Affection) programme (2016) promotes breastfeeding
  • IMS Act (Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods Act, 1992, amended 2003) prohibits promotion of breast-milk substitutes
  • ICDS/Anganwadi – supplementary nutrition and counselling; MCP card guidance; Poshan Maah

F. Role of the nurse

  • Counsel mothers during pregnancy about breastfeeding
  • Ensure skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding within one hour in the labour room and operation theatre
  • Help with positioning and attachment; manage problems – sore nipples, engorgement, "not enough milk"
  • Demonstrate preparation of low-cost complementary foods; counsel on hygiene and responsive feeding
  • Growth monitoring and early referral of faltering growth
  • Discourage bottle feeding and harmful practices (pre-lacteal feeds, discarding colostrum)

Conclusion WHO/UNICEF recommend initiating breastfeeding within one hour, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, and timely, adequate, safe and responsive complementary feeding from six months with continued breastfeeding to two years or beyond; nurses play a central role in putting these practices into action.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Define balanced diet.
answer_html:
Definition A balanced diet is one that contains different types of foods in such quantities and proportions that the need for energy, proteins, vitamins, minerals and other nutrients is adequately met, with a small provision for extra nutrients to withstand short periods of leanness.

Features

  • Includes foods from all food groups – cereals and millets, pulses, milk and animal foods, vegetables and fruits, fats and sugar in moderation
  • Energy distribution – carbohydrates 50–60%, proteins 10–15%, fats 20–30%
  • Varies with age, sex, activity and physiological state

Example – balanced diet for a sedentary adult man (ICMR, per day)

  • Cereals and millets 375 g, pulses 75 g, milk 300 ml, roots and tubers 200 g, green leafy vegetables 100 g, other vegetables 200 g, fruits 100 g, sugar 30 g, fats and oils 25 g

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: What is weaning? Write its principles.
answer_html:
Definition Weaning is the gradual introduction of foods other than breast milk into an infant's diet, starting at 6 months of age, while breastfeeding continues. WHO now prefers the term complementary feeding.

Why at 6 months

  • Breast milk alone no longer meets the baby's needs for energy, protein, iron and zinc
  • The baby's gut, kidneys and chewing–swallowing skills are ready

Principles

  1. Introduce one new food at a time, in small amounts (2–3 teaspoons), and increase gradually
  2. Start with thick, smooth mashed foods; progress to lumpy, then family foods
  3. Increase frequency, quantity and variety with age
  4. Make food energy-dense – add a little oil or ghee
  5. Use fresh, hygienically prepared food; feed with katori and spoon, not bottle
  6. Do not add much salt or sugar; no tea, biscuits or junk food
  7. Continue breastfeeding up to 2 years

Examples: mashed banana, dal-rice mash, khichdi, suji or ragi porridge, mashed potato, curd, egg.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the principles and steps of planning a balanced diet.
answer_html:
Introduction A balanced diet provides all nutrients in the right amounts and proportions to maintain health, vitality and well-being. Planning it requires knowledge of requirements, foods and the family's situation.

A. Principles

  1. Meet the RDA of the individual for energy, protein, vitamins and minerals
  2. Correct proportion of nutrients – carbohydrates 50–60%, proteins 10–15%, fats 20–30% of total energy
  3. Include all food groups daily – cereals and millets, pulses, milk and animal foods, vegetables (especially green leafy) and fruits, with fats and sugar in moderation
  4. Individual needs – consider age, sex, body weight, activity level and physiological state (growth, pregnancy, lactation, old age, illness)
  5. Economy – choose seasonal, local and affordable foods; pulses, groundnuts, millets and green leafy vegetables are cheap and nutritious
  6. Food habits – respect religion, region and preferences
  7. Quality protein – combine cereals with pulses; add milk, curd or egg
  8. Adequate fibre and water – whole grains, vegetables, fruits; 8–10 glasses of water
  9. Limit salt (less than 5 g), added sugar and fat; avoid junk foods
  10. Food safety and nutrient-preserving cooking methods
  11. Regular meal pattern – 3 meals and 1–2 healthy snacks

B. Steps in planning

  1. Collect information – age, sex, weight, occupation/activity, physiological state, health problems, food habits, income
  2. Calculate requirements – energy and protein (ICMR-NIN tables)
  3. Decide quantities of each food group using balanced-diet tables or exchange lists
  4. Distribute the day's food among meals
  5. Select specific foods and dishes – local, seasonal, liked and affordable
  6. Plan the menu with variety in colour, texture and cooking method
  7. Check the nutritive value using food composition tables; compare with RDA
  8. Evaluate and modify for cost, acceptability and practicality

C. Example – food groups per day for a sedentary adult woman (ICMR, approximate)

  • Cereals and millets about 270 g, pulses 60 g, milk 300 ml, roots and tubers 200 g, green leafy vegetables 100 g, other vegetables 200 g, fruits 100 g, sugar 20 g, fats and oils 20 g

D. Practical household tips

  • Half the plate with vegetables and fruits; a quarter cereals; a quarter pulses or protein foods
  • Use whole grains and millets at least for one meal
  • Include a green leafy vegetable daily and a seasonal fruit
  • Use iodised salt and a mix of oils

E. Nursing relevance

  • Teach families to plan low-cost balanced diets
  • Modify plans for pregnant women, children, elderly and patients

Conclusion A balanced diet is planned by assessing individual needs, choosing the right quantities from all food groups in the correct proportions, and selecting local, affordable and acceptable foods, then checking and adjusting the plan.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain food guides. Add a note on "My Plate for the Day".
answer_html:
Introduction Food guides are simple tools that translate scientific nutrient recommendations into practical advice about foods – what to eat, how much and how often. They are used for nutrition education of the public.

A. Types of food guides

1. Food groups

  • Foods grouped by similar nutrients – e.g. ICMR's five food groups (cereals; pulses; milk and meat products; fruits and vegetables; fats and sugars)
  • Advice: eat foods from every group daily

2. Food pyramid

  • A triangle showing proportions of foods:
    • base – cereals, millets, pulses – eat adequately
    • next – vegetables and fruits – eat liberally
    • upper – milk, eggs, meat, fish, nuts – eat moderately
    • tip – oils, fats, sugar, salt, junk food – eat sparingly
  • Often combined with advice on physical activity and water

3. Food plate

  • A picture of a plate divided into portions for each food group – easy to apply at every meal

B. "My Plate for the Day" (ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024)

  • A plate model showing the food groups and amounts for a day's diet of about 2,000 kcal
  • Half the plate – vegetables (including green leafy vegetables, roots and tubers) and fruits
  • The other half – cereals and millets, pulses/eggs/flesh foods, nuts and seeds, with milk or curd on the side
  • Approximate daily amounts: vegetables about 400 g, fruits about 100 g, cereals and millets about 250 g, pulses/eggs/flesh foods about 85 g, nuts and seeds about 35 g, milk/curd about 300 ml, fats and oils about 27 g
  • Key messages – sourcing nutrients from at least 8 food groups, using whole grains and millets, limiting oil, salt and sugar, and avoiding ultra-processed foods

C. Dietary Guidelines for Indians (NIN, 2024) – some key messages

  1. Eat a variety of foods to ensure a balanced diet
  2. Ensure extra food and health care during pregnancy and lactation
  3. Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then complementary foods with continued breastfeeding till 2 years
  4. Eat plenty of vegetables and pulses
  5. Use oils and fats in moderation; obtain good-quality protein and essential amino acids
  6. Restrict salt intake; minimise sugar and ultra-processed foods
  7. Ensure safe and clean food; drink plenty of water
  8. Read food labels
  9. Be physically active and maintain a healthy body weight

D. Uses of food guides

  • Nutrition education in schools, communities and hospitals
  • Planning balanced meals without calculations
  • Promoting healthy eating habits and prevention of non-communicable diseases

E. Limitations

  • Give general advice; individual needs differ (illness, pregnancy)
  • Need adaptation to regional foods and cultures

Conclusion Food guides – food groups, food pyramids and food plates such as ICMR-NIN's "My Plate for the Day" – convert nutrient requirements into simple food-based advice, with half the plate as vegetables and fruits and the rest from cereals, pulses, nuts and dairy.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Define RDA. Explain its uses and limitations.
answer_html:
A. Definition Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is the average daily dietary intake of a nutrient that is sufficient to meet the requirement of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals of a particular age, sex and physiological group.

  • In India, RDAs are given by the ICMR–National Institute of Nutrition (latest revision 2020)

B. Related terms

  • Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) – meets the need of half (50%) of healthy individuals in a group; RDA = EAR + 2 SD
  • Tolerable Upper Limit (TUL) – the highest daily intake that is unlikely to cause harm
  • Adequate Intake (AI) – used when data are not enough to set an RDA
  • Reference man and woman – healthy adults of standard weight (ICMR 2020: 65 kg man, 55 kg woman)

C. Uses of RDA

  1. Planning diets for individuals, families and institutions (hospitals, hostels, prisons)
  2. Evaluating dietary intake in diet surveys – identifying groups at risk of deficiency
  3. Nutrition programmes – fixing food norms for ICDS, PM POSHAN (mid-day meal), relief feeding
  4. Food and agricultural policy – estimating national food needs and production targets
  5. Food labelling and setting standards for fortification
  6. Nutrition education and counselling
  7. Research and development of new food products
  8. Setting standards for pregnant women, children, workers and athletes

D. Limitations

  1. Based on healthy people – not directly applicable to sick persons (therapeutic diets need different values)
  2. Represent group averages – individual requirements vary; may overestimate for many people
  3. Based on limited data for some nutrients and age groups
  4. Do not fully account for bioavailability, food–drug interactions and nutrient interactions
  5. Meant for intake averaged over time, not a single day
  6. Change with new research (revised periodically)
  7. Some nutrients have only AI values; values differ between countries
  8. Do not cover non-nutrients such as fibre or phytochemicals fully

E. Nursing relevance

  • Use RDA tables to plan diets for pregnant women, children and elderly
  • Remember that patients' needs differ – fever, burns and surgery raise needs; kidney disease limits some nutrients

Conclusion RDA is the daily intake that meets the needs of almost all healthy people in a group; it is widely used for planning and evaluating diets, programmes and policies, but has limitations for sick individuals and individual variation.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Write a note on dietary fibre.
answer_html:
Definition Dietary fibre is the part of plant foods – mainly non-starch polysaccharides and lignin – that resists digestion by human enzymes and reaches the large intestine largely intact.

A. Types

Type Examples Main sources Main action
Soluble fibre pectin, gums, mucilage, β-glucans oats, barley, pulses, apple, citrus fruits, isabgol (psyllium), fenugreek seeds forms a gel; lowers cholesterol and blood sugar
Insoluble fibre cellulose, lignin, some hemicelluloses whole wheat, bran, whole grains, vegetables, skins of fruits, nuts adds bulk; speeds movement through the bowel

B. Functions and health benefits

  1. Prevents constipation – increases stool bulk and softness
  2. Reduces risk of haemorrhoids, diverticulosis and possibly colon cancer
  3. Lowers blood cholesterol – binds bile acids and increases their excretion
  4. Controls blood sugar – slows absorption of glucose (low glycaemic index)
  5. Satiety and weight control – filling, low in calories
  6. Prebiotic – feeds healthy gut bacteria, which produce short-chain fatty acids
  7. Helps remove some toxins and carcinogens

C. Recommended intake

  • About 25–40 g per day for adults (ICMR suggests about 40 g per 2,000 kcal)
  • Most refined diets provide much less

D. Sources

  • Whole grains and millets – whole wheat atta (with bran), jowar, bajra, ragi, oats, brown rice
  • Pulses and legumes – whole moong, chana, rajma
  • Vegetables – green leafy vegetables, beans, carrots
  • Fruits with skin – guava, apple, pear
  • Nuts and seeds – flaxseed, isabgol

E. Excess fibre

  • Bloating and flatulence
  • Reduced absorption of iron, zinc and calcium (phytates)
  • Risk of intestinal obstruction if water intake is low

F. Practical advice

  • Increase fibre gradually and drink plenty of water
  • Do not sieve atta to remove bran; prefer whole fruits to juices
  • Include salads, sprouts and vegetables at every meal

G. Nursing relevance

  • High-fibre diet with fluids for constipation, bedridden patients, pregnancy, elderly, and patients on opioids
  • Soluble fibre for diabetes and high cholesterol
  • Low-fibre (low-residue) diet when advised – before bowel surgery or colonoscopy, acute diarrhoea, bowel obstruction

Conclusion Dietary fibre – soluble and insoluble – is the undigested part of plant foods that prevents constipation, lowers cholesterol and blood sugar and aids weight control; adults need about 25–40 g a day from whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruits, with adequate water.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain how to calculate the nutritive value of a recipe, with an example.
answer_html:
Introduction Calculating the nutritive value of a recipe or diet tells us how much energy, protein and other nutrients it provides. It is used to plan and evaluate diets, therapeutic menus and institutional meals.

A. Tools needed

  • Food composition tables – Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT, NIN, 2017) or Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (NIN)
  • Values are given per 100 g edible portion of raw food
  • Weighing scale and measuring cups/spoons

B. Steps

  1. List all ingredients of the recipe with their raw weights (in grams) per serving or for the whole recipe
  2. Find the nutrient content per 100 g of each ingredient from the tables

  3. Calculate the nutrients in the amount used: Nutrient = (nutrient per 100 g × weight used in g) ÷ 100

  4. Add the values of all ingredients for each nutrient

  5. Divide by the number of servings, if needed
  6. Compare with the RDA or the diet prescription
  7. Consider cooking losses for vitamins (e.g. vitamin C and thiamine)

C. Example – vegetable khichdi (one serving, approximate values)

Ingredient Amount Energy (kcal) Protein (g)
Rice (raw) 60 g 60 × 345 ÷ 100 = 207 60 × 6.8 ÷ 100 = 4.1
Moong dal (split) 30 g 30 × 348 ÷ 100 = 104 30 × 24 ÷ 100 = 7.2
Oil / ghee 5 g 5 × 900 ÷ 100 = 45 0
Mixed vegetables 50 g about 15 about 0.8
Total about 371 kcal about 12 g
  • This serving gives about 370 kcal and 12 g protein – roughly one-fifth of an adult woman's daily protein need

D. Precautions

  • Always use raw weights and the edible portion (remove peels, seeds, bones)
  • Use the same units throughout; record accurately
  • Values are approximate – varieties, soil and cooking methods differ
  • For cooked dishes, weigh the total cooked amount to find the size of one serving

E. Uses

  • Planning therapeutic diets (diabetic, renal, high-protein)
  • Evaluating hospital, hostel and school meals (PM POSHAN norms)
  • Nutrition education and research; preparing low-cost nutritious recipes

Conclusion The nutritive value of a recipe is calculated by multiplying the nutrient content per 100 g (from food composition tables) by the weight of each raw ingredient, adding the values and dividing by the number of servings, then comparing the result with the RDA.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the advantages of breastfeeding.
answer_html:
Introduction Breast milk is the ideal food for infants. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and continued breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond. Breastfeeding benefits the baby, the mother, the family and the nation.

A. Advantages to the baby

  1. Ideal nutrition – right amount of nutrients for growth; easily digested; composition changes as the baby grows (colostrum → transitional → mature milk; thin foremilk and fat-rich hindmilk)
  2. Protection against infections – contains antibodies (secretory IgA), lactoferrin, lysozyme, white cells and bifidus factor; fewer episodes of diarrhoea, pneumonia and ear infections
  3. Lower infant deaths – breastfed babies are much less likely to die from infections
  4. Clean and safe – no contamination; always at the right temperature
  5. Brain development – DHA and other factors; better IQ and school performance
  6. Less allergy and asthma
  7. Long-term health – lower risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes and high BP later in life
  8. Emotional bonding and security through close contact
  9. Proper development of jaws, teeth and speech
  10. Early, frequent feeding prevents hypoglycaemia and hypothermia; colostrum helps pass meconium and reduces jaundice

B. Advantages to the mother

  1. Uterine involution – suckling releases oxytocin, which contracts the uterus and reduces postpartum bleeding
  2. Natural child spacing – lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) is highly effective when the baby is under 6 months, exclusively breastfed and periods have not returned
  3. Helps return to pre-pregnancy weight (uses about 500 kcal a day)
  4. Lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer, type 2 diabetes and heart disease
  5. Bonding and satisfaction; reduces postpartum depression risk
  6. Convenient – no preparation, no bottles, available at night and during travel

C. Advantages to the family and society

  • Saves money – no formula, bottles or fuel; fewer doctor visits
  • Reduces health-care costs and absenteeism of working parents
  • Environment-friendly – no waste or packaging
  • Contributes to lower infant mortality and healthier future generations

D. Role of the nurse

  • Educate mothers antenatally; ensure early initiation and correct attachment
  • Support working mothers with expressed breast milk
  • Help mothers overcome myths ("not enough milk", discarding colostrum)

Conclusion Breastfeeding provides complete nutrition and protection against infection to the baby, helps the mother recover and space births, and saves money and lives – making it the most effective, natural and economical way to feed infants.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: What is colostrum? State its importance.
answer_html:
Definition Colostrum is the thick, yellowish milk secreted during the first 2–4 days after delivery. It is small in quantity (a few teaspoons per feed), which is just right for the newborn's small stomach.

Composition

  • Rich in protein, antibodies (especially secretory IgA), white blood cells, vitamin A (yellow colour from carotene) and zinc
  • Lower in fat and lactose than mature milk

Importance

  1. The baby's first immunisation – protects against infections
  2. Laxative effect – helps pass meconium, reducing neonatal jaundice
  3. Growth factors help the gut mature and prevent entry of germs
  4. Prevents hypoglycaemia in the newborn
  5. Rich vitamin A protects eyes and reduces infection

Nursing point: counsel families not to discard colostrum and not to give pre-lacteal feeds.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Write the hazards of bottle feeding.
answer_html:
Hazards to the baby

  1. Infections – bottles and teats are hard to clean; diarrhoea, oral thrush
  2. Malnutrition – over-dilution of costly formula causes marasmus; over-concentration causes dehydration and obesity
  3. No antibodies – more pneumonia, ear infections and deaths
  4. Allergy to cow's milk protein
  5. Nipple confusion – baby refuses the breast → lactation failure
  6. Dental caries ("bottle caries") and faulty jaw development
  7. Ear infections when fed lying down
  8. Higher later risk of obesity and diabetes; less bonding

Hazards to the mother and family

  • Loss of the protective effects of breastfeeding; earlier return of fertility
  • Expensive – formula, bottles and fuel

Advice: if breast milk cannot be given directly, feed expressed breast milk or other milk with a katori and spoon or paladai.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: What is the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative?
answer_html:
Definition The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) was launched by WHO and UNICEF in 1991 to protect, promote and support breastfeeding in maternity facilities. A hospital is declared "Baby-Friendly" when it follows the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding and the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes.

Ten Steps (revised 2018) – in brief

  1. Follow the Code; have a written infant feeding policy; monitor practices
  2. Train staff to support breastfeeding
  3. Inform pregnant women about breastfeeding
  4. Ensure immediate skin-to-skin contact and early initiation after birth
  5. Help mothers start and maintain breastfeeding and manage difficulties
  6. Give no food or fluid other than breast milk unless medically indicated
  7. Rooming-in – mother and baby together 24 hours a day
  8. Support responsive feeding (feeding on cues)
  9. Counsel about the risks of bottles, teats and pacifiers
  10. Arrange continued support after discharge

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: How is breast milk expressed and stored?
answer_html:
When needed: working mothers, sick or preterm babies who cannot suck, separation of mother and baby, breast engorgement.

Expression

  1. Wash hands; use a clean, boiled, wide-mouthed steel or glass container
  2. Sit comfortably; massage the breast gently; place thumb and finger on the areola (C-hold)
  3. Press back towards the chest, then compress and release rhythmically; rotate around the areola
  4. Express each breast for 3–5 minutes, repeating 2–3 times (20–30 minutes in all); a breast pump may also be used

Storage (common Indian guidance)

  • Room temperature – about 6–8 hours
  • Refrigerator – about 24 hours
  • Deep freezer – about 3 months

Feeding

  • Warm by keeping the container in warm water (do not boil or microwave); mix gently
  • Feed with a katori-spoon or paladai, not a bottle
  • Use within an hour of warming; do not refreeze

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the nutritional requirements and dietary management during pregnancy.
answer_html:
Introduction Good nutrition during pregnancy is essential for healthy fetal growth, prevention of low birth weight and anaemia, and for building maternal stores for lactation. Needs increase due to growth of the fetus, placenta, uterus and breasts, a 40–50% rise in blood volume and a higher BMR.

A. Weight gain

  • A woman of normal weight should gain about 10–12 kg (11.5–16 kg) during pregnancy; more if underweight, less if obese
  • About 1–2 kg in the first trimester, then about 0.4 kg per week

B. Additional requirements (ICMR-NIN 2020, approximate)

Nutrient Requirement in pregnancy
Energy +350 kcal/day in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters
Protein +9.5 g/day (2nd trimester), +22 g/day (3rd trimester)
Iron 27 mg/day + daily IFA tablet
Calcium 1,000 mg/day + calcium tablets (500 mg twice daily)
Folic acid about 570 µg/day; 400 µg tablets in the first trimester
Iodine 220–250 µg/day – iodised salt
Vitamin A about 900 µg/day (from food; no high-dose supplements)
ω-3 fatty acids (DHA) for fetal brain and eyes – fish, flaxseed, walnuts

C. Dietary advice

  1. Eat one extra meal or nutritious snack daily from the second trimester
  2. Milk or curd – 2–3 cups a day; pulses, eggs, fish or meat for protein
  3. Green leafy vegetables and seasonal fruits daily – iron, folate, vitamin C
  4. Whole grains and millets; fibre and 8–10 glasses of water to prevent constipation
  5. Use iodised salt; limit very salty and sugary foods
  6. Small, frequent meals for nausea and heartburn; dry snacks in the morning
  7. Avoid alcohol, tobacco and excess tea or coffee; avoid raw or undercooked meat and eggs and unpasteurised milk
  8. No fasting or dieting; counter harmful food taboos (e.g. avoiding papaya, eggs or milk)

D. Supplements and services (national guidelines)

  • Folic acid 400 µg daily in the first trimester
  • IFA tablet (60 mg iron + 500 µg folic acid) daily from the second trimester for at least 180 days
  • Calcium 1 g daily from the second trimester; deworming (albendazole) once in the second trimester
  • Take-home ration from Anganwadi (ICDS); maternity benefit under PMMVY

E. Common problems and diet

  • Nausea and vomiting – dry carbohydrate foods, small frequent meals, avoid fatty foods
  • Heartburn – small meals, do not lie down after eating
  • Constipation – fibre, fluids, activity
  • Gestational diabetes – controlled carbohydrate, high-fibre diet

F. Nurse's role

  • Monitor weight gain and Hb at each visit; counsel on diet using locally available foods
  • Ensure IFA and calcium compliance; link to ICDS services

Conclusion Pregnancy needs about 350 kcal and extra protein daily from the second trimester, along with more iron, calcium, folate and iodine; a varied diet with extra milk, pulses, vegetables and fruits, plus IFA and calcium supplements, ensures a healthy mother and baby.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain anaemia in pregnancy – causes, effects, dietary management and IFA supplementation.
answer_html:
Introduction Anaemia in pregnancy is defined by WHO as haemoglobin below 11 g/dl. It is the commonest medical disorder of pregnancy in India – about 52% of pregnant women are anaemic (NFHS-5).

A. Grades (haemoglobin)

  • Mild – 10–10.9 g/dl
  • Moderate – 7–9.9 g/dl
  • Severe – below 7 g/dl

B. Causes

  1. Iron deficiency – the commonest; increased demand plus low intake and poor absorption
  2. Folate and vitamin B₁₂ deficiency – megaloblastic anaemia
  3. Hookworm infestation, malaria
  4. Haemoglobinopathies – sickle cell disease, thalassaemia
  5. Repeated pregnancies, short birth intervals, teenage pregnancy
  6. Blood loss – heavy periods before pregnancy, antepartum haemorrhage
  7. Poor diet, food taboos, tea with meals

C. Effects

  • On the mother: fatigue, breathlessness, palpitation, poor work capacity; infections; heart failure in severe anaemia; poor tolerance to postpartum haemorrhage → maternal death; poor lactation
  • On the baby: low birth weight, preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction, stillbirth, low iron stores and anaemia in infancy

D. Dietary management

  • Iron-rich foods – green leafy vegetables (amaranth, drumstick leaves), garden cress seeds, jaggery, dates, millets (bajra, ragi), pulses, poha, meat, liver, fish, eggs
  • Vitamin C with meals – amla, guava, lemon, orange
  • Folate-rich foods – green leafy vegetables, pulses
  • Avoid tea and coffee with meals; cook in iron vessels; use sprouted and fermented foods

E. IFA supplementation (Anaemia Mukt Bharat)

  • Prophylaxis: 1 IFA tablet daily (60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid) from the second trimester for at least 180 days, and for 180 days after delivery
  • Folic acid 400 µg daily in the first trimester
  • Treatment of mild–moderate anaemia: 2 IFA tablets daily (therapeutic dose) with follow-up Hb
  • IV iron (iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose) for moderate–severe anaemia or poor response, especially in later pregnancy
  • Blood transfusion for severe anaemia close to term or with complications
  • Deworming with albendazole once after the first trimester
  • Hb testing at every antenatal visit (digital haemoglobinometer)

F. Nurse's role

  • Screen every pregnant woman for anaemia; counsel on diet
  • Explain side effects of IFA – black stools, constipation, nausea – take after meals or at bedtime
  • Check compliance (count tablets, MCP card); follow up and refer severe cases
  • Ensure institutional delivery for anaemic women; birth preparedness

Conclusion Anaemia in pregnancy (Hb below 11 g/dl), mostly due to iron deficiency, endangers both mother and baby; it is prevented and treated by an iron- and vitamin C-rich diet, daily IFA for 180 days in pregnancy and after delivery, deworming and timely treatment of moderate and severe anaemia.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the nutritional requirements and diet during lactation.
answer_html:
Introduction A lactating mother produces about 750–850 ml of milk per day in the first six months. Milk production requires extra energy and nutrients; if the diet is poor, the mother's own stores are used and her health suffers.

A. Additional requirements (ICMR-NIN 2020, approximate)

Nutrient 0–6 months 7–12 months
Energy +600 kcal/day +520 kcal/day
Protein +17 g/day +13 g/day
  • Calcium – 1,000 mg/day plus calcium tablets for 6 months after delivery
  • Iron – about 23 mg/day; IFA daily for 180 days after delivery
  • Iodine – about 250–290 µg/day; vitamin A about 950 µg/day
  • Fluids – about 3 litres a day

B. Dietary advice

  1. Eat more of the normal balanced diet – an extra meal or two nutritious snacks daily
  2. Milk and milk products – 3 cups a day for calcium and protein
  3. Pulses, eggs, fish, meat, groundnuts and soya for protein
  4. Green leafy vegetables and fruits daily
  5. Plenty of fluids – a glass of water, milk or soup each time she breastfeeds
  6. Traditional foods such as methi (fenugreek), dill seeds, garlic, cumin, gond or dry-fruit laddoos and dalia are nutritious and culturally welcome (evidence for increasing milk is limited; frequent suckling is the main stimulus)
  7. Avoid alcohol, smoking and excess tea/coffee; take medicines only as prescribed
  8. Do not diet for weight loss in the early months; weight reduces gradually with breastfeeding

C. Harmful practices to correct

  • Restricting water, vegetables, pulses or fruits after delivery
  • Giving only rice and ghee or very limited diets in the postnatal period
  • Belief that certain foods "spoil" the milk

D. Sample day's menu (vegetarian)

  • Early morning – milk with a few dry fruits
  • Breakfast – vegetable upma or poha with sprouts
  • Mid-morning – fruit and buttermilk
  • Lunch – chapatis, rice, dal, green leafy vegetable, curd, salad
  • Evening – methi laddoo or roasted chana, milk
  • Dinner – khichdi or chapati, mixed vegetable curry, dal
  • Bedtime – a glass of milk

E. Nurse's role

  • Counsel on diet and fluids during postnatal visits
  • Ensure continuation of IFA and calcium
  • Encourage frequent breastfeeding and rest; refer if the mother is undernourished or anaemic

Conclusion Lactation needs about 600 kcal and 17 g of extra protein daily in the first six months, with more calcium, iron and fluids; a varied diet with milk, pulses, vegetables, fruits and plenty of fluids keeps the mother healthy and supports good milk production.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the dietary needs of toddlers, preschool and school-age children.
answer_html:
Introduction After infancy, growth slows but children remain very active and are building bones, muscles and brain. Healthy food habits formed in childhood last for life.

A. Toddlers and preschool children (1–6 years)

Needs

  • Energy roughly 1,000–1,100 kcal (1–3 years) and about 1,350 kcal (4–6 years); protein and energy per kg body weight are high
  • Iron, calcium, vitamin A, zinc and iodine – common deficiencies in this age group

Feeding guidelines

  1. 3 main meals and 2 nutritious snacks – small stomach, high needs
  2. Family foods cut or mashed as needed; include cereals, dal, vegetables, curd, egg/meat, fruit
  3. Milk about 2–3 cups a day – but not too much milk, which reduces appetite and causes iron deficiency
  4. Add ghee or oil for energy density
  5. Encourage self-feeding; make food colourful and attractive; small portions
  6. Do not force-feed or bribe with sweets; be patient with food jags and picky eating
  7. Avoid junk foods, sugary drinks, chips, tea
  8. Hygiene – handwashing; safe water
  9. Growth monitoring, deworming, vitamin A and IFA syrup as per programmes

B. School-age children (6–12 years)

Needs

  • Energy about 1,700 kcal (7–9 years) rising to about 2,000–2,200 kcal (10–12 years)
  • Protein, calcium (bone growth), iron, vitamins

Feeding guidelines

  1. Never skip breakfast – improves attention and learning
  2. Nutritious tiffin – paratha with sabzi, idli, sandwiches, sprouts, fruit; avoid instant noodles and packaged snacks
  3. PM POSHAN (mid-day meal) provides a hot cooked meal at school
  4. Milk, pulses, eggs, green leafy vegetables and fruits daily
  5. Limit fast foods, sweets and soft drinks; limit screen time
  6. At least one hour of physical activity daily
  7. Plenty of water

C. Common nutritional problems

  • Under-nutrition – underweight, stunting, wasting
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia, vitamin A deficiency
  • Dental caries from sweets and sticky foods
  • Overweight and obesity in urban children
  • Worm infestation affecting appetite and nutrition
  • Poor appetite, picky eating

D. Role of parents and nurse

  • Parents should eat with children and model healthy eating
  • Nurse – growth monitoring, nutrition education of mothers, school health check-ups, referral of malnourished children, promoting ICDS and PM POSHAN services

Conclusion Toddlers, preschool and school-age children need frequent, energy-dense and varied meals with adequate protein, calcium, iron and vitamins, a regular breakfast and limited junk food, supported by growth monitoring and programmes such as ICDS and PM POSHAN.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the nutritional needs of adolescents.
answer_html:
Introduction Adolescence (10–19 years) is a period of rapid growth (growth spurt) – about 20% of adult height and 50% of adult weight are gained. Nutritional needs are among the highest in life. Good nutrition now also prepares girls for healthy motherhood.

A. Special nutritional needs

  1. Energy – high, especially in boys and active adolescents
  2. Protein – for growth of muscles and tissues
  3. Calcium and vitamin D – nearly half of adult bone mass is laid down; peak bone mass protects against osteoporosis later
  4. Iron – increased blood volume and muscle mass; menstrual losses in girls
  5. Zinc – growth and sexual maturation
  6. Folic acid – especially for girls (future pregnancy)
  7. Iodine – growth and brain function

B. Nutritional problems

  • Anaemia – about 59% of adolescent girls and 31% of boys (15–19 years, NFHS-5)
  • Thinness and stunting due to under-nutrition
  • Overweight and obesity – junk food, soft drinks, screen time
  • Skipping breakfast, irregular meals, frequent snacking
  • Unhealthy dieting and body-image concerns; eating disorders in some
  • Teenage pregnancy – double nutritional burden
  • Tobacco, alcohol and other substance use

C. Dietary guidelines

  1. Three regular meals and healthy snacks; never skip breakfast
  2. Milk, curd, paneer, ragi and sesame for calcium; sunlight for vitamin D
  3. Iron-rich foods – green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery, dates, eggs, meat – with vitamin C sources
  4. Pulses, eggs, fish, soya for protein
  5. Choose healthy snacks – fruits, roasted chana, sprouts, peanuts – instead of chips and cold drinks
  6. Limit fast food, sweets and sugary beverages
  7. Physical activity at least 60 minutes daily; adequate sleep and water

D. Programmes

  • WIFS – weekly IFA blue tablet and biannual albendazole for adolescents
  • Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK, 2014) – nutrition is a key theme; adolescent friendly health clinics
  • School Health and Wellness Programme (Ayushman Bharat), PM POSHAN in schools
  • Schemes for adolescent girls through Anganwadi centres

E. Nurse's role

  • Nutrition education in schools; screening for anaemia, BMI and growth
  • Ensure WIFS and deworming coverage; counsel on healthy eating and body image
  • Refer adolescents with severe thinness, obesity or eating problems

Conclusion Adolescents need more energy, protein, calcium, iron and zinc than at any other time except pregnancy; regular balanced meals, iron and calcium-rich foods, healthy snacks, activity and programmes such as WIFS and RKSK protect them from anaemia, under-nutrition and obesity.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Balanced Diet and Nutrition across the Life Cycle
question: Explain the nutritional needs and dietary guidelines for the elderly.
answer_html:
