Introduction With ageing, physical activity and BMR decrease, but the need for most nutrients does not. Elderly people are at risk of both under-nutrition and over-nutrition, and good nutrition helps them stay independent and active.

A. Physiological changes affecting nutrition

  • Lower BMR and activity → fewer calories needed
  • Loss of muscle (sarcopenia) and bone (osteoporosis)
  • Reduced taste, smell and appetite; poor teeth or dentures → difficulty chewing
  • Less saliva and gastric acid → poor absorption of vitamin B₁₂, iron and calcium
  • Constipation – slow bowel, low fibre and fluids, inactivity
  • Reduced thirst → risk of dehydration
  • Less vitamin D formation in skin
  • Chronic diseases and many medicines (drug–nutrient interactions)
  • Social factors – loneliness, depression, poverty, dependence, living alone

B. Nutritional needs

  • Energy – about 10–20% less than younger adults
  • Protein – the same or more (about 1–1.2 g/kg) to preserve muscle
  • Calcium (about 1,200 mg/day) and vitamin D – for bones
  • Vitamin B₁₂, folate, iron, zinc
  • Fibre and fluids – 6–8 glasses of water a day

C. Dietary guidelines

  1. Small, frequent meals at regular times
  2. Soft, easily chewed foods – dalia, khichdi, idli, upma, porridge, mashed vegetables, stewed fruits
  3. Protein at every meal – milk, curd, dal, paneer, eggs, fish
  4. Plenty of vegetables, fruits and whole grains for fibre and vitamins
  5. Limit salt, sugar and fat; avoid fried and heavy foods, especially at night
  6. Drink fluids even without thirst
  7. Get sunlight and do light exercise (walking, yoga) to keep muscles and bones strong
  8. Eat with family; make meals pleasant
  9. Regular dental care; well-fitting dentures
  10. Supplements (vitamin D, calcium, B₁₂) as prescribed

D. Common nutritional problems

  • Under-nutrition and weight loss; obesity, diabetes, hypertension
  • Osteoporosis and fractures; anaemia
  • Dehydration and constipation

E. Nurse's role

  • Nutritional screening (weight, BMI, appetite, Mini Nutritional Assessment)
  • Assist with feeding when needed; check swallowing and dentition
  • Educate family members; link to old-age support schemes

Conclusion The elderly need fewer calories but adequate protein, calcium, vitamin D, B₁₂, fibre and fluids; small, frequent, soft and nutritious meals, sunlight, exercise and social support help prevent malnutrition and chronic disease in old age.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define protein-energy malnutrition (PEM). Explain its causes, classification, clinical features, management, prevention and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Introduction Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) is one of the most important public health problems of India. It affects mainly children under five years, contributes to about one-third to half of all under-five deaths and leads to stunted growth, poor learning and low productivity in adult life.

A. Definition

  • WHO: PEM is a range of pathological conditions arising from a lack, in varying proportions, of protein and calories, occurring most frequently in infants and young children and commonly associated with infections
  • Today it is described as under-nutrition – wasting, stunting and underweight

B. Magnitude (NFHS-5, 2019–21 – children under 5)

  • Stunting 35.5%, wasting 19.3% (severe wasting 7.7%), underweight 32.1%

C. Causes

1. Immediate causes

  • Inadequate dietary intake – too little food, dilute feeds, late or poor complementary feeding
  • Infections – diarrhoea, measles, respiratory infections, tuberculosis, worm infestation – reduce appetite, increase needs and losses (malnutrition–infection cycle)

2. Underlying causes

  • Household food insecurity
  • Poor feeding and care practices – no exclusive breastfeeding, bottle feeding, discarding colostrum, food taboos
  • Poor sanitation and unsafe water; inadequate health services

3. Basic causes

  • Poverty, illiteracy (especially of mothers), unemployment
  • Large family, short birth intervals, low birth weight, maternal malnutrition
  • Gender discrimination, social customs, urban slums, natural calamities

D. Classification

1. IAP classification (weight-for-age, % of expected)

  • Normal – above 80%
  • Grade I – 71–80%; Grade II – 61–70%; Grade III – 51–60%; Grade IV – 50% or less
  • Add "K" when oedema is present

2. Gomez classification (weight-for-age)

  • Grade I – 75–90%; Grade II – 60–75%; Grade III – below 60%

3. Wellcome classification

Weight-for-age With oedema Without oedema
60–80% kwashiorkor underweight
Below 60% marasmic kwashiorkor marasmus

4. Waterlow classification – wasting (low weight-for-height – acute) and stunting (low height-for-age – chronic)

5. WHO classification (Z-scores) – used in programmes

  • Underweight – weight-for-age below –2 SD
  • Stunting – height-for-age below –2 SD
  • Wasting – weight-for-height below –2 SD
  • Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) – weight-for-height between –3 and –2 SD, or MUAC 11.5–12.5 cm
  • Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) – weight-for-height below –3 SD, or MUAC below 11.5 cm, or bilateral pitting oedema (6–59 months)

E. Clinical features

1. Marasmus (usually below 1 year; severe deficiency of energy)

  • Severe wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat – "skin and bones"
  • Old-man (wizened) face; loose skin folds over the buttocks ("baggy pants")
  • Weight below 60% of expected; no oedema
  • Child is alert, irritable and hungry
  • Hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, diarrhoea, infections

2. Kwashiorkor (usually 1–4 years, after weaning; protein deficiency with infection)

  • Pitting oedema – starting in the feet and legs; moon face
  • Growth failure; muscle wasting hidden by oedema
  • Mental changes – apathy, misery, irritability
  • Hair changes – thin, sparse, easily pluckable, hypopigmented; flag sign (alternate light and dark bands)
  • Skin changes – flaky-paint dermatosis, crazy-pavement skin, patches of hyper- and hypopigmentation
  • Enlarged fatty liver, anaemia, diarrhoea, vitamin deficiencies; low serum albumin

3. Marasmic kwashiorkor – features of both: severe wasting with oedema

F. Complications

  • Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance (low potassium)
  • Serious infections – septicaemia, pneumonia
  • Severe anaemia, heart failure, vitamin A deficiency (blindness), refeeding syndrome, death
  • Long-term – stunting, poor intelligence and school performance

G. Management

1. Moderate malnutrition – in the community

  • Supplementary nutrition through Anganwadi (ICDS take-home ration, hot cooked meals)
  • Energy-dense home foods – adding oil, ghee, jaggery, groundnuts to cereal–pulse mixtures
  • Treat infections, deworming, micronutrients
  • Nutrition counselling and growth monitoring every month

2. Severe acute malnutrition

  • With complications or poor appetite → admission to a Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC); treatment follows the WHO 10 steps: prevent/treat hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and dehydration (ReSoMal), correct electrolytes, treat infections, give micronutrients (iron only later), cautious feeding with F-75, catch-up growth with F-100, sensory stimulation and emotional support, and prepare for follow-up
  • Uncomplicated SAM with good appetite → community-based management with energy-dense therapeutic food and regular follow-up

H. Prevention

1. Health promotion

  • Maternal nutrition – antenatal care, IFA, take-home ration, adequate weight gain
  • Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months; timely, adequate complementary feeding
  • Birth spacing; nutrition education; improvement of sanitation and safe water

2. Specific protection

  • Immunisation (especially measles-rubella)
  • Supplementary feeding – ICDS, PM POSHAN
  • Vitamin A prophylaxis, IFA syrup/tablets, deworming, food fortification

3. Early diagnosis and treatment

  • Growth monitoring on the growth chart (MCP card); MUAC screening; checking for oedema
  • Early treatment of diarrhoea (ORS + zinc) and pneumonia
  • Prompt referral of SAM children

4. Rehabilitation – NRC care and follow-up; social support

5. Programmes – ICDS/Poshan 2.0, POSHAN Abhiyaan, NFSA/PDS, PM POSHAN, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, MAA, RBSK

I. Role of the nurse

  1. Identify malnourished children – weight, height, MUAC, oedema, growth charts
  2. Refer SAM children with complications to NRC; follow up after discharge
  3. In hospital/NRC – keep the child warm, prevent hypoglycaemia (2-hourly feeds), maintain hygiene and infection control, monitor weight, intake–output and vital signs
  4. Counsel mothers on feeding, hygiene, responsive feeding; demonstrate low-cost recipes
  5. Ensure immunisation, deworming and micronutrient supplements
  6. Work with Anganwadi workers and ASHAs; home visits; maintain records

Conclusion PEM is a spectrum of under-nutrition – from underweight to marasmus and kwashiorkor – caused by inadequate food and repeated infections against a background of poverty and poor feeding practices; it is prevented through good maternal and infant feeding, immunisation, supplementary nutrition and growth monitoring, and treated in the community or NRCs with the active involvement of nurses.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Differentiate between kwashiorkor and marasmus.
answer_html:
Point Kwashiorkor Marasmus
Main deficiency mainly protein (with infection) mainly energy (calories)
Usual age 1–4 years (after weaning) below 1 year
Oedema present – feet, legs, face absent
Wasting moderate – hidden by oedema severe – "skin and bones"
Face moon face old-man (wizened) face
Mental state apathetic, miserable alert, irritable
Appetite poor good (hungry)
Hair thin, sparse, pluckable, flag sign usually normal or thin
Skin flaky-paint dermatosis dry, loose skin folds
Liver enlarged (fatty) normal
Serum albumin very low normal or slightly low
Weight-for-age 60–80% below 60%
Prognosis higher mortality if untreated better with feeding

Common to both: growth failure, diarrhoea, infections and associated vitamin deficiencies; both are forms of severe acute malnutrition and need urgent nutritional rehabilitation.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is osteomalacia?
answer_html:
Definition Osteomalacia is the softening of bones in adults due to defective mineralisation of bone, caused mainly by deficiency of vitamin D (and/or calcium or phosphate). It is the adult form of rickets.

Common in

  • Women with repeated pregnancies and prolonged lactation, women who stay indoors or are fully covered
  • Elderly, housebound people; patients with malabsorption, liver or kidney disease, or on anticonvulsants

Features

  • Diffuse bone pain and tenderness – pelvis, spine, ribs, legs
  • Proximal muscle weakness – difficulty climbing stairs, waddling gait
  • Fractures, pseudo-fractures (Looser's zones); deformity of the pelvis may cause obstructed labour

Investigations: low calcium and phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase, low vitamin D.

Treatment: vitamin D and calcium supplements, sunlight exposure, calcium-rich diet.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Name the iron and iodine deficiency diseases.
answer_html:
A. Iron deficiency diseases

  1. Iron-deficiency anaemia – microcytic, hypochromic anaemia; pallor, fatigue, breathlessness
  2. Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), angular stomatitis, glossitis
  3. Pica – craving to eat mud, chalk or ice
  4. Plummer–Vinson syndrome – difficulty in swallowing (rare)
  5. Reduced work capacity, poor learning and cognition in children
  6. In pregnancy – low birth weight, preterm birth, maternal deaths

B. Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD)

  1. Goitre (enlarged thyroid) – the commonest visible sign
  2. Hypothyroidism
  3. Cretinism – intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, short stature, spastic gait
  4. Abortions, stillbirths, congenital anomalies
  5. Low IQ, poor school performance, impaired mental function
  6. Neonatal hypothyroidism

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is scurvy?
answer_html:
Definition Scurvy is a disease caused by deficiency of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), which leads to defective collagen formation and weak blood vessels.

Features in adults

  • Swollen, spongy, bleeding gums; loosening of teeth
  • Perifollicular haemorrhages, petechiae, easy bruising, corkscrew hairs
  • Poor wound healing; old wounds may reopen
  • Joint pain and swelling (bleeding into joints), anaemia, weakness

Infantile scurvy (Barlow's disease) – 6–12 months, babies fed only boiled or formula milk

  • Painful swelling of the legs; baby lies in "frog position" (pseudoparalysis)
  • Scorbutic rosary; subperiosteal bleeding

Treatment: vitamin C (about 100–300 mg/day for children, more for adults) until recovery; amla, guava, citrus fruits.

Prevention: fresh fruits and vegetables daily; proper cooking practices.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain severe acute malnutrition (SAM) – criteria and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is the most serious form of under-nutrition in children. Children with SAM are about nine times more likely to die than well-nourished children, but with correct treatment most recover.

A. Criteria (children 6–59 months) – any one of

  1. Weight-for-height (length) below –3 SD of WHO growth standards
  2. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below 11.5 cm
  3. Bilateral pitting oedema (nutritional)

B. Assessment

  • Appetite test and check for medical complications – lethargy, inability to drink, convulsions, hypothermia, severe dehydration, severe anaemia, pneumonia, high fever, extensive skin lesions, severe oedema
  • SAM with complications, failed appetite test or infants below 6 months → facility-based care in a Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC)
  • Uncomplicated SAM with good appetite → community-based management (CMAM)

C. Facility-based management – WHO 10 steps

Stabilisation phase (days 1–7)

  1. Treat/prevent hypoglycaemia – blood glucose below 54 mg/dl → 50 ml of 10% glucose or sugar solution; feed every 2 hours, day and night
  2. Treat/prevent hypothermia – keep warm, kangaroo care, cover including the head, warm room
  3. Treat/prevent dehydration – use ReSoMal (low-sodium ORS for malnourished children) orally or by NG tube; avoid IV fluids except in shock
  4. Correct electrolyte imbalance – extra potassium and magnesium; restrict sodium
  5. Treat infections – give broad-spectrum antibiotics to all; measles vaccination if due
  6. Correct micronutrient deficiencies – vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, copper, multivitamins; do not give iron in this phase
  7. Start cautious feeding – F-75 (75 kcal/100 ml), about 130 ml/kg/day (100 ml/kg if oedema), in small frequent feeds

Rehabilitation phase (weeks 2–6)

  1. Achieve catch-up growth – change to F-100 (100 kcal/100 ml) or therapeutic food; 150–220 kcal/kg/day; target weight gain more than 10 g/kg/day; start iron
  2. Provide sensory stimulation and emotional support – play therapy, mother's involvement, loving care

Follow-up

  1. Prepare for follow-up after recovery – teach the mother feeding and care; discharge when oedema has gone, weight gain is satisfactory (about 15%) and the child is well; follow-up visits after discharge

D. Community-based management

  • Energy-dense therapeutic or home-made foods, oral antibiotics, weekly or fortnightly follow-up by Anganwadi workers/ASHAs; referral if the child worsens

E. Nursing responsibilities

  • Screening with MUAC tapes and checking for oedema
  • 2-hourly feeding, accurate preparation of F-75/F-100, recording intake and daily weight
  • Keeping the child warm, preventing infections, monitoring for refeeding problems (oedema, breathlessness, fast pulse)
  • Counselling and training mothers; ensuring follow-up and linking with ICDS

Conclusion SAM is diagnosed by weight-for-height below –3 SD, MUAC below 11.5 cm or bilateral oedema; complicated cases are treated in NRCs using the WHO 10 steps in stabilisation and rehabilitation phases, while uncomplicated cases are managed in the community.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain calcium deficiency – causes, effects, prevention and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Calcium is essential for bones, teeth, muscle contraction, nerve conduction and blood clotting. Normal serum calcium is 8.5–10.5 mg/dl. Long-term low intake mainly affects bones, while a sudden fall in blood calcium affects nerves and muscles.

A. Causes

  1. Low dietary intake – diets low in milk and milk products, ragi and green leafy vegetables
  2. Vitamin D deficiency – lack of sunlight; poor absorption of calcium
  3. Increased needs – pregnancy, lactation, growth in childhood and adolescence
  4. Poor absorption – phytates and oxalates (excess bran, spinach), malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea
  5. Increased loss – high salt and caffeine intake, some diuretics
  6. Hormonal – menopause (low oestrogen), hypoparathyroidism (e.g. after thyroid surgery)
  7. Kidney and liver disease – vitamin D not activated
  8. Drugs – corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, long-term antacids (PPIs)
  9. Old age, inactivity, alcohol, smoking

B. Effects

1. Chronic deficiency – bone disorders

  • Rickets in children – soft, deformed bones
  • Osteomalacia in adults – bone pain, weakness
  • Osteoporosis – reduced bone mass; fractures of hip, spine and wrist in the elderly and post-menopausal women
  • Poor teeth, delayed dentition, dental caries

2. Acute fall in blood calcium (hypocalcaemia)

  • Tetany – tingling around the mouth and fingers, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
  • Chvostek's sign (twitching of facial muscles on tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm with BP cuff)
  • Laryngospasm, convulsions, cardiac arrhythmias (prolonged QT)

3. In pregnancy

  • Higher risk of pre-eclampsia, maternal bone loss, poor fetal bone mineralisation

C. Investigations

  • Serum calcium (total and ionised), phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D, parathyroid hormone; X-ray and bone density (DEXA) scan

D. Prevention

  1. Calcium-rich diet – milk, curd, paneer, buttermilk, ragi, sesame seeds (til), green leafy vegetables (amaranth, drumstick leaves, methi), soya, small fish eaten with bones, almonds
  2. Requirement – 1,000 mg/day for adults (ICMR-NIN 2020)
  3. Vitamin D – sunlight; fortified milk and oil
  4. Weight-bearing exercise – walking, yoga
  5. Limit cola drinks, excess salt and caffeine; avoid smoking and alcohol
  6. Calcium supplementation in pregnancy and lactation – 500 mg twice daily from the second trimester to 6 months after delivery

E. Management

  • Treat the cause; oral calcium and vitamin D supplements as prescribed
  • Acute tetany – IV 10% calcium gluconate given slowly with cardiac monitoring

F. Nurse's role

  • Diet counselling; ensure supplement compliance (calcium not taken with iron)
  • Watch for tetany after thyroid surgery; keep calcium gluconate ready
  • Fall prevention in elderly with osteoporosis

Conclusion Calcium deficiency results from low intake, lack of vitamin D, increased needs and poor absorption; it causes rickets, osteomalacia and osteoporosis in the long term and tetany when blood calcium falls suddenly, and is prevented by a calcium-rich diet, sunlight, exercise and supplementation in pregnancy.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the role of the nurse in the prevention and control of iodine deficiency disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD) are the world's leading preventable cause of brain damage. Iodine is needed for thyroid hormones, which control metabolism and brain development. Soils in many parts of India, especially hilly and flood-prone regions, are poor in iodine, so the whole population is considered at risk. Daily requirement is 150 µg for adults, 220–250 µg in pregnancy.

A. Spectrum of IDD (in brief)

  • Fetus – abortion, stillbirth, congenital anomalies, cretinism
  • Newborn – neonatal goitre, neonatal hypothyroidism
  • Child and adolescent – goitre, impaired mental and physical development, low IQ
  • Adult – goitre, hypothyroidism, impaired mental function

B. Role of the nurse

1. Health education

  • Explain the importance of iodised salt to families, pregnant women, schools and community groups
  • Teach correct storage – airtight container, away from moisture, heat and sunlight; buy packed iodised salt; add salt after cooking
  • Explain that non-iodised salt is banned for human consumption
  • Observe Global IDD Prevention Day (21 October) with awareness activities

2. Promotion and monitoring of iodised salt

  • Test household and shop salt using salt testing kits (STK); train ASHAs and school children to test
  • Encourage shopkeepers to sell only iodised salt; report sale of non-iodised salt

3. Surveys and screening

  • Assist in goitre surveys of school children (6–12 years) by palpation and grading
  • Help collect urine samples for urinary iodine estimation
  • Support newborn screening (TSH) for congenital hypothyroidism

4. Care of vulnerable groups

  • Pregnant and lactating women – ensure iodised salt and iodine-rich foods (seafood, milk, eggs); counsel on the effect of iodine deficiency on the baby's brain
  • Adolescent girls – education before marriage and pregnancy

5. Early detection, referral and follow-up

  • Identify persons with goitre, hypothyroidism or cretinism; refer for evaluation
  • Ensure regular thyroxine therapy and follow-up when prescribed

6. Implementation of NIDDCP activities

  • Participate in surveys, IEC campaigns, monitoring and record keeping
  • Coordinate with PHC, Anganwadi workers, schools, panchayats and NGOs

7. Community mobilisation and research

  • Involve local leaders, self-help groups and teachers
  • Participate in surveillance and research on IDD

C. Expected outcomes

  • More than 90% households using adequately iodised salt (15 ppm or more)
  • Reduction of goitre prevalence below 5% in school children
  • Normal urinary iodine levels in the community

Conclusion The nurse prevents and controls iodine deficiency disorders through education on use and storage of iodised salt, salt testing, goitre surveys, care of pregnant women, early detection and referral, and active participation in the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain childhood obesity – causes, consequences, prevention and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Childhood obesity is an excessive accumulation of body fat in children that harms health. It is increasing rapidly in India, especially in urban and affluent families, and often continues into adult life.

A. Definition and assessment

  • Children 5–19 years (WHO): BMI-for-age above +1 SD – overweight; above +2 SD – obesity
  • Under 5 years: weight-for-height above +2 SD – overweight; above +3 SD – obesity
  • IAP growth charts are used for Indian children; waist circumference indicates abdominal fat
  • NFHS-5: 3.4% of children under five are overweight (up from 2.1% in NFHS-4)

B. Causes and risk factors

  1. Unhealthy diet – junk and fast foods, fried snacks, sugar-sweetened drinks, sweets, large portions
  2. Physical inactivity – little outdoor play, travel by vehicle
  3. Screen time – TV, mobile phones, video games (more than 2 hours a day); eating while watching screens
  4. Inadequate sleep
  5. Family factors – obese parents, family eating habits, using food as reward, overfeeding
  6. Genetic tendency
  7. Socio-economic – urban affluence; aggressive food advertising
  8. Psychological – stress and emotional eating
  9. Medical (uncommon) – hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, steroids, genetic syndromes

C. Consequences

  • Physical – type 2 diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, fatty liver, sleep apnoea, asthma, flat feet and knock knees, early puberty, PCOS in girls
  • Psychological – low self-esteem, teasing and bullying, depression, poor school performance
  • Long-term – adult obesity and heart disease

D. Prevention and management (family-based lifestyle change, not strict dieting)

  1. Healthy diet
    • regular meals including breakfast; family meals without TV
    • more vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses; low-fat milk
    • limit junk food, fried snacks, sweets and sugary drinks; water instead of soft drinks
    • age-appropriate portions; do not use food as reward
  2. Physical activity – at least 60 minutes daily of active play, sports, cycling, yoga
  3. Limit recreational screen time to under 2 hours; no screens in the bedroom
  4. Adequate sleep (9–12 hours for school children)
  5. Behaviour change – goal setting, praise, involving the whole family
  6. School measures – healthy canteens, physical education, nutrition education; FSSAI restricts sale and advertising of high-fat, sugar and salt foods near schools ("Eat Right School")
  7. Medical treatment – rarely drugs or surgery in severe adolescent obesity, under specialists
  8. Screening and treatment of complications – BP, blood sugar, lipids

E. Nurse's role

  • Measure height, weight and BMI of children regularly (school health)
  • Counsel parents on diet, activity and screen time; promote breastfeeding in infancy
  • Health education in schools; support the child's self-esteem; refer for evaluation

Conclusion Childhood obesity, defined by BMI-for-age above +2 SD, results mainly from unhealthy diets, inactivity and screen time; it leads to diabetes, hypertension and psychological problems, and is best prevented and managed by family-based changes in diet, activity, sleep and school environment.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain vitamin A deficiency – clinical features, treatment and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) is the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness and also increases illness and death from measles, diarrhoea and respiratory infections. Pre-school children are most affected.

A. Causes

  • Diets poor in vitamin A – few green leafy vegetables, yellow fruits, milk, eggs
  • Low fat intake (needed for absorption)
  • Protein-energy malnutrition and zinc deficiency
  • Infections – measles, diarrhoea, respiratory infections, worms
  • Not giving colostrum; early stopping of breastfeeding
  • Poverty and lack of awareness

B. Eye changes – WHO classification of xerophthalmia

Code Sign
XN Night blindness – earliest symptom
X1A Conjunctival xerosis – dry, wrinkled conjunctiva
X1B Bitot's spots – foamy, triangular white spots on the conjunctiva
X2 Corneal xerosis – dry, hazy cornea
X3A Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia – less than one-third of the cornea
X3B Keratomalacia – one-third or more of the cornea (melting of cornea)
XS Corneal scar – permanent blindness
XF Xerophthalmic fundus

C. Other features

  • Rough, dry skin with follicular hyperkeratosis
  • Frequent infections, poor growth, anaemia
  • Higher child mortality

D. Treatment (WHO schedule)

  • Oral vitamin A on day 0 (diagnosis), day 1 and day 14:
    • below 6 months – 50,000 IU
    • 6–12 months – 1,00,000 IU
    • above 12 months – 2,00,000 IU
  • Women of reproductive age with night blindness or Bitot's spots – low daily or weekly doses (no high single dose, as it may harm a fetus)
  • Eye care – antibiotic ointment for corneal ulcers, protect eyes; treat measles, diarrhoea and malnutrition

E. Prevention

  1. Short-term – biannual high-dose vitamin A prophylaxis for children 9 months to 5 years (national programme)
  2. Medium-term – fortification of edible oil and milk with vitamin A (+F logo)
  3. Long-term – dietary diversification: green leafy vegetables, carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango, milk, eggs; kitchen gardens
  4. Breastfeeding and colostrum
  5. Measles immunisation, diarrhoea control, deworming
  6. Nutrition education – cooking vegetables with a little oil

F. Nurse's role

  • Ask about night blindness; examine eyes for Bitot's spots in children
  • Give vitamin A doses correctly and record them
  • Educate mothers on vitamin A-rich foods; refer eye changes urgently

Conclusion Vitamin A deficiency progresses from night blindness to Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis and keratomalacia, leading to blindness; it is treated with high-dose vitamin A on days 0, 1 and 14, and prevented by prophylaxis, fortification and a diet rich in green and yellow vegetables and fruits.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the deficiency disorders of B-complex vitamins.
answer_html:
Introduction B-complex vitamins are water-soluble and are not stored (except B₁₂), so deficiency develops when the diet is poor for some time. Deficiencies are common with polished-rice and maize diets, alcoholism, poverty and malabsorption, and often occur together.

1. Thiamine (B₁) deficiency – beriberi

  • Causes – diets of highly polished rice, repeated washing of rice and discarding cooking water, alcoholism, chronic diarrhoea, hyperemesis
  • Dry beriberi – peripheral neuropathy: numbness, burning feet, muscle wasting, foot drop, difficulty rising from squatting
  • Wet beriberi – cardiac: oedema, breathlessness, palpitation, enlarged heart, heart failure
  • Infantile beriberi – breastfed infants (2–6 months) of deficient mothers: hoarse or absent cry, vomiting, cyanosis, heart failure, sudden death
  • Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome (alcoholics) – confusion, ataxia, eye-muscle palsy; memory loss
  • Treatment – thiamine (injection in severe cases, before giving glucose in alcoholics); whole grains, parboiled rice, pulses

2. Riboflavin (B₂) deficiency – ariboflavinosis

  • Angular stomatitis (cracks at the corners of the mouth), cheilosis, glossitis (magenta tongue)
  • Seborrhoeic dermatitis around the nose, photophobia, corneal vascularisation, scrotal dermatitis
  • Causes – diets low in milk and green leafy vegetables
  • Treatment – riboflavin, milk, green leafy vegetables

3. Niacin (B₃) deficiency – pellagra

  • "3 Ds" – dermatitis (on sun-exposed parts; Casal's necklace around the neck), diarrhoea, dementia; untreated – death (4th D)
  • Causes – maize- or jowar-based diets, alcoholism, carcinoid syndrome, Hartnup disease, isoniazid
  • Treatment – nicotinamide; groundnuts, pulses, meat, milk

4. Pyridoxine (B₆) deficiency

  • Peripheral neuropathy, convulsions in infants, microcytic anaemia, glossitis
  • Common with isoniazid therapy – prevented by giving pyridoxine with INH

5. Folic acid deficiency

  • Megaloblastic anaemia, glossitis, diarrhoea
  • In pregnancy – neural tube defects in the baby
  • Causes – poor diet, overcooking, pregnancy, malabsorption, alcohol, drugs (phenytoin, methotrexate)

6. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency

  • Megaloblastic anaemia with neurological features – tingling, numbness, loss of position sense, memory loss (subacute combined degeneration)
  • Causes – strict vegetarian diet, pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, ileal disease, metformin
  • Treatment – B₁₂ injections

Summary table

Vitamin Disease Key features
B₁ beriberi neuropathy, heart failure
B₂ ariboflavinosis angular stomatitis, glossitis
B₃ pellagra dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia
B₆ – neuropathy, fits
Folate megaloblastic anaemia neural tube defects
B₁₂ megaloblastic anaemia neurological damage

Prevention

  • Whole grains, parboiled or less-polished rice, pulses, milk, eggs, groundnuts, green leafy vegetables
  • Avoid repeated washing of rice and discarding cooking water
  • Supplements for pregnant women, alcoholics, TB patients and the elderly; reduce alcohol

Conclusion Deficiencies of B-complex vitamins cause beriberi (B₁), ariboflavinosis (B₂), pellagra (B₃), neuropathy (B₆) and megaloblastic anaemia (folate and B₁₂); they are prevented by a varied diet of whole grains, pulses, milk and vegetables and by correct cooking practices.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain rickets – causes, clinical features, treatment and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Rickets is a disease of growing children in which the bones are not properly mineralised, mainly due to deficiency of vitamin D (and/or calcium). Bones become soft and deformed. It is commonest between 6 months and 2 years of age.

A. Causes

  1. Lack of sunlight – infants kept indoors or fully covered, pollution, winter, dark skin
  2. Low dietary vitamin D and calcium
  3. Exclusively breastfed babies of vitamin D-deficient mothers without supplementation
  4. Prematurity (low stores)
  5. Malabsorption – coeliac disease, chronic diarrhoea
  6. Liver and kidney disease (renal rickets); anticonvulsant drugs
  7. Genetic forms (vitamin D-resistant rickets)

B. Clinical features

1. Head

  • Craniotabes – soft skull bones that dent on pressure (ping-pong ball feel)
  • Frontal and parietal bossing (square head)
  • Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle; delayed teething, dental caries

2. Chest

  • Rickety rosary – beading at the junction of ribs and cartilages
  • Harrison's sulcus – a groove along the lower chest
  • Pigeon chest

3. Limbs

  • Widening of wrists and ankles
  • Bow legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum) after the child starts walking

4. Spine and pelvis

  • Kyphosis, scoliosis; pelvic deformity (in girls may cause obstructed labour later)

5. General

  • Delayed motor milestones (sitting, standing, walking), hypotonia, pot belly
  • Irritability, sweating of the head, frequent respiratory infections
  • Fractures; tetany or convulsions due to low calcium; short stature

C. Investigations

  • Serum calcium normal or low, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, 25(OH) vitamin D low, PTH high
  • X-ray of wrist – cupping, fraying and splaying of the ends of long bones

D. Treatment

  • Vitamin D as prescribed – daily oral doses (about 2,000 IU) for 3 months, or a single large oral dose (stoss therapy), followed by maintenance doses
  • Calcium about 500 mg/day
  • Sunlight, calcium-rich diet; orthopaedic correction of severe deformities later

E. Prevention

  1. Sunlight exposure of infants and children regularly
  2. Vitamin D supplementation – 400 IU/day for infants, especially breastfed and preterm babies
  3. Adequate vitamin D in pregnancy – mothers' sunlight and diet
  4. Calcium-rich foods – milk, curd, ragi, green leafy vegetables; fortified milk and oil
  5. Health education to mothers

F. Nursing points

  • Handle gently – bones fracture easily; prevent deformities by proper positioning
  • Teach mothers about sun exposure and correct supplement doses
  • Monitor growth and milestones

Conclusion Rickets is defective bone mineralisation in children due mainly to vitamin D deficiency, producing craniotabes, rickety rosary, wrist widening and bow legs; it is treated with vitamin D and calcium and prevented by sunlight, infant vitamin D supplementation and a calcium-rich diet.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain iron-deficiency anaemia – causes, clinical features, management and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Iron-deficiency anaemia (IDA) is anaemia due to insufficient iron for haemoglobin formation. It is the commonest nutritional deficiency in India – NFHS-5 found anaemia in 67% of children (6–59 months), 57% of women and 25% of men.

A. Diagnosis of anaemia (WHO haemoglobin cut-offs)

  • Children 6–59 months – below 11 g/dl
  • Children 5–11 years – below 11.5 g/dl; 12–14 years – below 12 g/dl
  • Non-pregnant women – below 12 g/dl; pregnant women – below 11 g/dl; men – below 13 g/dl

B. Causes

  1. Inadequate intake – cereal-based vegetarian diets low in iron and vitamin C
  2. Poor absorption – tea and coffee with meals, phytates, achlorhydria, malabsorption
  3. Increased requirements – infancy, adolescence (growth spurt), pregnancy
  4. Blood loss – hookworm infestation, heavy menstruation, bleeding piles, peptic ulcer
  5. Repeated pregnancies, short birth spacing
  6. Low stores at birth – prematurity, low birth weight, early cord clamping
  7. Early introduction of cow's milk in infancy; malaria and chronic infections

C. Clinical features

  • Tiredness, weakness, breathlessness on exertion, palpitation, giddiness, headache
  • Pallor of conjunctiva, tongue, palms and nail beds
  • Koilonychia (spoon nails), brittle nails, angular stomatitis, glossitis
  • Pica – eating mud, chalk, raw rice or ice
  • Poor concentration and school performance; reduced work output; frequent infections
  • Severe anaemia – tachycardia, oedema, heart failure
  • Children – irritability, poor appetite, delayed development

D. Investigations

  • Haemoglobin; red cell indices (low MCV, MCH – microcytic hypochromic); peripheral smear
  • Low serum ferritin (best indicator of iron stores), low serum iron, high TIBC
  • Stool for hookworm ova, occult blood

E. Management

  • Treat the cause – deworming (albendazole), treat bleeding
  • Oral iron – ferrous salts; children about 3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron; adults 60–120 mg/day; continue for 3 months after Hb becomes normal to refill stores
  • Take with vitamin C; avoid tea, milk and calcium with the dose
  • Parenteral iron for intolerance, poor compliance or severe anaemia
  • Blood transfusion in very severe anaemia with heart failure
  • Iron-rich diet

F. Prevention

  1. Anaemia Mukt Bharat – prophylactic IFA for children, adolescents and women; biannual deworming
  2. Dietary diversification – green leafy vegetables, pulses, millets, jaggery, meat, liver, eggs with vitamin C foods
  3. Food fortification – double-fortified salt, fortified rice and wheat flour
  4. Delayed cord clamping at birth; exclusive breastfeeding
  5. Sanitation, use of footwear and toilets to prevent hookworm; malaria control
  6. Birth spacing and adolescent health programmes

G. Nurse's role

  • Screen for anaemia (Hb testing); look for pallor at every contact
  • Counsel on IFA – take after meals, expect black stools, constipation; compliance checks
  • Diet education; deworming campaigns; follow up and refer severe cases

Conclusion Iron-deficiency anaemia, caused by low intake, poor absorption, increased needs and blood loss (especially hookworm), produces fatigue, pallor, koilonychia and poor work and school performance; it is treated with oral iron and prevented through IFA supplementation, deworming, fortification and iron- and vitamin C-rich diets.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define therapeutic diet. Write its purposes. Plan a menu for a patient with chronic kidney disease. (2 + 3 + 5)
answer_html:
A. Definition (2 marks)

  • A therapeutic diet is a modification of the normal diet to meet the special nutritional needs of a patient during illness, in order to aid treatment and recovery
  • It is prescribed by the physician, planned by the dietitian, and served and supervised by the nurse
  • Diet therapy – use of food as part of treatment

B. Purposes (3 marks)

  1. Maintain or improve nutritional status of the patient
  2. Correct nutritional deficiencies – high-protein diet in malnutrition, iron-rich diet in anaemia
  3. Maintain or attain ideal body weight – low-calorie diet in obesity, high-calorie diet in underweight
  4. Give rest to a diseased organ – low-protein diet in kidney failure, low-fat diet in gallbladder disease
  5. Adjust to the body's ability to digest, absorb and use food – diabetes, liver disease, malabsorption
  6. Remove foods that cause harm – gluten-free in coeliac disease, lactose-free in lactose intolerance
  7. Control symptoms – high-fibre for constipation, soft bland diet in gastritis
  8. Meet increased needs – fever, burns, surgery, infections
  9. Prevent complications and recurrence – kidney stones, hypertension
  10. Help in diagnosis – test diets (e.g. before certain laboratory tests)
  11. Improve comfort, morale and quality of life

Principles of therapeutic diets

  • Based on the normal balanced diet, changed only as much as necessary
  • Consider food habits, religion, economic status and likes and dislikes
  • Palatable, attractive and simple to prepare at home
  • Nutritionally adequate as far as possible; changes made gradually
  • Explain the diet to the patient and family

Types of modification

  • Consistency – liquid, soft, pureed
  • Energy – high or low calorie
  • Nutrients – protein, fat, carbohydrate, sodium, potassium, fibre, fluid
  • Frequency – small, frequent meals
  • Elimination of specific foods

C. Menu for a patient with chronic kidney disease (5 marks)

Dietary principles in CKD (not yet on dialysis)

  1. Energy – adequate (30–35 kcal/kg/day) so that body protein is not broken down; use low-protein energy sources – sugar, oil, sabudana, arrowroot, cornflour
  2. Protein – restricted to about 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day, mostly of high biological value (milk in limited amount, egg white, paneer); on dialysis, protein is increased (about 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day)
  3. Sodium – restricted (about 2 g sodium = 5 g salt or less) if oedema or hypertension – no pickles, papad, chutneys, namkeen, processed foods
  4. Potassium – restricted if serum potassium is high – avoid banana, coconut water, oranges, sweet lime, potato, tomato, dried fruits; leach vegetables (cut, soak in warm water for 2–4 hours, discard water, boil in plenty of water)
  5. Phosphorus – restricted – limit milk products, colas, nuts and processed foods; phosphate binders with meals as prescribed
  6. Fluids – in oliguria, previous day's urine output + about 500 ml
  7. Avoid salt substitutes (contain potassium) and star fruit
  8. Control blood sugar in diabetic kidney disease

Sample one-day menu – about 1,800 kcal, 40 g protein, low salt, low potassium (for a 55–60 kg adult)

Meal Menu Amount
Early morning tea with a little milk and sugar; unsalted rusk or homemade biscuit 1 cup (50 ml milk); 2 pieces
Breakfast suji upma with leached vegetables (cooked in oil, little salt) 1 plate (40 g suji)
Mid-morning apple or papaya (low-potassium fruit) 1 small / 1 slice
Lunch rice; chapati without salt; thin dal; leached bottle gourd or ridge gourd vegetable; cucumber salad 1 cup rice; 1 chapati; ½ katori dal; 1 katori vegetable
Evening sabudana khichdi or puffed rice (murmura) chivda without salt; tea 1 small bowl
Dinner chapatis; leached cabbage or cauliflower vegetable; egg-white curry or a small piece of paneer 2 chapatis; 1 katori vegetable; 1 egg white / 25 g paneer
Bedtime – (or fluids as allowed)
  • Oil about 25–30 g/day and sugar about 30–40 g/day to provide energy without protein
  • Avoid: pickles, papad, salted snacks, banana, coconut water, citrus fruits, potato, tomato excess, dry fruits, colas, salt substitutes

Nursing responsibilities

  • Daily weight, intake–output chart, BP and oedema
  • Monitor serum potassium, creatinine and urea; report high potassium
  • Educate patient and family on leaching, salt and fluid limits, measuring fluids
  • Encourage compliance while keeping meals tasty (lemon, herbs, spices instead of salt)

Conclusion A therapeutic diet is a modified normal diet used to treat disease – to correct deficiencies, rest organs, control symptoms and meet special needs; in chronic kidney disease the diet provides adequate energy with restricted protein, sodium, potassium, phosphorus and fluids, planned to remain acceptable to the patient.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the diet for a patient with constipation.
answer_html:
Introduction Constipation is infrequent (fewer than three times a week) or difficult passage of hard, dry stools. It is common in elderly, pregnant women, bedridden and post-operative patients and those on opioids, iron or antacids. Diet is the first line of management.

A. Dietary causes

  • Low fibre intake – refined foods (maida, polished rice, bakery products)
  • Low fluid intake
  • Irregular meals, skipping breakfast
  • Excess milk, cheese, fried and processed foods

B. Objectives of diet

  • Increase bulk and softness of stools
  • Stimulate peristalsis; establish a regular bowel habit

C. Dietary management

1. High-fibre diet (25–40 g/day) – increase gradually

  • Whole grains – whole wheat atta with bran (do not sieve), dalia, oats, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), brown rice
  • Whole pulses and sprouts – rajma, chana, whole moong
  • Vegetables – green leafy vegetables, beans, carrots, salads
  • Fruits with skin – guava, papaya, pear, apple, figs (anjeer), prunes, soaked raisins
  • Isabgol (psyllium husk) with a glass of water or milk at bedtime
  • Flaxseed, nuts

2. Fluids

  • 8–10 glasses (2–3 litres) of water daily
  • Warm water on rising stimulates the bowel; soups, buttermilk, juices (prune juice)

3. Probiotics – curd and buttermilk improve gut bacteria

4. Regular meals – breakfast triggers the gastrocolic reflex; small amount of oil or ghee helps

5. Foods to limit

  • Maida products, white bread, biscuits, cakes, fried and fast foods, excess tea/coffee, excess milk and cheese

D. Sample menu

  • Early morning – 1–2 glasses of warm water; soaked raisins or figs
  • Breakfast – vegetable dalia or oats porridge; a guava
  • Mid-morning – buttermilk; papaya
  • Lunch – whole-wheat chapatis, brown rice, whole dal, green leafy vegetable, salad, curd
  • Evening – sprouts chaat; water
  • Dinner – jowar or bajra roti, mixed vegetables, dal
  • Bedtime – isabgol in water or warm milk

E. Other measures

  • Exercise – walking, yoga; early ambulation after surgery
  • Regular toilet time (after breakfast); never ignore the urge
  • Privacy and proper position (squatting or footstool)
  • Review drugs causing constipation

F. Precautions

  • Increase fibre slowly to avoid bloating; always with enough water
  • In elderly and bedridden patients use soft fibre (stewed fruits, dalia, mashed vegetables)
  • High fibre is not suitable in bowel obstruction

Conclusion The diet for constipation is high in fibre from whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruits, with plenty of fluids, probiotics and regular meals, supported by exercise and a regular bowel routine.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the dietary management of diabetes mellitus.
answer_html:
Introduction Diet is the foundation of diabetes treatment. Even with drugs or insulin, good control is not possible without proper diet. The diabetic diet is a healthy balanced diet with control of quantity, type and timing of carbohydrates.

A. Objectives

  • Keep blood glucose near normal – avoid both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia
  • Achieve and maintain healthy body weight
  • Keep blood lipids and BP normal
  • Prevent or delay complications
  • Provide adequate nutrition for growth, pregnancy and activity

B. Principles

  1. Energy – according to ideal body weight and activity; reduce by about 500 kcal/day in overweight patients
  2. Carbohydrates – about 50–55% of energy, mainly complex carbohydrates with fibre and low glycaemic index; avoid simple sugars
  3. Fibre – 25–40 g/day (whole grains, pulses, vegetables, methi seeds)
  4. Protein – about 15–20% of energy (0.8–1 g/kg); restricted in diabetic kidney disease
  5. Fat – less than 30% of energy; saturated fat below 10%; no trans fat; use a mix of oils
  6. Salt – less than 5 g/day
  7. Meal pattern – 3 meals + 2–3 small snacks at regular times; consistent carbohydrate in each meal; never skip meals (especially on insulin or sulphonylureas); bedtime snack if advised
  8. Food exchange lists for variety
  9. Alcohol – avoid (risk of hypoglycaemia); sweeteners (sucralose, stevia, aspartame) in moderation

C. Foods

  • Include: whole wheat, millets (ragi, jowar, bajra), oats, dalia, whole pulses, sprouts, green leafy and other vegetables, salads, soaked methi seeds, bitter gourd, toned or skimmed milk, curd, egg white, fish, chicken, a few nuts, low-sugar fruits in moderation – guava, apple, orange, papaya, pear, jamun
  • Avoid: sugar, jaggery, honey, sweets, cakes, pastries, soft drinks, fruit juices, maida products, fried foods; limit mango, banana, chikoo, grapes, potatoes and large amounts of white rice

D. Sample day's menu (about 1,600 kcal)

  • Early morning – tea without sugar; soaked methi seeds water
  • Breakfast – 2 ragi dosas or vegetable oats upma; sambar
  • Mid-morning – guava or a small apple
  • Lunch – 2 multigrain chapatis, ½ cup rice, dal, green vegetable, salad, curd
  • Evening – roasted chana or sprouts; tea without sugar
  • Dinner – 2 chapatis, vegetable curry, dal or fish/chicken curry, salad
  • Bedtime – a glass of toned milk (if on insulin)

E. Special situations

  • Hypoglycaemia – 15 g fast sugar, then a snack
  • Sick days – continue insulin, take fluids and easily digested carbohydrates, monitor sugar
  • Exercise – extra snack before heavy exercise

F. Nurse's role

  • Teach the patient to plan meals using exchange lists and the plate method (half vegetables, a quarter whole grains, a quarter protein)
  • Teach blood glucose self-monitoring and recognition of hypoglycaemia
  • Ensure meals are served on time in relation to insulin

Conclusion The diabetic diet is a balanced, calorie-appropriate diet rich in complex carbohydrates and fibre, low in sugar and saturated fat, taken at regular times in consistent amounts, which, with exercise and drugs, keeps blood glucose, weight and lipids under control.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the dietary management of hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
answer_html:
Introduction Diet plays a major role in preventing and controlling hypertension, coronary heart disease and heart failure. The aim is to reduce BP, blood cholesterol and body weight and to lessen the workload of the heart.

A. Objectives

  • Lower BP and LDL cholesterol; raise HDL
  • Achieve healthy weight
  • Prevent atherosclerosis, heart attack and stroke
  • Reduce cardiac workload in heart disease

B. Principles

1. Restrict sodium

  • Less than 5 g of salt a day (about 2 g sodium); stricter in heart failure
  • Avoid pickles, papad, chutneys, namkeen, chips, salted butter, cheese, sauces, processed and bakery foods, ajinomoto (MSG), baking soda
  • Do not add salt at the table; flavour food with lemon, herbs, spices
  • Read food labels for sodium

2. DASH-type diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension)

  • Plenty of fruits and vegetables (rich in potassium – unless kidney disease), whole grains, pulses, nuts, low-fat dairy
  • Less red meat, sweets and sugary drinks

3. Fats

  • Total fat below 30% of energy; saturated fat below 7–10%; avoid trans fats (vanaspati, reused oil)
  • Use MUFA/PUFA oils in combination; include ω-3 – fish, flaxseed, walnuts
  • Limit ghee, butter, egg yolk, organ meats, fried foods; cholesterol below about 200 mg/day in heart disease

4. Fibre – soluble fibre (oats, barley, pulses, fruits) lowers cholesterol

5. Weight reduction if overweight – about 1 mmHg fall in BP per kg of weight lost

6. Others

  • Avoid alcohol and stop smoking; limit caffeine
  • Small, frequent meals – heavy meals increase cardiac work
  • After a heart attack – soft, light diet in small amounts for the first few days
  • Heart failure – strict salt restriction and fluid restriction (often 1–1.5 L/day) as advised

C. Sample menu (low salt, low fat)

  • Breakfast – oats porridge with toned milk or vegetable poha; fruit
  • Mid-morning – buttermilk without salt (with jeera)
  • Lunch – chapatis, rice, dal, green vegetable, salad with lemon, curd
  • Evening – sprouts or roasted chana (unsalted); tea
  • Dinner – chapatis, vegetable curry, grilled fish or dal
  • Use 3–4 teaspoons of oil for the whole day

D. Lifestyle measures

  • Regular exercise (30 minutes, most days), stress management, adequate sleep
  • Regular BP and lipid checks; drugs as prescribed

E. Nurse's role

  • Teach hidden sources of salt and fat; demonstrate low-salt cooking
  • Monitor weight, BP, intake–output and oedema in heart failure
  • Encourage adherence to diet, exercise and medicines

Conclusion Dietary management of hypertension and heart disease involves restricting salt, saturated and trans fats, increasing fruits, vegetables, whole grains and fibre, achieving healthy weight, and avoiding alcohol and smoking, with fluid restriction and small meals in heart failure.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the dietary management of obesity.
answer_html:
Introduction Obesity is excess body fat that impairs health. For Asian Indians, BMI 23–24.9 is overweight and 25 or more is obese; waist circumference above 90 cm (men) and 80 cm (women) indicates abdominal obesity. Weight reduction lowers the risk of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and joint problems.

A. Objectives

  • Gradual weight loss of about 0.5–1 kg per week (5–10% of body weight in 6 months)
  • Preserve muscle mass and nutritional adequacy
  • Develop lasting healthy habits; prevent weight regain

B. Principles of diet

  1. Calorie deficit of 500–1,000 kcal/day – usually 1,200–1,500 kcal/day for women and 1,500–1,800 kcal/day for men; not below about 1,000–1,200 kcal without medical supervision
  2. Adequate protein (1–1.2 g/kg) – gives satiety and protects muscle – pulses, sprouts, toned milk, curd, paneer, egg white, fish, chicken
  3. Complex carbohydrates and high fibre – whole grains, millets, salads, vegetables
  4. Low fat – about 20–25% of energy; measured oil (3–4 teaspoons/day)
  5. Avoid sugar, sweets, fried snacks, bakery items, soft drinks, fruit juices, alcohol
  6. Plenty of vegetables – low-calorie bulk; whole fruits instead of juice
  7. Free foods – clear soups, buttermilk, lemon water without sugar, salads, green tea
  8. Low-fat cooking methods – steaming, boiling, grilling, baking, pressure cooking

C. Eating habits (behaviour modification)

  • Small, frequent meals; never skip breakfast
  • Eat slowly, chew well; use smaller plates
  • Avoid eating while watching TV or mobile; no late-night snacking
  • Drink a glass of water before meals
  • Keep a food diary; weigh weekly; set realistic goals
  • Avoid crash or fad diets, which cause muscle loss and regain of weight

D. Sample 1,400 kcal menu

  • Early morning – lemon water or green tea
  • Breakfast – 2 vegetable besan chillas or moong dal dosa with mint chutney
  • Mid-morning – one fruit (apple/orange)
  • Lunch – 2 multigrain chapatis, dal, green vegetable, big salad, buttermilk
  • Evening – sprouts salad; tea without sugar
  • Dinner – 1–2 chapatis or a small bowl of brown rice, vegetable curry, grilled fish/paneer, salad
  • Bedtime – a small glass of toned milk (optional)

E. Physical activity and other measures

  • 150–300 minutes per week of moderate activity (brisk walking, cycling, yoga) plus muscle-strengthening exercise
  • Adequate sleep, stress management
  • Drugs or bariatric surgery only for selected severe cases under specialists

F. Nurse's role

  • Assess BMI and waist circumference; screen for diabetes and hypertension
  • Counsel on diet, activity and behaviour change; involve family
  • Provide motivation and regular follow-up; avoid blaming the patient

Conclusion Obesity is managed by a moderate calorie-deficit diet that is high in protein, fibre and vegetables and low in sugar and fat, combined with regular physical activity and behaviour change to produce slow, steady and lasting weight loss.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the dietary management of liver diseases.
answer_html:
Introduction The liver is central to the metabolism of all nutrients. In liver disease, appetite is poor, nutrients are not used well, and malnutrition is common. Proper diet helps liver cells regenerate, prevents complications and improves survival.

A. Acute viral hepatitis

  • Objectives – rest to the liver, regeneration of liver cells, maintain nutrition
  • High energy (about 35–40 kcal/kg) – mainly easily digested carbohydrates: rice, chapati, potatoes, sugar, glucose, fruits and fruit juices, sugarcane juice (hygienically prepared)
  • Adequate protein (about 1–1.2 g/kg) – milk, curd, paneer, dal, eggs, fish – unless encephalopathy develops
  • Moderate fat as tolerated – avoid fried, greasy and spicy foods
  • Small, frequent, attractive meals – nausea and anorexia are common
  • Plenty of fluids; safe boiled water (hepatitis A and E spread through water)
  • No alcohol; avoid unnecessary medicines and herbal remedies
  • Avoid unnecessary restrictions (such as banning all fat or turmeric) that worsen malnutrition

B. Cirrhosis of liver

  • Energy – 35–40 kcal/kg/day; protein – about 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day (protein is not routinely restricted)
  • Late-evening snack rich in complex carbohydrate (e.g. chapati with milk) to prevent overnight starvation
  • Small, frequent meals (4–6 per day)
  • Sodium restriction (about 2 g sodium/day) for ascites and oedema; fluid restriction only if serum sodium is very low
  • Soft foods if oesophageal varices – avoid hard, sharp foods
  • Vitamins and minerals – B-complex (thiamine), zinc, vitamin K as needed
  • Total abstinence from alcohol

C. Hepatic encephalopathy

  • Previously protein was severely restricted; now adequate protein is maintained (1.2–1.5 g/kg), preferring vegetable and dairy protein, spread through the day
  • Only brief reduction during acute severe episodes, as advised
  • Lactulose; prevent constipation, GI bleeding and infection, which raise ammonia
  • Tube feeding if the patient cannot eat

D. Foods to avoid in liver disease

  • Alcohol, fried and fatty foods, very spicy foods, pickles and salty foods (in ascites), raw or unhygienic street foods

E. Nurse's role

  • Encourage small frequent meals and record food intake
  • Monitor weight, abdominal girth, oedema, intake–output, mental status
  • Counsel on alcohol abstinence and safe water and food

Conclusion In liver disease the diet provides high energy and adequate protein in small, frequent meals, with sodium restriction in ascites, a late-evening snack in cirrhosis, and complete avoidance of alcohol; protein is no longer routinely restricted even in hepatic encephalopathy.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the dietary management of diarrhoea.
answer_html:
Introduction Diarrhoea is the passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours. It is a leading cause of illness and death in children under five. The main dangers are dehydration and malnutrition, so fluids and continued feeding are the key treatment.

A. Objectives

  • Prevent and correct dehydration and electrolyte loss
  • Maintain nutrition and prevent weight loss
  • Reduce severity and duration

B. Fluid management

  1. ORS (low-osmolarity WHO ORS) – the most important; sodium 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, osmolarity 245 mOsm/L
    • Below 2 years – 50–100 ml after each loose stool
    • 2–10 years – 100–200 ml after each loose stool
    • Older children and adults – as much as they want
    • Some dehydration – 75 ml/kg over 4 hours at the health facility
  2. Home-available fluids – rice water (kanji), dal water, buttermilk with salt, coconut water, lemon water with a pinch of salt and sugar, thin soups
  3. Avoid sugary soft drinks, packaged fruit juices, sweetened tea – they worsen diarrhoea

C. Continued feeding

  • Continue breastfeeding – more often
  • Give usual foods – soft, easily digested and energy-rich: khichdi with a little oil, curd rice, mashed potato, banana, idli, suji, dalia, boiled egg
  • Small, frequent meals (every 3–4 hours)
  • After recovery – one extra meal a day for 2 weeks (catch-up growth)
  • Avoid fried, fatty and very spicy foods, raw salads and whole pulses initially
  • Milk may be continued; curd is better tolerated; lactose-free feeds only if diarrhoea persists due to lactose intolerance

D. Zinc

  • 10 mg/day (2–6 months) and 20 mg/day (above 6 months) for 14 days

E. Diarrhoea in adults

  • ORS and clear fluids → bland, low-residue diet (khichdi, curd rice, toast, banana) → gradual return to normal diet

F. Danger signs needing referral

  • Unable to drink, repeated vomiting, blood in stools, very sunken eyes, lethargy, fever, skin pinch going back very slowly

G. Prevention

  • Handwashing with soap, safe drinking water, toilets
  • Exclusive breastfeeding, safe complementary foods, food hygiene
  • Rotavirus and measles vaccination; vitamin A

H. Nurse's role

  • Teach mothers to prepare and give ORS correctly; demonstrate feeding
  • Assess dehydration; monitor intake–output and weight
  • Counsel on zinc, hygiene and danger signs

Conclusion Dietary management of diarrhoea rests on ORS and home fluids to prevent dehydration, continued breastfeeding and feeding with soft energy-rich foods, zinc for 14 days, and an extra meal during recovery, along with hygiene measures to prevent recurrence.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the pre-operative and post-operative diet.
answer_html:
Introduction Good nutrition before and after surgery improves wound healing, resistance to infection and recovery, and reduces complications and hospital stay. Malnourished patients have more wound infections and poor healing.

A. Pre-operative diet

1. Build up nutritional status (for planned surgery)

  • High-calorie, high-protein diet for 1–2 weeks before major surgery in malnourished patients
  • Correct anaemia (iron), low albumin, vitamin deficiencies (vitamins C and K, zinc)
  • Weight reduction in obese patients where possible
  • Control blood glucose in diabetics

2. Fasting before anaesthesia (to prevent aspiration)

  • Solid food/light meal – stop about 6 hours before (8 hours for fried or fatty meals)
  • Clear fluids (water, clear juice without pulp) – allowed up to 2 hours before
  • Infants – breast milk up to 4 hours, formula up to 6 hours before
  • Avoid unnecessarily long fasting; carbohydrate drinks before surgery are used in enhanced recovery (ERAS) protocols

3. Special preparation

  • Low-residue diet and bowel preparation before bowel surgery or colonoscopy

B. Post-operative diet

1. Early feeding

  • Most patients can start oral fluids within hours and food within 24 hours of surgery (ERAS), once awake, without nausea, and with bowel activity
  • After major abdominal/GI surgery, feeding begins as advised by the surgeon

2. Progression

  • Sips of water → clear liquids (water, coconut water, clear soup, dal water, ORS, strained juice) → full liquids (milk, lassi, custard, thin porridge) → soft diet (khichdi, dalia, idli, mashed vegetables, eggs) → normal diet

3. Nutrient needs

  • Energy – about 30–35 kcal/kg/day
  • Protein – 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day or more for wound healing – milk, eggs, dal, paneer, fish
  • Vitamin C, zinc, vitamin A, iron, B-complex – collagen formation and healing
  • Fluids and electrolytes – replace losses
  • Fibre and fluids – prevent constipation from opioids and immobility

4. Special situations

  • Tonsillectomy – cold, soft foods (cold milk, ice cream, custard); avoid hot, spicy and hard foods
  • Abdominal surgery – avoid gas-forming foods initially
  • Cholecystectomy – low-fat diet at first
  • Gastrectomy – small, frequent, dry meals; avoid sweets and fluids with meals (prevent dumping syndrome)
  • If oral intake is not possible for more than 5–7 days – enteral (tube) feeding; if the gut does not work – parenteral nutrition

C. Nurse's role

  • Assess nutritional status pre-operatively; ensure correct fasting instructions
  • Check bowel sounds, nausea, and gradually advance the diet as ordered
  • Record intake–output and weight; encourage protein-rich foods
  • Monitor blood glucose in diabetics

Conclusion Pre-operative nutrition aims to correct deficiencies and follow safe fasting rules, while post-operative feeding starts early and progresses from clear liquids to a normal high-protein diet rich in vitamin C and zinc, promoting healing and quick recovery.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the types of hospital diets based on consistency.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospital diets are often modified in consistency (texture) according to the patient's ability to chew, swallow and digest. The common progression is clear liquid → full liquid → soft → normal diet.

1. Clear liquid diet

  • Foods – water, ORS, glucose water, strained clear soups, dal water, rice water, coconut water, strained fruit juice (apple, sweet lime), tea without milk, plain jelly, ice chips
  • Uses – immediately after surgery, before and after some procedures (colonoscopy), acute vomiting or diarrhoea, first feed after NPO
  • Features – provides fluid and electrolytes, leaves little residue; only about 400–600 kcal – inadequate, so used for 24–48 hours only

2. Full liquid diet

  • Foods – all clear liquids plus milk, milkshakes, lassi, buttermilk, thin strained porridges (ragi, suji), custard, thin kheer, pureed vegetable soups, ice cream, egg-nog, protein drinks
  • Uses – after clear liquids post-operatively, difficulty in chewing or swallowing (oral or jaw surgery), oesophageal disease, very weak patients
  • Features – can give 1,500–2,000 kcal if planned; feeds every 2–3 hours

3. Soft diet

  • Foods – soft, easily chewed, low-fibre, mildly seasoned: khichdi, dal-rice, curd rice, idli, upma, dalia, soft chapati soaked in dal, mashed or boiled vegetables (without skins and seeds), eggs, fish, minced chicken, banana, papaya, stewed apple, custard
  • Avoid – fried foods, raw salads, whole pulses, nuts, coarse cereals, strong spices
  • Uses – transition from liquid to normal diet, after surgery, fever, GI disturbances, elderly with chewing problems

4. Mechanical soft and pureed diets

  • Foods that are minced, mashed or blended; liquids may be thickened
  • Uses – dysphagia after stroke, dental problems, head and neck surgery
  • Textures are graded (e.g. IDDSI levels) to prevent aspiration

5. Bland diet

  • Non-irritating – no strong spices, chillies, pickles, alcohol, caffeine, not too hot or cold
  • Uses – gastritis, peptic ulcer (according to individual tolerance)

6. Low-residue diet

  • Low in fibre and residue – refined cereals, well-cooked vegetables without skins
  • Uses – before bowel surgery or colonoscopy, during flares of inflammatory bowel disease

7. Regular (normal/house) diet

  • A normal balanced diet for patients without special needs

Nursing responsibilities

  • Check the diet order and the patient's ability to chew and swallow
  • Position the patient upright; assist with feeding; observe tolerance
  • Progress the diet as ordered; record intake; explain the reason for the diet

Conclusion Hospital diets based on consistency – clear liquid, full liquid, soft, pureed, bland, low-residue and regular – are matched to the patient's condition and gradually progressed towards a normal diet.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the methods of feeding a patient – oral, enteral and parenteral.
answer_html:
Introduction When a patient cannot eat normally, nutrition must be given by the most natural route possible. The rule is: "If the gut works, use it."

A. Oral feeding (preferred)

  • Self-feeding with encouragement; oral nutritional supplements between meals if intake is poor
  • Assisted feeding for weak, elderly, blind, paralysed or stroke patients:
    • sit the patient upright (90°); protect clothing
    • give small mouthfuls, allow time to chew and swallow; alternate solids and liquids
    • check swallowing; use thickened liquids if dysphagia
    • use adaptive devices (spoons with large handles, plate guards, two-handled cups)
    • give mouth care before and after meals; make food attractive

B. Enteral (tube) feeding

  • Indications – the gut works but the patient cannot or should not eat by mouth:
    • unconscious patients, dysphagia (stroke), head and neck surgery or cancer
    • oesophageal obstruction, severe burns, severe anorexia, preterm babies
  • Routes
    • Nasogastric (NG) tube – short-term (up to 4–6 weeks)
    • Nasoduodenal/nasojejunal – when risk of aspiration is high
    • Gastrostomy (PEG) or jejunostomy – long-term
  • Feeds – blenderised kitchen feeds (milk, egg, dal water, strained cereal, oil, sugar) or commercial formulas (standard, high-protein, diabetic, renal)
  • Methods – bolus (200–400 ml by syringe or gravity every 3–4 hours), intermittent drip, or continuous by pump
  • Nursing care
    • check tube position before every feed (aspirate pH; X-ray confirms initial placement)
    • head end raised 30–45° during and for 30–60 minutes after feeding
    • give feeds at room temperature, slowly; flush with 20–30 ml water before and after feeds and medicines
    • check gastric residual volume as per policy
    • mouth and nostril care; secure the tube; record intake–output, weight, blood sugar
  • Complications – aspiration pneumonia, diarrhoea, tube blockage or displacement, nasal ulcers, dehydration, refeeding syndrome

C. Parenteral nutrition

  • Meaning – nutrients (dextrose, amino acids, lipid emulsion, electrolytes, vitamins, trace elements) given intravenously
  • Indications – non-functioning gut: intestinal obstruction, prolonged paralytic ileus, short bowel syndrome, high-output fistula, severe pancreatitis or inflammatory bowel disease; when enteral feeding is not possible for more than 5–7 days
  • Types
    • Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) – through a central venous line (high concentration)
    • Peripheral parenteral nutrition (PPN) – short-term, less concentrated, through a peripheral vein
  • Nursing care
    • strict asepsis; use a dedicated lumen; do not give other drugs through it
    • give by infusion pump at a steady rate; never stop suddenly (risk of hypoglycaemia)
    • monitor blood glucose, electrolytes, liver function, weight, intake–output, temperature
    • change bags and tubing as per policy (usually every 24 hours)
  • Complications – catheter infection and sepsis, thrombosis, pneumothorax (insertion), hyper- or hypoglycaemia, fluid overload, liver dysfunction, refeeding syndrome

D. Comparison

Point Enteral Parenteral
Route gut (tube) vein
Physiology natural; keeps gut healthy bypasses gut
Cost low high
Infection risk lower higher
Main use functioning gut non-functioning gut

Conclusion Patients are fed orally whenever possible, by tube (enteral feeding) when the gut works but oral intake is impossible, and intravenously (parenteral nutrition) only when the gut cannot be used; each method needs careful nursing care to prevent complications.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Write the dietary management of an underweight person.
answer_html:
Definition: underweight – BMI below 18.5 kg/m².

Objectives: gradual weight gain (about 0.5 kg per week), improved nutrition and strength.

Dietary management

  1. High-calorie diet – about 500 kcal/day extra
  2. High protein – 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day – milk, curd, paneer, eggs, pulses, soya, meat
  3. Energy-dense foods – ghee, oil, sugar, jaggery, nuts and dry fruits, banana, potatoes, peanut chikki
  4. Small, frequent meals (5–6 a day); milkshakes, lassi, kheer between meals
  5. Avoid filling low-calorie foods and too much water just before meals
  6. Make meals attractive; include favourite foods

Other measures

  • Treat causes – tuberculosis, worms, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, depression, poverty
  • Exercise to build muscle; vitamin and mineral supplements if needed

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is a ketogenic diet?
answer_html:
Definition A ketogenic diet is a very high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet with adequate protein, which makes the body use ketone bodies (from fat) instead of glucose as its main fuel.

Composition

  • Fat about 70–90% of energy; carbohydrate very low (often below 20–50 g/day)
  • Classical diet uses a 4 : 1 ratio of fat to protein + carbohydrate (by weight)

Uses

  • Drug-resistant epilepsy in children – reduces seizures
  • Some metabolic disorders (e.g. GLUT-1 deficiency)
  • Popular for weight loss, but long-term safety is uncertain

Side effects

  • Constipation, nausea, kidney stones, high cholesterol, poor growth in children, low blood sugar, acidosis

Note: must be started and monitored under medical and dietitian supervision.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is a gluten-free diet?
answer_html:
Definition A gluten-free diet completely excludes gluten – a protein found in wheat, barley and rye (and oats contaminated with them).

Uses

  • Coeliac disease – lifelong; gluten damages the small intestine and causes malabsorption, diarrhoea, anaemia and poor growth
  • Gluten sensitivity and dermatitis herpetiformis

Foods to avoid

  • Wheat – atta, maida, suji/rava, dalia, bread, biscuits, cakes, pasta, noodles
  • Barley, rye, malt; many processed foods, soups and sauces thickened with wheat flour

Foods allowed

  • Rice, maize, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), rajgira (amaranth), kuttu (buckwheat), sabudana, quinoa
  • Pulses, besan, potatoes, milk, eggs, meat, fish, fruits, vegetables, nuts

Points: read food labels; avoid cross-contamination (separate utensils, grinding mills).

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Write a note on the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
answer_html:
Introduction The Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Act, 1954 was enacted by the Government of India to protect consumers from adulterated and misbranded food. It came into force on 1 June 1955 along with the PFA Rules, 1955, and was amended several times (1964, 1976, 1986) to make it stricter.

A. Objectives

  1. Protect the public from poisonous and harmful foods
  2. Prevent sale of sub-standard food
  3. Protect consumers from fraud and deception (misbranding)
  4. Encourage fair trade practices

B. Adulterated food (as defined in the Act) – a food is adulterated if:

  • It is not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the buyer
  • It contains a substance that affects its quality or is injurious to health
  • A cheaper or inferior substance is substituted wholly or partly
  • A valuable constituent has been removed (e.g. cream from milk)
  • It was prepared, packed or stored under insanitary conditions
  • It is filthy, putrid, rotten, decomposed or insect-infested, or from a diseased animal
  • It contains a poisonous ingredient, a prohibited colour or preservative, or permitted ones in excess
  • Its quality or purity is below the prescribed standard

C. Administrative machinery

  1. Central Committee for Food Standards (CCFS) – advises the government on standards
  2. Central Food Laboratories – for appeals and final analysis (e.g. Kolkata, Mysore, Ghaziabad, Pune)
  3. Public Analysts – analyse samples in each state
  4. Food Inspectors – power to enter premises, take samples, seize adulterated food and launch prosecutions
  5. Local (Health) Authority – supervises implementation

D. Sampling procedure

  • The Food Inspector purchases a sample, divides it into three parts, seals and labels them:
    • one sent to the Public Analyst
    • one given to the vendor
    • one kept with the Local Health Authority
  • The vendor may have his part analysed by the Central Food Laboratory, whose report is final
  • Consumers and consumer associations could also get food analysed by paying a fee

E. Penalties

  • Imprisonment (minimum six months, extendable to three years) and fine
  • Life imprisonment when the adulterant is likely to cause death or grievous harm

F. Present status

  • The PFA Act was repealed and replaced by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which came into force on 5 August 2011; the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) now regulates food safety

G. Role of the nurse

  • Educate the public about common adulterants and simple tests
  • Encourage buying labelled, licensed foods; report suspected adulteration
  • Recognise and report outbreaks such as epidemic dropsy

Conclusion The PFA Act, 1954 defined adulteration, set food standards, created Food Inspectors and Public Analysts and prescribed strict penalties; it has now been replaced by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, administered by FSSAI.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Define food additives. Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Food additives are substances that are not normally eaten as food by themselves but are intentionally added in small amounts to food during manufacture, processing, packing or storage to improve its keeping quality, colour, flavour, texture or nutritive value.

Purposes

  • Preserve food and prevent spoilage
  • Improve colour, taste, flavour and appearance
  • Improve texture and consistency
  • Increase nutritive value (fortification)
  • Aid processing (leavening, emulsifying)

Examples

  • Preservatives – salt, sugar, vinegar, sodium benzoate, potassium metabisulphite
  • Colours – turmeric, saffron, tartrazine
  • Flavours – vanilla essence, MSG
  • Sweeteners – saccharin, sucralose
  • Antioxidants – BHA, BHT, vitamin E
  • Emulsifiers – lecithin; fortificants – iodine, iron, vitamins A and D

Regulation: only additives permitted by FSSAI within prescribed limits may be used; they are shown on labels by INS numbers.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Classify food additives with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Food additives are substances added intentionally, in small quantities, to improve the keeping quality, appearance, flavour, texture or nutritive value of foods. In India they are regulated by FSSAI (Food Products Standards and Food Additives Regulations, 2011).

Classification

1. Preservatives – prevent spoilage by microbes

  • Class I (natural) – salt, sugar, vinegar, spices, honey, oil, wood smoke
  • Class II (chemical) – sodium benzoate (squashes, sauces), potassium metabisulphite / sulphur dioxide (pickles, juices), sorbic acid, propionates (bread), nitrites (cured meats)

2. Antioxidants – prevent rancidity of fats and oils

  • BHA, BHT, propyl gallate, TBHQ; natural – vitamin E, vitamin C

3. Colouring agents

  • Natural – turmeric (curcumin), saffron, caramel, annatto, chlorophyll, beetroot
  • Permitted synthetic – tartrazine, sunset yellow, carmoisine, ponceau 4R, erythrosine, brilliant blue (within limits, about 100 ppm)
  • Non-permitted (harmful) – metanil yellow, Sudan dyes, rhodamine B, auramine

4. Flavouring agents and flavour enhancers

  • Natural – spices, herbs, vanilla; synthetic – essences (vanillin)
  • Flavour enhancer – monosodium glutamate (MSG) – not permitted in foods for infants below 12 months

5. Sweeteners

  • Nutritive – sugar, glucose, honey
  • Non-nutritive (artificial) – saccharin, aspartame, sucralose, acesulfame-K; natural – stevia
  • Not for infants; aspartame must be avoided in phenylketonuria

6. Emulsifiers and stabilisers

  • Lecithin, mono- and diglycerides, gums (guar gum, gum arabic, xanthan), pectin, agar, carrageenan, gelatine – used in ice cream, sauces, mayonnaise

7. Thickening and gelling agents – starch, pectin, agar

8. Leavening agents – baking soda, baking powder, yeast

9. Acidulants (acidity regulators) – citric acid, acetic acid (vinegar), lactic acid, tartaric acid

10. Anti-caking agents – calcium silicate, magnesium carbonate (in salt, milk powder)

11. Nutritive additives (fortificants) – iodine (salt), iron, folic acid, vitamin B₁₂ (fortified rice, wheat flour), vitamins A and D (oil, milk)

12. Others – bleaching and maturing agents for flour, humectants (glycerol), firming agents (calcium chloride), glazing and anti-foaming agents

Health concerns
