  • Allergic reactions (tartrazine, sulphites – may trigger asthma)
  • Hyperactivity in some children (synthetic colours)
  • Non-permitted colours can cause cancer and organ damage
  • Nitrites form nitrosamines (carcinogens)

Nurse's role

  • Teach people to read labels, limit packaged and brightly coloured foods, especially for children

Conclusion Food additives include preservatives, antioxidants, colours, flavours, sweeteners, emulsifiers, thickeners, leavening agents, acidulants, anti-caking agents and fortificants; only FSSAI-permitted additives within limits are safe, and non-permitted colours are harmful.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: What is food preservation? Name the methods.
answer_html:
Definition Food preservation is the process of treating and handling food to prevent or slow down spoilage (caused by microbes, enzymes, oxidation, insects and moisture) so as to extend its shelf life while retaining its nutritive value, quality and safety.

Methods

  1. Low temperature – refrigeration (0–5 °C), freezing (–18 °C)
  2. High temperature – boiling, pasteurisation of milk (63 °C for 30 minutes or 72 °C for 15 seconds), sterilisation, canning
  3. Drying/dehydration – sun drying (papad, vadi, dried fish, raisins), spray drying (milk powder)
  4. Preservatives – salt (pickles, fish), sugar (jams, murabba), vinegar, oil, smoking; chemical preservatives (sodium benzoate, potassium metabisulphite)
  5. Fermentation – curd, idli batter, pickles
  6. Irradiation – gamma rays for spices, onions, potatoes
  7. Modern packaging – vacuum packing, modified-atmosphere packaging

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Explain the methods of cooking with their advantages and disadvantages.
answer_html:
Introduction Cooking is the application of heat to food. It makes food tasty, digestible and safe, but the method chosen affects nutrient losses and fat content.

Purposes of cooking

  • Improves taste, flavour, appearance and texture
  • Makes food easier to digest (gelatinises starch, softens fibre)
  • Destroys microorganisms and natural toxins (trypsin inhibitors in pulses, avidin in raw egg white)
  • Gives variety; improves keeping quality

Methods

Method Examples Advantages Disadvantages
Boiling rice, dal, eggs, vegetables simple, cheap; food soft and digestible water-soluble vitamins and minerals lost if water is discarded
Simmering/stewing stews, curries slow cooking; nutrients stay in the liquid takes time and fuel
Steaming idli, dhokla, momos, steamed vegetables good nutrient retention; no fat; light and digestible takes longer; needs a steamer
Pressure cooking dal, rice, meat, vegetables saves time and fuel; less water and air, so better vitamin retention overcooking if not timed; safety precautions needed
Roasting chana, groundnuts, papad, sweet potato good flavour; no fat some loss of B-vitamins; charring
Baking bread, cakes, biscuits even cooking; attractive products needs an oven; loss of thiamine; often high fat/sugar products
Grilling / tandoor tandoori roti, paneer tikka, fish fat drips away; tasty charring forms harmful compounds
Shallow frying / sautéing parathas, cutlets, tadka quick, tasty adds fat and calories
Deep frying puri, pakoda, samosa quick, crisp, tasty high fat and calories, difficult to digest, vitamin loss; reused oil forms trans fats and toxic compounds
Microwave cooking reheating, steaming vegetables very fast; little water; good nutrient retention uneven heating; special containers; no browning
Solar cooking rice, dal saves fuel; no smoke slow; depends on sunlight

Healthy cooking choices

  • Prefer steaming, pressure cooking, boiling (using the water), stewing and grilling
  • Limit deep frying; do not reuse frying oil repeatedly
  • Use minimum water and short cooking times; cook with lids on

Nursing relevance

  • Advise steamed and pressure-cooked foods for patients with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and digestive problems
  • Teach families methods that save nutrients and fuel

Conclusion Moist-heat methods (boiling, steaming, pressure cooking), dry-heat methods (roasting, baking, grilling), frying and microwave cooking each have advantages and drawbacks; steaming and pressure cooking retain nutrients best, while deep frying adds fat and destroys nutrients.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Explain how nutrients are lost during preparation and cooking, and how they can be preserved.
answer_html:
Introduction A considerable part of the nutrients in food can be lost before it reaches the plate – during storage, milling, washing, cutting, cooking and serving. Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C) and minerals are most affected. Simple household practices can prevent much of this loss.

A. Causes of nutrient loss

Factor Nutrients affected
Heat (long cooking, reheating) vitamin C, thiamine, folate
Air (oxidation) vitamins C, A, E
Light riboflavin, vitamin A
Water (washing, soaking, discarding cooking water) B-vitamins, vitamin C, minerals
Alkali (baking soda) thiamine, vitamin C
Copper vessels vitamin C
Milling and polishing thiamine, fibre, minerals
Long storage vitamin C in fruits and vegetables; rancidity of fats

B. Ways to preserve nutrients

1. Storage

  • Buy fresh foods in quantities that can be used soon
  • Store vegetables in a cool place or refrigerator; keep oils in closed, dark containers
  • Keep milk away from sunlight (riboflavin)

2. Cereals and pulses

  • Do not wash rice repeatedly – wash gently once or twice
  • Do not discard rice water (kanji) – cook rice with just enough water (absorption method)
  • Use parboiled, hand-pounded or less-polished rice
  • Use whole-wheat atta without sieving the bran
  • Germinate and ferment pulses and cereals – increases vitamins

3. Vegetables and fruits

  • Wash before cutting, not after
  • Cut into large pieces just before cooking; do not soak cut vegetables
  • Peel thinly or cook with skins where possible
  • Do not keep cut vegetables or fruits exposed to air
  • Eat fruits and salads raw where safe

4. Cooking

  • Use minimum water and use the leftover water in dal, soups or gravies
  • Add vegetables to boiling water rather than cold water
  • Cook covered, for the shortest time – pressure cooking and steaming are best
  • Do not add baking soda
  • Add lemon juice after cooking
  • Avoid overcooking, repeated reheating and repeated frying in the same oil

5. Serving

  • Serve food soon after cooking; avoid keeping it hot for long hours
  • Avoid reheating leftover food many times

C. Nursing relevance

  • Teach mothers and hospital kitchen staff these practices
  • In hospitals, ensure food is cooked close to serving time and served promptly

Conclusion Nutrients, especially vitamins B and C and minerals, are lost through milling, washing, soaking, heat, air, light, alkali and discarding cooking water; washing before cutting, cooking covered for short times in little water, avoiding soda and serving promptly preserve most of them.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Explain food adulteration – common adulterants, simple tests, health hazards and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Food adulteration is the addition or removal of any substance to or from food so that its natural composition and quality are affected, making it unsafe, sub-standard or misbranded. It is done mainly for profit and is a serious public health problem in India.

A. Types

  1. Intentional – deliberate mixing of cheaper or harmful substances (water in milk, sand in spices, colours in sweets)
  2. Incidental – accidental contamination (pesticide residues, insect parts, rodent hair, droppings)
  3. Metallic contamination – lead, arsenic, mercury from containers or environment

B. Common adulterants and simple home tests (FSSAI "DART" – Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test)

Food Adulterant Simple test
Milk water a drop on a slanting surface: pure milk flows slowly leaving a white trail
Milk starch add iodine – blue colour
Milk detergent shake with water – persistent lather
Ghee / butter mashed potato, starch, vanaspati iodine test – blue colour
Turmeric metanil yellow, lead chromate add a few drops of concentrated HCl – pink/violet colour
Chilli powder brick powder, sand, colour sprinkle on water – brick powder sinks, colour streaks
Black pepper papaya seeds papaya seeds float on water/alcohol; shrunken and oval
Tea leaves used tea leaves, colour, iron filings colour spreads on wet blotting paper; magnet attracts iron
Mustard seeds argemone seeds argemone seeds are rough, black and conical
Mustard oil argemone oil nitric acid test – orange-red colour
Arhar (tur) dal khesari dal; metanil yellow khesari is wedge-shaped; HCl test for colour
Sugar chalk dissolve in water – chalk settles
Silver leaf (varak) aluminium aluminium leaf forms a grey ball on burning
Green vegetables malachite green cotton dipped in paraffin turns green when rubbed

C. Health hazards

  • Epidemic dropsy – argemone oil in mustard oil
  • Lathyrism – khesari dal
  • Cancer and organ damage – metanil yellow, Sudan dyes, lead chromate
  • Lead poisoning – lead chromate in turmeric
  • Gastrointestinal disorders, kidney and liver damage, allergies
  • Loss of nutrients – diluted milk, sub-standard foods

D. Prevention

  1. Buy from reliable shops; prefer packaged foods with the FSSAI licence number, label and expiry date
  2. Look for quality marks – AGMARK (agricultural products), ISI/BIS marks
  3. Avoid loose, unusually cheap or very brightly coloured foods
  4. Use simple home tests
  5. Report complaints to the Food Safety Officer or through the FSSAI helpline/app
  6. Strict enforcement of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006
  7. Consumer education and awareness campaigns

E. Role of the nurse

  • Educate families on recognising adulteration and buying safe foods
  • Identify and report clusters of illness (e.g. epidemic dropsy) suggesting adulteration

Conclusion Food adulteration – intentional, incidental or metallic – affects common foods such as milk, spices, oils and pulses and causes serious diseases; consumer awareness, simple tests, buying licensed and labelled products and strict enforcement of food laws prevent it.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: What is lathyrism?
answer_html:
Definition Lathyrism (neurolathyrism) is a paralytic disease of the lower limbs caused by eating large amounts of khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) for a long period (usually more than one-third of the diet for 2–6 months).

Cause: a neurotoxin, BOAA (β-N-oxalyl-amino-L-alanine), present in the dal. Khesari is drought-resistant and cheap, so it is eaten in famine or drought; it is also used to adulterate arhar dal and besan. Cases have been reported from Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and Maharashtra.

Features – spastic paraplegia in stages:

  • Latent → no-stick (stiff, jerky gait) → one-stick → two-stick → crawler stage
  • The damage is irreversible

Prevention

  • Avoid khesari as a staple; steeping (soaking in hot water and discarding the water) or parboiling removes most of the toxin
  • Vitamin C prophylaxis; low-toxin varieties; legal control of sale; health education

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: What is epidemic dropsy?
answer_html:
Definition Epidemic dropsy is a disease caused by consuming mustard oil adulterated with argemone oil. Argemone (Argemone mexicana) seeds look like mustard seeds and may be mixed accidentally or deliberately.

Toxin: sanguinarine in argemone oil.

Features

  • Bilateral pitting oedema of the legs – the main sign
  • Diarrhoea, vomiting, skin erythema and mottling
  • Breathlessness, heart failure
  • Glaucoma – may cause blindness
  • Usually affects several members of a family who use the same oil

Outbreaks: a large outbreak occurred in Delhi in 1998.

Detection: nitric acid test (orange-red colour) and paper chromatography of the oil.

Prevention and control

  • Stop the suspected oil immediately; buy packaged, branded oil
  • Legal action against adulterators; public education; surveillance of cases

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: What is food fortification? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Food fortification is the deliberate addition of one or more essential micronutrients to a food, whether or not they are normally present in it, to improve its nutritional quality and provide a public health benefit with minimal risk.

Examples in India

  1. Iodised salt – iodine (universal salt iodisation)
  2. Double-fortified salt – iodine + iron
  3. Edible oil and milk – vitamins A and D
  4. Fortified rice – iron, folic acid and vitamin B₁₂ – supplied through PDS, ICDS and PM POSHAN
  5. Fortified wheat flour (atta) – iron, folic acid, B₁₂

Regulation: FSSAI (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, 2018; fortified foods carry the "+F" logo.

Advantages

  • No change in food habits needed; reaches large populations
  • Cost-effective, safe and sustainable

Note: enrichment means restoring nutrients lost during processing, while fortification may add new ones.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: What is parboiling of rice? State its advantages.
answer_html:
Definition Parboiling is the process in which paddy (unhusked rice) is soaked in water, steamed or partially boiled and then dried before milling.

How it helps

  • During soaking and steaming, water-soluble vitamins (thiamine, niacin) and minerals move from the bran and germ into the grain (endosperm), so they are retained even after milling and polishing

Advantages

  1. Higher thiamine and niacin – helps prevent beriberi
  2. Less breakage during milling – better yield
  3. Better keeping quality; resistant to insects
  4. Cooked rice is firmer and less sticky; less nutrient loss on washing
  5. Somewhat lower glycaemic response

Disadvantages: slight change in colour, smell and taste; takes longer to cook and needs more fuel.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: Cookery Rules and Preservation of Nutrients
question: Explain the principles and methods of food preservation with household examples. Add a note on their effect on the nutritive value of food. (3 + 5 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction Food spoils because of microorganisms (bacteria, yeasts, moulds), enzymes in the food, oxidation, insects and rodents and moisture. Food preservation prevents or slows spoilage so that food remains safe, nutritious and acceptable for a longer time, reduces wastage and makes seasonal foods available throughout the year.

A. Principles of food preservation (3 marks)

  1. Prevent or delay microbial growth
    • remove water (drying)
    • lower the temperature (refrigeration, freezing)
    • raise the osmotic pressure (salt, sugar)
    • increase acidity (vinegar, lemon, fermentation)
    • exclude air (canning, vacuum packing)
    • add preservatives
  2. Destroy microorganisms – heat (boiling, pasteurisation, sterilisation), irradiation
  3. Inactivate food enzymes – blanching, heating
  4. Prevent contamination and damage – clean handling, proper packaging, protection from insects, rodents and moisture

B. Methods of preservation (5 marks)

1. Low temperature

  • Refrigeration (0–5 °C) – slows bacterial growth; milk, curd, cooked food, fruits and vegetables for short periods
  • Freezing (–18 °C or below) – stops growth; meat, fish, peas; vegetables are blanched first to inactivate enzymes
  • Thaw frozen food in the refrigerator; do not refreeze

2. High temperature

  • Boiling – milk and drinking water at home
  • Pasteurisation – milk heated to 63 °C for 30 minutes (holding method) or 72 °C for 15 seconds (flash/HTST method) and cooled quickly; kills disease-causing germs
  • UHT treatment – about 135–140 °C for a few seconds; packed aseptically (tetra packs) – long shelf life without refrigeration
  • Sterilisation and canning – food sealed in cans and heated under pressure; faulty canning can cause botulism

3. Drying (dehydration)

  • Sun drying – papad, vadi, sandge, chillies, dried fish, raisins, mango slices
  • Mechanical drying – spray-dried milk powder, dried vegetables; freeze drying for instant foods

4. Salt

  • Pickles, salted fish, amla – high salt draws water from microbes
  • Disadvantage – high sodium (harmful in hypertension and kidney disease)

5. Sugar

  • Jams, jellies, murabba, squashes, sharbat – high sugar concentration prevents growth

6. Acid

  • Vinegar pickles, lemon pickles; fermentation produces lactic acid

7. Oil

  • Covering pickles with oil keeps out air and microbes

8. Fermentation

  • Curd, idli–dosa batter, dhokla, kanji, fermented bamboo shoots – useful microbes produce acid and alcohol and suppress harmful ones

9. Smoking – fish and meat (also flavours food)

10. Chemical preservatives

  • Potassium metabisulphite (KMS) in light-coloured squashes and pickles; sodium benzoate in coloured squashes and sauces – only within FSSAI limits

11. Irradiation

  • Controlled exposure to gamma rays to prevent sprouting (onions, potatoes) and kill insects and microbes (spices); irradiated foods carry the Radura symbol

12. Modern packaging

  • Vacuum packing, modified-atmosphere packaging, aseptic packaging

13. Household storage of grains and pulses

  • Clean and sun-dry before storage; store in airtight bins off the floor
  • Traditional methods – neem leaves, coating pulses with a little oil; protect from rats and moisture

C. Effect on nutritive value (2 marks)

  • Refrigeration and freezing – retain most nutrients; small losses of vitamin C during blanching and long storage
  • Heat processing (canning, boiling) – losses of vitamin C, thiamine and folate; proteins become more digestible
  • Pasteurisation – small loss of vitamin C and B-vitamins; protein and calcium unaffected
  • Sun drying – large losses of vitamin C and carotene; minerals concentrated
  • Salting – adds sodium; sugar preserves – add empty calories
  • Fermentation – increases B-vitamins, improves digestibility, reduces phytates
  • Irradiation – minor vitamin losses at permitted doses
  • Milling and polishing (processing) – loss of thiamine and fibre

Nursing relevance

  • Teach families safe home preservation and storage; caution about salty pickles for hypertensive and renal patients
  • Recognise risks – botulism from bulging cans, mould on stored grains (aflatoxin)

D. Signs of spoilage – when food should be discarded

  • Bulging, leaking or rusted cans; spurting liquid on opening
  • Mould growth, unusual colour or slime on food
  • Sour or putrid smell, frothing or gas in pickles and sauces
  • Discoloured or musty grains and groundnuts (risk of aflatoxin)
  • Curdling of milk on boiling, off-flavour

E. Choosing a method

  • Depends on the type of food, storage period needed, cost and facilities available, and the effect on nutrients and safety
  • Short-term storage – refrigeration; long-term – drying, canning, freezing

F. Advantages of food preservation – prevents wastage, makes seasonal foods available all year, reduces cost, supports food security and trade, and provides convenient, safe foods during travel and disasters.

Conclusion Food preservation is based on preventing microbial growth, destroying microbes, inactivating enzymes and preventing contamination, using methods such as refrigeration, heating, drying, salting, sugaring, fermentation, preservatives and irradiation; each method affects nutrients differently, so it should be chosen and used wisely.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the principles and methods of nutrition education. Plan a nutrition education session for a group of antenatal mothers. (4 + 3 + 3)
answer_html:
Introduction Nutrition education is the process of helping people gain knowledge, develop positive attitudes and adopt healthy food practices voluntarily, so that their nutritional status improves. Food habits are deeply rooted in culture; changing them needs patience and a planned approach. Nurses, ANMs, Anganwadi workers and ASHAs are the main nutrition educators in India.

A. Principles of nutrition education (4 marks)

  1. Know the audience – their needs, interests, beliefs, literacy, income and local foods
  2. Felt needs and relevance – start with problems people consider important (e.g. a child who is not gaining weight)
  3. Known to unknown, simple to complex – build on existing knowledge and practices
  4. Simple, clear and practical messages in the local language, using local foods and recipes
  5. Few messages at a time – focus on 2–3 key actions
  6. Active participation – discussion, questions, demonstrations, return demonstrations
  7. Learning by doing – cooking demonstrations, preparing ORS
  8. Motivation and reinforcement – praise, recognition, examples of healthy children ("positive deviance")
  9. Respect for culture – retain good traditional practices; change harmful ones tactfully
  10. Affordability and feasibility – advice must fit the family's budget and resources
  11. Credibility and consistency – the same messages from all health workers
  12. Repetition through different channels
  13. Involvement of leaders – local leaders, elders, teachers, SHG members, mothers-in-law
  14. Evaluation and feedback – check understanding and practice

B. Methods and media (3 marks)

1. Individual methods

  • Counselling at antenatal clinics, immunisation sessions, NRCs and home visits
  • Most effective for behaviour change; allows personalised advice

2. Group methods

  • Talks/lectures, group discussions, demonstrations (cooking, recipe preparation, IYCF), role plays, puppet shows, workshops, exhibitions, field visits
  • Community events – Godh Bharai, Annaprashan, Poshan Maah (September), National Nutrition Week (1–7 September), World Breastfeeding Week (1–7 August)

3. Mass methods

  • Radio, TV, newspapers, posters, hoardings, films
  • Internet, social media and mobile messages
  • Folk media – street plays (nukkad natak), songs, kirtans, puppetry

Audio-visual aids

  • Food models and real foods, flash cards, flip charts, posters, flannel graphs, MCP card, charts, videos

C. Steps in planning a nutrition education programme

  1. Assess needs – nutritional problems, food habits, resources of the group
  2. Set objectives – general and specific (knowledge, attitude, practice)
  3. Select content – simple, relevant messages
  4. Choose methods and aids
  5. Implement – at a convenient time and place
  6. Evaluate – questions, return demonstrations, follow-up of practices (weight gain, IFA intake)

D. Plan of a nutrition education session for antenatal mothers (3 marks)

  • Topic: Nutrition during pregnancy
  • Group: 15 antenatal mothers at an Anganwadi centre / PHC
  • Duration: 45 minutes
  • Educator: nursing student / staff nurse
  • AV aids: real foods, food models, flash cards, MCP card, IFA and calcium tablets, a low-cost recipe demonstration
  • General objective: mothers will understand the importance of good nutrition in pregnancy and adopt healthy dietary practices
  • Specific objectives – at the end of the session, mothers will be able to:
    1. explain why good nutrition is important in pregnancy
    2. state the extra food needed daily
    3. identify local iron-, calcium- and protein-rich foods
    4. describe the correct way to take IFA and calcium tablets
    5. list foods and practices to avoid
Time Specific objective Content Teaching–learning activity AV aid Evaluation
5 min introduction greeting; ask about their usual diet discussion – participation
8 min 1 healthy baby, prevents anaemia and low birth weight, strength for delivery and breastfeeding explanation with examples flash cards "Why should a pregnant woman eat more?"
8 min 2 one extra meal or snack daily; more milk, dal, vegetables, fruits; weight gain of 10–12 kg discussion food models "How much extra food do you need?"
10 min 3 iron – green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates, bajra; calcium – milk, curd, ragi, til; protein – dal, eggs, groundnuts, soya show real foods; cooking demonstration of green moong–spinach khichdi real foods mothers name three local iron-rich foods
7 min 4 IFA daily after meals for 180 days with lemon water; calcium separately; black stools are normal; deworming demonstration with tablets IFA, calcium tablets, MCP card return explanation
5 min 5 avoid tobacco, alcohol, excess tea with meals, unsafe food; no fasting; correct food taboos discussion posters "What should you avoid?"
2 min summary key messages repeated question–answer – –

E. Evaluation

  • Immediate – oral questions, return demonstration
  • Follow-up – home visits to check diet, IFA compliance (tablet count), weight gain and Hb

F. Role of the nurse

  • Plan regular sessions; use local foods and language; involve family members, especially husbands and mothers-in-law
  • Link mothers with ICDS take-home ration and PMMVY benefits

Conclusion Nutrition education follows principles of relevance, simplicity, participation, cultural respect and repetition, and uses individual, group and mass methods with suitable aids; a well-planned session for antenatal mothers, with demonstrations and follow-up, can improve their diet, IFA intake and pregnancy outcomes.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the methods of nutritional assessment.
answer_html:
Introduction Nutritional assessment is the evaluation of the nutritional status of individuals or communities. The main methods are remembered as "ABCD" – Anthropometry, Biochemical, Clinical and Dietary – supported by vital statistics and ecological study.

A. Anthropometry (body measurements)

  • Weight, length/height, head and chest circumference, MUAC, skinfold thickness, waist and hip circumference
  • Indices – weight-for-age (underweight), height-for-age (stunting), weight-for-height (wasting), BMI
  • Compared with WHO growth standards using growth charts and Z-scores
  • Advantages – simple, cheap, objective; limitation – does not identify specific nutrient deficiencies

B. Biochemical (laboratory) assessment

  • Haemoglobin (anaemia), serum ferritin (iron stores)
  • Serum albumin, total protein (protein status)
  • Serum retinol (vitamin A), 25(OH) vitamin D, vitamin B₁₂, folate
  • Urinary iodine (iodine status)
  • Blood glucose, lipid profile; stool for parasites
  • Advantages – objective, detects sub-clinical deficiency early; limitations – costly, needs laboratory facilities

C. Clinical examination

  • Head-to-toe examination for signs of malnutrition – hair (pluckable, flag sign), eyes (Bitot's spots), lips (angular stomatitis), tongue (glossitis), gums (bleeding), thyroid (goitre), skin (dermatosis), nails (koilonychia), oedema, bone deformities
  • Advantages – simple, quick, no equipment; limitations – signs appear late, are non-specific and subjective

D. Dietary assessment

  • 24-hour dietary recall, food frequency questionnaire, diet history, food diary, weighment method (household diet survey)
  • Nutrient intake calculated from food composition tables and compared with RDA
  • Advantages – shows the cause and helps plan interventions; limitations – depends on memory and honesty

E. Vital and health statistics

  • Infant and under-five mortality, 1–4 year mortality (a sensitive indicator of malnutrition), low birth weight rate, morbidity from diarrhoea, measles and respiratory infections

F. Assessment of ecological factors

  • Food production and availability, food prices, income, socio-cultural practices, sanitation, health services, infections

G. Other methods

  • Functional tests – hand-grip strength, dark adaptation test
  • Radiology – rickets, scurvy
  • Screening tools – Subjective Global Assessment (SGA), MUST, Mini Nutritional Assessment (elderly)

Nursing relevance

  • Nurses measure weight, height and MUAC, examine for clinical signs, take diet histories and collect blood and urine samples

Conclusion Nutritional status is assessed by anthropometry, biochemical tests, clinical examination and dietary surveys, supplemented by vital statistics and ecological factors; combining these methods gives the most accurate picture.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the purposes of nutrition education.
answer_html:
Introduction Nutrition education helps people acquire knowledge, attitudes and skills to make healthy food choices voluntarily. It is a key part of health education and of every national nutrition programme.

Purposes (objectives)

  1. Create awareness about the importance of nutrition for health, growth, work capacity and resistance to disease
  2. Promote healthy eating habits – balanced diet, dietary diversity, regular meals
  3. Promote optimal infant and young child feeding – early and exclusive breastfeeding, timely complementary feeding
  4. Improve maternal nutrition – diet in pregnancy and lactation, weight gain, IFA and calcium intake
  5. Prevent nutritional deficiency diseases – PEM, anaemia, vitamin A deficiency, iodine deficiency, rickets
  6. Prevent diet-related non-communicable diseases – obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease – by reducing salt, sugar and fat
  7. Correct food fads, taboos and misconceptions – e.g. avoiding colostrum, eggs or green vegetables in pregnancy
  8. Make the best use of available resources – low-cost nutritious foods, seasonal foods, kitchen gardens, wise spending of the family food budget
  9. Teach correct cooking, storage and hygiene – preserving nutrients and preventing food-borne diseases
  10. Promote fortified foods – iodised salt, double-fortified salt, fortified rice and oil
  11. Encourage use of government programmes – ICDS, PM POSHAN, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, PDS
  12. Promote growth monitoring and early detection of malnutrition
  13. Support patients to follow therapeutic diets (diabetes, kidney and heart disease)
  14. Encourage healthy lifestyle – physical activity, avoiding tobacco and alcohol
  15. Empower women and communities – self-reliance and community participation in nutrition

Target groups

  • Mothers, pregnant and lactating women, adolescents, school children, elderly, patients and families, community leaders, food handlers

Expected outcomes

  • Improved knowledge and practices, better nutritional status, fewer deficiency diseases and lower infant and maternal mortality

Role of the nurse

  • Use every contact – clinics, wards, home visits, schools – to give simple, practical nutrition messages

Approach to achieve these purposes

  • Use simple, practical messages in the local language
  • Demonstrations (cooking, ORS, complementary foods) rather than lectures alone
  • Involve families and community leaders; repeat messages through different channels

Conclusion The purposes of nutrition education are to create awareness, promote healthy eating and feeding practices, prevent deficiency and lifestyle diseases, correct harmful beliefs, make the best use of resources and programmes, and empower families to maintain good nutrition.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the anthropometric measurements used for assessing the nutritional status of children.
answer_html:
Introduction Anthropometry is the measurement of the physical dimensions and composition of the body. It is the most widely used method of nutritional assessment in children because it is simple, cheap and objective.

1. Weight

  • The most sensitive indicator of current nutrition
  • Measured with an infant weighing scale, Salter (hanging) scale or digital scale; minimal clothing; check the zero error
  • Normal pattern – birth weight about 3 kg; doubles by 5 months, triples by 1 year, about four times by 2 years
  • Weight-for-age below –2 SD = underweight

2. Length / height

  • Length (lying, using an infantometer) below 2 years; height (standing, using a stadiometer) above 2 years
  • Birth length about 50 cm; about 75 cm at 1 year
  • Height-for-age below –2 SD = stunting (chronic malnutrition)

3. Weight-for-height

  • Below –2 SD = wasting (acute malnutrition); below –3 SD = SAM

4. Head circumference

  • Measured with a non-stretchable tape around the occipitofrontal area
  • About 33–35 cm at birth; reflects brain growth – small in microcephaly, large in hydrocephalus

5. Chest circumference

  • Measured at the nipple level during quiet breathing
  • At birth about 2 cm less than head circumference; equal at about 1 year; afterwards chest exceeds head
  • Chest–head ratio below 1 after one year suggests malnutrition

6. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)

  • Measured at the midpoint between acromion and olecranon of the left arm
  • Children 6–59 months: below 11.5 cm – SAM, 11.5–12.5 cm – moderate, above 12.5 cm – normal

7. Skinfold thickness

  • Triceps and subscapular skinfolds measured with calipers – estimate body fat

8. BMI-for-age – for children 5–19 years

Growth charts and Z-scores

  • Measurements are plotted on WHO growth standards (MCP card)
  • The direction of the growth curve matters more than its position – a flat or falling curve shows growth faltering

Precautions

  • Use standard, calibrated instruments and correct techniques
  • Record the exact age; repeat measurements; record and plot immediately

Nursing relevance

  • Nurses and Anganwadi workers measure and plot growth monthly, counsel mothers and refer faltering children

Conclusion Weight, length/height, their indices, head and chest circumference, MUAC and skinfold thickness, plotted on WHO growth charts, help identify underweight, stunting, wasting and obesity in children early and guide timely action.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Describe the clinical signs of malnutrition.
answer_html:
Introduction Clinical examination is a simple method of nutritional assessment that looks for physical signs of deficiency in tissues such as hair, eyes, mouth, skin and bones. It needs no equipment but signs appear late and may be non-specific.

Head-to-toe clinical signs and their probable causes

Area Sign Probable deficiency
General wasting, thinness protein-energy (marasmus)
oedema protein (kwashiorkor)
apathy, misery PEM
Hair thin, sparse, dull, easily pluckable, depigmented; flag sign PEM
Face moon face kwashiorkor
nasolabial seborrhoea riboflavin
Eyes pale conjunctiva iron (anaemia)
Bitot's spots, conjunctival and corneal xerosis, keratomalacia vitamin A
angular palpebritis riboflavin
Lips angular stomatitis, cheilosis riboflavin, B₆, iron
Tongue magenta tongue riboflavin
raw, red, painful (glossitis) niacin, folate, B₁₂
pale, smooth iron
Teeth mottled enamel excess fluoride
caries excess sugar, low fluoride
Gums spongy, bleeding vitamin C
Glands thyroid enlargement (goitre) iodine
parotid enlargement PEM
Skin dry, rough; follicular hyperkeratosis vitamin A, essential fatty acids
petechiae, perifollicular bleeding vitamin C
pellagrous dermatitis (sun-exposed) niacin
flaky-paint dermatosis kwashiorkor
Nails koilonychia (spoon nails) iron
Muscles wasting PEM
Bones craniotabes, frontal bossing, rickety rosary, wrist widening, bow legs vitamin D (rickets)
painful swelling of legs vitamin C (scurvy)
Internal organs enlarged liver PEM
rapid pulse, enlarged heart anaemia, thiamine (wet beriberi)
Nervous system numbness, burning feet, calf tenderness, loss of reflexes thiamine
mental confusion, dementia thiamine, niacin, B₁₂

Advantages of clinical assessment

  • Simple, quick, cheap; useful in field surveys and at the bedside

Limitations

  • Signs appear only in advanced deficiency
  • Many signs are non-specific (caused by more than one deficiency or by other factors)
  • Subjective – depends on the examiner's skill
  • Must be confirmed with dietary and biochemical assessment

Points while examining

  • Examine in good daylight; compare with other members of the family or community
  • Record signs systematically (WHO-style check-list) and grade them where possible

  • Combine with weight, height, MUAC and haemoglobin before concluding

  • Look for more than one sign of the same deficiency before drawing a conclusion

Conclusion Clinical examination detects malnutrition through characteristic signs in the hair, eyes, mouth, skin, nails, thyroid, bones and internal organs; it is simple and useful but should be combined with anthropometric, dietary and laboratory methods.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the methods of dietary assessment.
answer_html:
Introduction Dietary assessment measures what and how much people eat. It helps identify inadequate or excessive intake before clinical signs appear, finds the causes of malnutrition and guides diet counselling and programmes.

A. Methods for individuals

1. 24-hour dietary recall

  • The person recalls all foods and drinks taken in the previous 24 hours, with amounts estimated using standard cups, spoons and food models
  • Advantages – quick, cheap, little burden; suitable for illiterate people
  • Limitations – depends on memory; one day may not be typical – repeat on 2–3 days, including a holiday

2. Food frequency questionnaire (FFQ)

  • A list of foods with how often each is eaten (daily, weekly, monthly, rarely)
  • Shows usual intake and food patterns; semi-quantitative forms include portion sizes
  • Useful in large surveys and studies on diet and disease

3. Diet history

  • A detailed interview about usual eating pattern over weeks or months, often combined with a 24-hour recall and checklist
  • Gives a complete picture but is time-consuming and needs a trained interviewer

4. Food diary (food record)

  • The person records everything eaten at the time of eating for 3–7 days, by estimation or by weighing
  • Accurate; but needs a literate, motivated person and may change eating behaviour

B. Methods for families and communities

5. Weighment method (household diet survey)

  • All raw foods used for cooking are weighed, along with leftovers, usually for 1–7 days
  • Intake is calculated per consumption unit
  • Most accurate community method (used by the National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau), but time-consuming and intrusive

6. Food balance sheet

  • Estimates the food available per person in a country (production + imports – exports – losses)
  • Shows national trends, not individual intake

7. Duplicate diet method – an identical portion of all food eaten is collected and analysed in the laboratory (research)

8. Observation / plate-waste method – used in hospitals and institutions

C. Analysis

  • Foods are converted into nutrients using food composition tables (IFCT, NIN) or software
  • Intake is compared with RDA – e.g. a protein intake below about 70% of RDA indicates inadequacy

D. Precautions

  • Build rapport; use local measures and recipes
  • Probe for snacks, drinks, oil and sugar, which are often forgotten
  • Avoid leading questions

E. Nursing relevance

  • Nurses take diet histories and 24-hour recalls in hospitals and the community to plan diets and counselling

Conclusion Dietary assessment uses 24-hour recall, food frequency questionnaires, diet history and food records for individuals, and the weighment method and food balance sheets for communities; the results, compared with RDAs, show nutrient gaps and guide action.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define nutritional assessment. State its objectives.
answer_html:
Definition Nutritional assessment is the evaluation of the nutritional status of individuals or population groups by measuring food intake, body dimensions, biochemical parameters and clinical signs, and by studying related factors.

Objectives

  1. To find the nutritional status – normal, under-nourished or over-nourished
  2. To identify specific deficiencies (anaemia, vitamin A deficiency, PEM)
  3. To find the magnitude and distribution of malnutrition in the community
  4. To identify high-risk groups (children, pregnant women, elderly)
  5. To find the causes (dietary, social, economic, disease)
  6. To plan nutrition interventions and programmes
  7. To monitor and evaluate the effect of programmes and treatment

Methods (ABCD): Anthropometry, Biochemical tests, Clinical examination, Dietary assessment; plus vital statistics and ecological factors.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is BMI? Give its classification.
answer_html:
Definition Body mass index (BMI) is the ratio of body weight to the square of height: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²

WHO classification (adults)

  • Underweight – below 18.5
  • Normal – 18.5–24.9
  • Overweight – 25–29.9
  • Obese – 30 or more (class I 30–34.9; II 35–39.9; III 40 or more)

Asian Indian cut-offs (Indians have more body fat at lower BMI)

  • Normal 18.5–22.9; overweight 23–24.9; obese 25 or more

Example: 70 kg, 1.65 m → 70 ÷ 2.72 = 25.7 → obese by Indian cut-offs (overweight by WHO).

Limitations: does not distinguish muscle from fat or show fat distribution; not used in pregnancy; in children, BMI-for-age charts are used.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)? State its significance.
answer_html:
Definition MUAC is the circumference of the left upper arm measured at the midpoint between the tip of the shoulder (acromion) and the elbow (olecranon), with the arm hanging relaxed.

Measurement: a colour-coded MUAC tape (Shakir's tape) or non-stretchable tape; neither too tight nor too loose.

Interpretation (children 6–59 months)

  • Below 11.5 cm – red – severe acute malnutrition
  • 11.5–12.5 cm – yellow – moderate acute malnutrition
  • Above 12.5 cm – green – normal

Significance

  1. Remains fairly constant between 1 and 5 years, so age need not be known
  2. Simple, quick and cheap – used by Anganwadi workers and ASHAs for community screening
  3. Strong predictor of death in malnourished children
  4. In pregnant women, a low MUAC (below about 23 cm) indicates risk of low birth weight

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is growth monitoring?
answer_html:
Definition Growth monitoring is the regular measurement of a child's weight (and length/height) and plotting it on a growth chart to detect growth faltering early and take timely action.

Tools

  • WHO growth standards (2006); Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card with colour-coded zones
  • Done monthly by Anganwadi workers (more often in infancy), recorded on the Poshan Tracker

Interpretation

  • Upward curve parallel to the reference lines – good growth
  • Flat curve – danger (no weight gain)
  • Falling curve – very dangerous
  • The direction of the curve is more important than its position

Uses

  1. Early detection of under-nutrition before it becomes severe
  2. Education and motivation of mothers
  3. Guides referral and supplementary feeding
  4. Evaluates the effect of health and nutrition services

Note: growth monitoring is part of UNICEF's GOBI strategy (Growth monitoring, Oral rehydration, Breastfeeding, Immunisation).

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is waist–hip ratio? State its significance.
answer_html:
Definition Waist–hip ratio (WHR) = waist circumference ÷ hip circumference

  • Waist – measured midway between the lowest rib and the iliac crest after normal expiration
  • Hip – measured at the widest part of the buttocks

High-risk values (WHO)

  • Men – above 0.90; women – above 0.85

Waist circumference alone (Asian Indians)

  • Above 90 cm in men and above 80 cm in women indicates abdominal (central) obesity

Significance

  1. Measures abdominal fat, which is metabolically harmful
  2. Better predictor than BMI of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and heart disease
  3. Indians tend to have central obesity even with normal BMI ("thin-fat Indian")
  4. Simple, cheap screening tool in clinics and the community

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ)?
answer_html:
Definition A food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) is a dietary assessment tool consisting of a list of foods and asking how often each food is eaten over a period (per day, week or month).

Types

  • Qualitative – only frequency
  • Semi-quantitative – frequency plus usual portion size

Steps: prepare a list of commonly eaten local foods → ask the frequency of each → (estimate portions) → calculate approximate intake and patterns.

Advantages

  • Assesses usual, long-term intake and food patterns
  • Quick, inexpensive, can be self-administered; useful in large epidemiological studies (diet and disease)

Limitations

  • Limited to foods in the list; depends on memory
  • Less accurate for exact amounts; must be adapted to local diets

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain the role of the nurse in national nutritional programmes.
answer_html:
Introduction India runs several programmes to combat malnutrition – ICDS (Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0), POSHAN Abhiyaan, PM POSHAN (mid-day meal), Anaemia Mukt Bharat (including WIFS), vitamin A prophylaxis, NIDDCP, National Deworming Day, MAA, Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres, NFSA/PDS and food fortification. Nurses (staff nurses, ANMs, community health officers) are key to their success.

Role of the nurse

1. Assessment and surveillance

  • Identify vulnerable groups – pregnant and lactating women, children under 5, adolescent girls
  • Growth monitoring, MUAC screening, haemoglobin testing, goitre screening
  • Community surveys and diet surveys

2. Delivery of services

  • Distribute IFA tablets/syrup, calcium, vitamin A, albendazole, ORS and zinc
  • Provide services at Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days (VHSND) along with immunisation and antenatal care

3. Nutrition and health education

  • IYCF counselling – breastfeeding and complementary feeding
  • Balanced diet, use of iodised salt and fortified foods, food hygiene
  • Cooking demonstrations of low-cost recipes
  • Campaigns – Poshan Maah (September), National Nutrition Week, World Breastfeeding Week

4. Referral and management

  • Refer SAM children to Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres and follow them up after discharge
  • Refer severely anaemic pregnant women for treatment

5. Supervision, training and support

  • Train and supervise Anganwadi workers, ASHAs and helpers
  • Check quality and hygiene of supplementary nutrition and mid-day meals

6. Coordination and convergence

  • Work with ICDS, education, Panchayati Raj institutions, Jal Shakti/sanitation and NGOs
  • Participate in community-based events – Godh Bharai, Annaprashan

7. Records and reports

  • Maintain the MCP card, registers, HMIS and Poshan Tracker entries; report coverage

8. Monitoring and evaluation

  • Monitor coverage, compliance (e.g. IFA), and outcomes (weight gain, Hb)

9. Community mobilisation

  • Involve mothers' groups, self-help groups, Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committees

10. Research and advocacy

  • Participate in studies; advocate for nutrition in local planning

Challenges the nurse helps to overcome

  • Poor compliance with IFA and other supplements – counselling, follow-up
  • Food taboos and harmful practices – tactful education
  • Gaps in coverage of remote and migrant families – home visits, outreach
  • Poor record keeping – regular checking of registers and digital entries

Conclusion The nurse plays a central role in national nutrition programmes as an assessor, service provider, educator, referral link, trainer, supervisor, coordinator and record keeper, ensuring that programme benefits reach vulnerable mothers and children.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain the mid-day meal programme (PM POSHAN) – objectives, nutritional norms and principles.
answer_html:
Introduction The Mid-Day Meal (MDM) programme provides a hot cooked meal to school children. It began nationally as the National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education on 15 August 1995; cooked meals were made compulsory by the Supreme Court in 2001. In September 2021 it was renamed PM POSHAN (Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman). It is one of the largest school feeding programmes in the world.

A. Beneficiaries

  • Children in Balvatika (pre-primary) and classes 1–8 of government and government-aided schools

B. Objectives

  1. Improve the nutritional status of school children
  2. Increase enrolment, attendance and retention, and reduce dropouts
  3. Encourage children from poor families to attend school
  4. Promote social equity – children of all castes and religions eat together
  5. Reduce classroom hunger and improve concentration
  6. Provide nutritional support in drought-affected areas and during summer vacations

C. Nutritional norms (per child per day)

Level Energy Protein Cereals Pulses Vegetables Oil
Primary 450 kcal 12 g 100 g 20 g 50 g 5 g
Upper primary 700 kcal 20 g 150 g 30 g 75 g 7.5 g
  • Use of fortified rice and double-fortified salt; micronutrients, IFA and deworming through school health programmes

D. Principles of the mid-day meal

  1. It should supplement, not substitute, the home diet
  2. Provide about one-third of daily energy and half of protein requirements
  3. Use locally available, low-cost foods, including millets
  4. Easy to prepare, acceptable and tasty for children
  5. Variety in the weekly menu
  6. Hygienic preparation, storage and serving; safe water
  7. Served at a fixed time daily during school hours
  8. Community participation – School Management Committees, mothers' groups, Tithi Bhojan

E. Features of PM POSHAN

  • School nutrition gardens; cooking competitions
  • Tithi Bhojan – community members contribute special meals on festivals and occasions
  • Social audit and tasting of meals by teachers/SMC members before serving
  • Involvement of women's self-help groups as cooks; direct transfer of cooking cost to schools
  • Supplementary nutrition items in districts with high anaemia

F. Problems

  • Irregular supply, poor quality, food safety incidents, infrastructure gaps, leakages, social discrimination

G. Role of the nurse

  • Health check-ups of children; growth monitoring; detection and referral of deficiencies
  • Supervise kitchen hygiene, safe water and health of cooks
  • Health and nutrition education for children, teachers and parents

Conclusion PM POSHAN provides a hot cooked meal of 450 kcal and 12 g protein (primary) or 700 kcal and 20 g protein (upper primary), supplementing the home diet, improving nutrition and school attendance, and promoting social equity, when meals are nutritious, hygienic and regularly supplied.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain the major nutritional problems in India.
answer_html:
Introduction India faces a double (triple) burden of malnutrition – widespread under-nutrition and micronutrient deficiencies together with a rapid rise in obesity and diet-related diseases. The National Family Health Survey-5 (2019–21) shows the scale of the problem.

1. Low birth weight (LBW)

  • About 18% of babies weighed at birth are below 2.5 kg (NFHS-5)
  • Causes – maternal under-nutrition, anaemia, teenage pregnancy, short spacing
  • LBW babies are at higher risk of death, infections and stunting

2. Protein-energy malnutrition

  • Children under 5: stunting 35.5%, wasting 19.3%, underweight 32.1%
  • Contributes to a large share of child deaths

3. Nutritional anaemia

  • Children 6–59 months – 67%; women 15–49 years – 57%; pregnant women – 52%; adolescent girls – 59%; men – 25%
  • Mainly iron deficiency, with folate and B₁₂ deficiency, hookworm and malaria

4. Iodine deficiency disorders

  • Goitre, cretinism, low IQ; the whole country is considered at risk
  • About 94% of households use iodised salt (NFHS-5), but adequacy varies

5. Vitamin A deficiency

  • Night blindness and xerophthalmia; sub-clinical deficiency remains in young children

6. Vitamin D deficiency – very common in all age groups; rickets and osteomalacia

7. Other micronutrient deficiencies – zinc, folate, vitamin B₁₂ (especially in vegetarians), calcium

8. Fluorosis – endemic in many states due to high fluoride in groundwater

9. Food-toxin related problems

  • Lathyrism (khesari dal), epidemic dropsy (argemone oil), aflatoxicosis (mouldy groundnuts and maize – liver damage)

10. Over-nutrition and non-communicable diseases

  • Overweight/obesity – about 24% of women and 23% of men (NFHS-5)
  • Rising diabetes, hypertension, heart disease – linked to refined foods, excess salt, sugar and fat, and inactivity

Causes

  • Poverty, food insecurity, illiteracy, poor feeding practices, infections, poor sanitation, gender inequality, large families, urbanisation and nutrition transition

Strategies

  • ICDS/Poshan 2.0, POSHAN Abhiyaan, PM POSHAN, Anaemia Mukt Bharat, vitamin A prophylaxis, NIDDCP, food fortification, NFSA/PDS, MAA, NRCs, Eat Right India, Fit India, nutrition education

Conclusion India's major nutritional problems are low birth weight, protein-energy malnutrition, anaemia, iodine, vitamin A and vitamin D deficiencies, fluorosis and food-toxin diseases, along with rising obesity and NCDs; they require combined action through programmes, fortification, education and improved living conditions.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme.
answer_html:
Introduction The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme was launched on 2 October 1975 in 33 blocks and is now universal. It is run by the Ministry of Women and Child Development and is one of the world's largest programmes for early childhood care and development. Since 2021 it is implemented as part of Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0.

A. Objectives

  1. Improve the nutritional and health status of children 0–6 years
  2. Lay the foundation for proper psychological, physical and social development of the child
  3. Reduce mortality, morbidity, malnutrition and school dropouts
  4. Achieve effective coordination of policy and implementation among departments
  5. Enhance the capability of mothers to look after the health and nutrition of their children

B. Beneficiaries

  • Children 0–6 years
  • Pregnant women and lactating mothers
  • Adolescent girls (in selected districts through the Scheme for Adolescent Girls)

C. Package of six services

  1. Supplementary nutrition
  2. Pre-school non-formal education (children 3–6 years)
  3. Nutrition and health education (women 15–45 years)
  4. Immunisation
  5. Health check-up
  6. Referral services - Services 4–6 are delivered through the health system (ANM, MO) at the Anganwadi centre

D. Supplementary nutrition norms (per beneficiary per day)

Beneficiary Energy Protein
Children 6 months–6 years 500 kcal 12–15 g
Severely malnourished children 800 kcal 20–25 g
Pregnant and lactating women 600 kcal 18–20 g
  • Given for 300 days a year – take-home ration for children 6–36 months and mothers; morning snack and hot cooked meal for children 3–6 years at the centre
  • Use of fortified rice and millets

E. Infrastructure and staff

  • Anganwadi centre (AWC) – one per about 400–800 population (mini-AWC for smaller habitations)
  • Anganwadi worker (AWW) and helper at the AWC; supervisor (Mukhya Sevika); CDPO at block level

F. Other activities

  • Growth monitoring and Poshan Tracker app
  • Community-based events – Godh Bharai (for pregnant women), Annaprashan (start of complementary feeding)
  • Early childhood care and education; referral of SAM children

G. Role of the nurse/ANM

  • Immunisation, antenatal care and health check-ups at the AWC; VHSND
  • Training and supporting AWWs; referral and follow-up of malnourished children

Conclusion ICDS provides supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-ups and referral through Anganwadi centres to children under six, pregnant and lactating women and adolescent girls, forming the backbone of India's fight against child malnutrition.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain the Anaemia Mukt Bharat strategy.
answer_html:
Introduction Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2018 under POSHAN Abhiyaan to reduce anaemia. It uses a 6 × 6 × 6 strategy – 6 target groups, 6 interventions and 6 institutional mechanisms – and aimed at reducing anaemia prevalence by 3 percentage points every year.

A. Six target groups and IFA prophylaxis

Beneficiary Dose and regimen
Children 6–59 months 1 ml IFA syrup (20 mg iron + 100 µg folic acid) twice a week
Children 5–9 years 1 IFA pink tablet (45 mg iron + 400 µg folic acid) weekly
Adolescents 10–19 years 1 IFA blue tablet (60 mg iron + 500 µg folic acid) weekly
Women of reproductive age (20–24 years, not pregnant or lactating) 1 IFA red tablet (60 mg iron + 500 µg folic acid) weekly
Pregnant women 1 IFA red tablet daily from the second trimester for 180 days
Lactating mothers 1 IFA red tablet daily for 180 days after delivery

B. Six interventions

  1. Prophylactic iron–folic acid supplementation (as above)
  2. Deworming – albendazole twice a year (National Deworming Day – 10 February and 10 August); pregnant women once in the second trimester
  3. Intensified year-round behaviour change communication – including delayed cord clamping at birth, iron-rich diet, compliance with IFA
  4. Testing and treatment of anaemia using digital haemoglobinometers – "Test, Treat, Talk (T3)" camps
  5. Mandatory provision of IFA-fortified foods in government programmes (fortified rice, double-fortified salt)
  6. Addressing non-nutritional causes of anaemia in endemic areas – malaria, haemoglobinopathies (sickle cell), fluorosis

C. Six institutional mechanisms

  1. Intra-ministerial coordination
  2. National Anaemia Mukt Bharat Unit
  3. National Centre of Excellence and Advanced Research on Anaemia Control (AIIMS, New Delhi)
  4. Convergence with other ministries (WCD, Education, Panchayati Raj)
  5. Strengthening supply chain and logistics
  6. AMB dashboard and digital portal for monitoring

D. Role of the nurse

  • Screen for anaemia; give and supervise IFA intake; counsel on side effects
  • Conduct deworming and T3 camps; educate on iron-rich diets
  • Record and report on the AMB dashboard; refer severe anaemia

Conclusion Anaemia Mukt Bharat tackles anaemia through a 6 × 6 × 6 strategy – IFA prophylaxis for six age groups, deworming, behaviour change, digital testing and treatment, fortified foods and attention to non-nutritional causes – backed by strong institutional mechanisms.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain the national vitamin A prophylaxis programme.
answer_html:
Introduction The National Prophylaxis Programme against Nutritional Blindness due to Vitamin A Deficiency was started in 1970 and is now part of the Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) services under the National Health Mission. Its aim is to prevent blindness and deaths due to vitamin A deficiency in young children.

A. Objectives

  • Prevent xerophthalmia and nutritional blindness
  • Reduce childhood illness and deaths from measles, diarrhoea and respiratory infections

B. Schedule of vitamin A prophylaxis

Dose Age Amount
1st dose 9 months (with measles-rubella vaccine) 1,00,000 IU (1 ml)
2nd dose 16–18 months (with DPT booster) 2,00,000 IU (2 ml)
3rd to 9th doses every 6 months up to 5 years 2,00,000 IU each
  • Total – 9 doses (17 lakh IU) between 9 months and 5 years
  • Some states run biannual vitamin A supplementation rounds

C. Administration

  • Vitamin A solution contains 1,00,000 IU per ml; use only the marked spoon supplied with the bottle (marked at 1 ml and 2 ml)
  • Give orally; do not give by syringe directly into the mouth
  • Once opened, use the bottle within the period stated by the manufacturer; protect from sunlight
  • Record each dose in the MCP card and immunisation register

D. Therapeutic use

  • Xerophthalmia – doses on day 0, day 1 and day 14 (50,000 IU below 6 months; 1 lakh IU at 6–12 months; 2 lakh IU above 12 months)
  • Measles and severe acute malnutrition – vitamin A as per guidelines

E. Precautions

  • High doses are not given to pregnant women (risk to the fetus)
  • Do not exceed the scheduled dose; check previous doses to avoid toxicity

F. Other measures in the programme

  • Promotion of breastfeeding and colostrum
  • Dietary diversification – green leafy and yellow-orange vegetables and fruits; kitchen gardens
  • Fortification of oil and milk; measles immunisation; diarrhoea control

G. Role of the nurse

  • Give doses at the correct age with the correct spoon; maintain records
  • Educate mothers on vitamin A-rich foods; detect and refer eye signs

Conclusion The vitamin A prophylaxis programme gives 9 doses of vitamin A from 9 months to 5 years (1 lakh IU, then 2 lakh IU every 6 months), supported by breastfeeding, dietary diversification, fortification and immunisation, to prevent nutritional blindness and child deaths.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Explain POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission).
answer_html:
Introduction POSHAN Abhiyaan (Prime Minister's Overarching Scheme for Holistic Nourishment) – the National Nutrition Mission – was launched on 8 March 2018 at Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan by the Ministry of Women and Child Development. It aims to improve nutritional outcomes of children 0–6 years, adolescent girls, pregnant women and lactating mothers in a time-bound manner, focusing on the first 1,000 days of life.

A. Targets (original, to be achieved by 2022)

  • Reduce stunting by 2% per year
  • Reduce under-nutrition (underweight) by 2% per year
  • Reduce anaemia among young children, women and adolescent girls by 3% per year
  • Reduce low birth weight by 2% per year
  • "Mission 25 by 2022" – bring stunting down to 25%

B. Key pillars and components

  1. ICT-enabled real-time monitoring – Anganwadi workers use smartphones; now the Poshan Tracker app
  2. Convergence – of ICDS, National Health Mission, PMMVY, Swachh Bharat, Jal Jeevan, PDS, education (PM POSHAN), MGNREGA and Panchayati Raj
  3. Behaviour change communication – "Jan Andolan" (people's movement)
    • Poshan Maah every September; Poshan Pakhwada in March
    • Community-based events at Anganwadi centres
  4. Capacity building – incremental learning approach for frontline workers
  5. Growth monitoring devices – infantometers, stadiometers, weighing scales for every AWC
  6. Performance incentives for Anganwadi workers and teams

C. Thematic focus

  • Early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding, complementary feeding
  • Anaemia control (Anaemia Mukt Bharat), deworming
  • Diarrhoea management, hand-washing and sanitation
  • Food fortification, millets, kitchen gardens (Poshan Vatika)
  • Women's education, diet and age at marriage

D. Present status

  • Since 2021 it is part of Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, together with ICDS and the Scheme for Adolescent Girls

E. Role of the nurse

  • Participate in Poshan Maah activities and community-based events
  • Coordinate with AWWs and ASHAs; ensure growth monitoring, IFA, deworming and counselling
  • Use data for monitoring and follow-up

Progress and challenges

  • Child stunting and underweight have declined slowly, but anaemia remains very high
  • Challenges include inadequate infrastructure of some Anganwadi centres, workload of frontline workers, data quality and behaviour change at household level

Conclusion POSHAN Abhiyaan, launched in 2018, aims to reduce stunting, under-nutrition, anaemia and low birth weight through technology-based monitoring, convergence of schemes, a people's movement for nutrition and capacity building, now continued under Poshan 2.0.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Write the objectives of the Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) programme.
answer_html:
Introduction WIFS was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2012 for adolescents (10–19 years) – school-going boys and girls in classes 6–12 of government, government-aided and municipal schools, and out-of-school girls through Anganwadi centres. It is now part of Anaemia Mukt Bharat.

Objective

  • To reduce the prevalence and severity of nutritional anaemia among adolescents

Interventions to achieve it

  1. Weekly supervised IFA tablet – blue tablet (60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid) on a fixed day, after the mid-day meal
  2. Biannual deworming with albendazole 400 mg, six months apart
  3. Nutrition and health education – iron-rich diet, hygiene, prevention of anaemia
  4. Screening for moderate and severe anaemia and referral for treatment

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Write the objectives of the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP).
answer_html:
Introduction The National Goitre Control Programme was started in 1962 and renamed the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP) in 1992.

Objectives

  1. Surveys to assess the magnitude of iodine deficiency disorders in districts
  2. Supply of iodised salt in place of common salt
  3. Resurveys to assess the extent of IDD and the impact of iodised salt every 5 years
  4. Laboratory monitoring of iodised salt and urinary iodine excretion
  5. Health education and publicity

Goals

  • Reduce the prevalence of IDD below 5% in the country
  • Ensure 100% consumption of adequately iodised salt (15 ppm or more) at household level

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: What is the National Nutrition Policy, 1993?
answer_html:
Introduction The National Nutrition Policy was adopted by the Government of India in 1993 under the Department of Women and Child Development. It recognised that malnutrition has many causes and needs a multi-sectoral approach.

Direct (short-term) interventions

  1. Nutrition interventions for vulnerable groups – expansion of ICDS, adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women
  2. Fortification of essential foods (e.g. iodised salt)
  3. Popularisation of low-cost nutritious foods
  4. Control of micronutrient deficiencies in vulnerable groups

Indirect (long-term) interventions

  • Food security; improving dietary patterns through production and demonstration
  • Income transfers, land reforms, minimum wages, equal pay for women
  • Health and family welfare services; prevention of food adulteration
  • Nutrition surveillance, monitoring, research and communication
  • Education, literacy and improvement of the status of women; community participation

Follow-up: the National Plan of Action on Nutrition (1995) was prepared to implement it.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Write a note on the National Food Security Act, 2013.
answer_html:
Introduction The National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013 gives a legal right to subsidised foodgrains to about two-thirds of India's population – up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.

Entitlements

  1. Priority households – 5 kg of foodgrains per person per month
  2. Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) – the poorest households – 35 kg per household per month
  3. Grains were priced at ₹3/2/1 per kg (rice/wheat/coarse grains); they are free since 1 January 2023 under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana
  4. Pregnant women and lactating mothers – free meal through Anganwadi and maternity benefit of at least ₹6,000
  5. Children 6 months–6 years – meals through Anganwadi; 6–14 years – mid-day meal

Other features

  • The eldest woman (18 years or above) is the head of household for ration cards
  • Grievance redressal, State Food Commissions, vigilance committees, social audits
  • One Nation One Ration Card – portability across states

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
unit_title: National Nutritional Programmes and Role of Nurse
question: Describe the Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC) – objectives, admission and discharge criteria, services and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction A Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC) is a unit within a health facility (district hospital, CHC or medical college) where children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) are admitted for medical and nutritional therapeutic care. NRCs were established under the National Health Mission following national guidelines on facility-based care of SAM. They usually have 10–20 beds, and the mother or caregiver stays with the child.

A. Objectives

  1. Provide clinical management of SAM children, especially those with complications
  2. Promote physical and psychological recovery of the child
  3. Build the capacity of mothers/caregivers in appropriate feeding, hygiene and care practices
  4. Identify social and economic causes of malnutrition in the family and link the family with support schemes
  5. Reduce child deaths due to malnutrition

B. Staff

  • Medical officer/paediatrician, nursing staff, nutrition counsellor/feeding demonstrator, cook-cum-caretaker and attendants

C. Admission criteria

  1. Children 6–59 months with SAM – weight-for-height below –3 SD, MUAC below 11.5 cm or bilateral pitting oedema – plus any of:
    • failed appetite test or poor appetite
    • medical complications – fever, hypothermia, severe dehydration, severe anaemia, pneumonia, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy, extensive skin lesions
    • severe (+++) bilateral oedema
  2. Infants below 6 months with visible severe wasting or oedema, or with feeding difficulties
  3. Children referred by Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, RBSK teams or doctors after screening

D. Services

  1. Medical care following the WHO 10 steps – treatment of hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, infections and electrolyte and micronutrient deficiencies
  2. Therapeutic feeding – F-75 in the stabilisation phase and F-100 (or locally prepared energy-dense foods) for catch-up growth
  3. Counselling and training of mothers – breastfeeding, complementary feeding, cooking demonstrations with local low-cost foods, hygiene and handwashing
  4. Psycho-social stimulation – play activities, toys, mother–child interaction
  5. Immunisation, vitamin A, deworming, IFA as needed
  6. Linkages – ICDS, PDS, wage-loss compensation to mothers and travel support as per state norms, other social welfare schemes
  7. Follow-up after discharge

E. Discharge criteria

  • Weight gain of about 15% over the admission weight (or over the weight after oedema has gone), sustained
  • Oedema completely resolved
  • Medical complications treated, child alert and eating well
  • Mother trained in feeding and care
  • Average stay is about 2 weeks, longer if needed

F. Follow-up

  • Usually 4 follow-up visits at 15-day intervals after discharge (about 2 months)
  • Weight, MUAC and oedema checked; feeding reviewed; Anganwadi worker and ASHA support at home
  • Children who relapse are re-referred

G. Monitoring indicators

  • Recovery (cure) rate – should be high (more than 75%)
  • Death rate – should be low (below 10%; ideally below 5%)
  • Defaulter rate – below 15%
  • Average weight gain (g/kg/day) and length of stay; bed occupancy

H. Role of the nurse

  1. Admission assessment – weight, length/height, MUAC, oedema, appetite test, vital signs, danger signs
  2. Round-the-clock care – 2-hourly feeds day and night in the stabilisation phase, accurate preparation of F-75/F-100
  3. Monitoring – temperature, pulse, respiration, hydration, daily weight, intake–output; watch for refeeding problems and fluid overload
  4. Prevention of hypothermia and hypoglycaemia – kangaroo care, warm room, night feeds
  5. Infection prevention – hand hygiene, clean feeding utensils, isolation when needed
  6. Medication administration – antibiotics, vitamin A, micronutrients as prescribed
  7. Counselling and demonstration for mothers; involving them in feeding and play
  8. Records – NRC registers, growth charts, online reporting
  9. Discharge planning and follow-up – coordinate with AWWs, ASHAs and families

I. Common problems in NRC functioning

  • Low bed occupancy due to poor referral or reluctance of families (loss of wages, other children at home)
  • Defaulting before discharge and poor follow-up after discharge
  • Shortage of trained staff; irregular supply of therapeutic feeds
  • Relapse when household food insecurity and poor hygiene are not addressed

J. Link with community-based management

  • Children without complications and with good appetite are treated at home through community-based management of acute malnutrition, with weekly or fortnightly follow-up by AWWs and ASHAs
  • NRCs and community programmes together form a continuum of care

Conclusion NRCs provide facility-based medical and nutritional care for children with severe acute malnutrition, train mothers in feeding and care, and ensure follow-up after discharge; nurses are central to their functioning through round-the-clock feeding, monitoring, infection prevention, counselling and record keeping.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain safe food handling – storage, preparation, cooking and serving.
answer_html:
Introduction Unsafe food containing bacteria, viruses, parasites or chemicals causes more than 200 diseases. WHO estimates that about 600 million people (almost 1 in 10) fall ill and 420,000 die every year from contaminated food. Safe handling at every step – from purchase to serving – prevents most food-borne illness.

1. Purchase (selection)

  • Buy fresh foods from clean, licensed shops; check expiry date, FSSAI licence number and intact packaging (no bulging or rusty cans)
  • Use pasteurised milk; buy meat and fish from hygienic, licensed outlets
  • Avoid cut fruits and foods kept uncovered by the roadside

2. Storage

  • Refrigerate perishables promptly – below 5 °C; freezer at –18 °C
  • Keep raw meat and fish in sealed containers on the lowest shelf, below cooked foods
  • Cover all food; store cooked and raw foods separately
  • Dry stores – cool, dry, airtight, off the floor, pest-free; follow first in, first out
  • Never store chemicals or pesticides near food

3. Preparation

  • Wash hands with soap before handling food and after handling raw meat, toilet use, touching waste or animals
  • Wash fruits and vegetables in clean running water before cutting
  • Use separate chopping boards and knives for raw meat and for vegetables/cooked food
  • Thaw frozen food in the refrigerator, not at room temperature
  • Keep kitchen surfaces and utensils clean; use safe water

4. Cooking

  • Cook thoroughly – especially meat, poultry, eggs and seafood – until the centre reaches 70 °C (juices run clear, no pink meat)
  • Boil milk; cook eggs until the yolk is firm
  • Reheat leftovers until steaming hot throughout – only once

5. Serving and holding

  • Serve hot foods hot (above 60 °C) and cold foods cold (below 5 °C)
  • Do not keep cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours
  • Use clean serving spoons; do not touch food with bare hands; protect from flies

6. Leftovers

  • Cool quickly and refrigerate in shallow, covered containers; use within a day

7. Personal hygiene of food handlers

  • Clean clothes, apron, head cover, short clean nails, no jewellery
  • Cover cuts with waterproof dressings; no smoking, spitting or sneezing near food
  • Sick handlers (diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, skin infection) must not handle food

8. Kitchen hygiene

  • Clean and sanitise surfaces and utensils; wash dishcloths daily
  • Covered dustbins; regular waste disposal; pest and rodent control; good ventilation and lighting

Nursing relevance

  • Supervise hygiene in hospital kitchens and food trolleys; ensure correct temperatures
  • Educate families, especially those caring for infants, pregnant women, elderly and immunocompromised patients

Conclusion Safe food handling means buying fresh food, storing it at correct temperatures, preventing cross-contamination during preparation, cooking thoroughly, serving promptly and maintaining personal and kitchen hygiene at every step.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the role of food handlers in the spread of food-borne diseases and the measures to control it.
answer_html:
Introduction A food handler is any person who handles food, food utensils or food-contact surfaces – cooks, helpers, waiters, street vendors, hospital kitchen staff and mothers at home. Food handlers can contaminate food and cause outbreaks of food-borne disease affecting many people at once.

A. How food handlers spread disease

  1. As carriers (look healthy but excrete germs)
    • Typhoid (chronic carriers – e.g. "Typhoid Mary"), amoebiasis (cysts), shigellosis, cholera
    • Hepatitis A and E, norovirus
    • Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, throat and skin
  2. During active illness – diarrhoea, vomiting, jaundice, sore throat, boils and infected cuts
  3. Poor personal hygiene – not washing hands after using the toilet → faeco-oral spread; dirty, long nails; coughing and sneezing over food
  4. Unsafe practices
    • cross-contamination from raw to cooked food
    • inadequate cooking, keeping food at room temperature, repeated reheating
    • use of unsafe water and unclean utensils

B. Diseases spread through food handlers

  • Bacterial food poisoning (Staphylococcus, Salmonella, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens)
  • Typhoid, cholera, bacillary and amoebic dysentery
  • Hepatitis A and E, viral gastroenteritis
  • Intestinal worms (e.g. pinworm, tapeworm)

C. Control measures

  1. Pre-employment medical examination
    • General examination, skin and nails
    • Stool examination for ova, cysts and pathogens (Salmonella, Shigella)
    • Vaccination – typhoid and hepatitis A; deworming
  2. Periodic medical examination – at least once a year (FSSAI requires medical fitness and vaccination of food handlers)
  3. Exclusion from work when ill – diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, skin infections – until symptom-free and cleared
  4. Treatment of carriers
  5. Training and health education – personal hygiene, handwashing, safe food handling; FSSAI's FoSTaC training programme
  6. Good personal hygiene practices
    • handwashing with soap for at least 20 seconds at critical times
    • short, clean nails; clean uniform, apron, cap or hair net, gloves where needed
    • waterproof dressings on cuts; no jewellery
    • no smoking, chewing tobacco, spitting or touching face and hair while handling food
