  7. Facilities – adequate handwashing stations with soap and water, toilets, changing rooms
  8. Supervision and inspection – by food safety officers and kitchen supervisors; licensing of food businesses

D. Role of the nurse

  • In hospitals – supervise kitchen staff hygiene, check health records, participate in infection control
  • Investigate outbreaks of food poisoning; collect samples
  • Educate food handlers in schools (mid-day meal cooks), hostels and the community

Conclusion Food handlers spread food-borne diseases as carriers, during illness and through poor hygiene and unsafe practices; pre-employment and periodic medical examinations, vaccination, exclusion of sick handlers, training and strict personal hygiene control this risk.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Explain the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the functions of FSSAI.
answer_html:
Introduction The Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006 is India's main food law. It consolidated eight earlier food laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the Fruit Products Order, the Meat Food Products Order and the Milk and Milk Products Order. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) was set up in 2008 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and the Act came into force on 5 August 2011 with the FSS Rules and Regulations.

A. Objectives

  • Lay down science-based standards for food
  • Regulate manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import of food
  • Ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human consumption

B. Functions of FSSAI

  1. Frame regulations and standards – food products, additives, contaminants, pesticide residues, labelling, packaging, fortification
  2. Licensing and registration of food businesses
    • registration for petty food businesses (small turnover)
    • state licence and central licence for larger businesses
  3. Accreditation of food laboratories; food testing, including mobile labs ("Food Safety on Wheels")
  4. Surveillance, inspection and enforcement
  5. Food safety audits; risk assessment; recall of unsafe food
  6. Import control of food
  7. Training – Food Safety Training and Certification (FoSTaC)
  8. Consumer awareness and information

C. Enforcement structure

  • Commissioner of Food Safety (state) → Designated Officer (district) → Food Safety Officers (inspection and sampling)
  • Food Analysts and accredited laboratories
  • Adjudicating Officers, Food Safety Appellate Tribunal and special courts

D. Penalties (graded by severity)

  • Fines for sub-standard, misbranded food, misleading advertisements and unhygienic processing
  • For unsafe food: imprisonment and fine increasing with harm – up to 6 months when no injury, up to 6 years for grievous injury, and 7 years to life imprisonment with a fine of at least ₹10 lakh if it causes death

E. Important initiatives

  • Eat Right India (2018) – "Sahi Bhojan, Behtar Jeevan"; Eat Right School, Eat Right Campus, Clean Street Food Hubs
  • "+F" logo for fortified foods; trans-fat limit of 2% in oils and fats
  • "Aaj se thoda kam" – gradual reduction of salt, sugar and oil
  • DART book for testing adulteration at home; Food Safety Connect app and helpline
  • World Food Safety Day – 7 June

F. Other related laws

  • AGMARK (Agricultural Produce Grading and Marking Act, 1937), BIS (ISI mark), Consumer Protection Act 2019, Legal Metrology Act 2009, Infant Milk Substitutes Act 1992, Essential Commodities Act 1955

G. Role of the nurse

  • Educate consumers to buy licensed, labelled food; report food safety complaints
  • Ensure hospital food services follow FSSAI hygiene requirements

Conclusion The FSS Act, 2006 replaced older food laws and created FSSAI to set science-based standards, license food businesses, test and monitor food, enforce graded penalties and promote safe and healthy eating through initiatives such as Eat Right India.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Name the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food.
answer_html:
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food

  1. Keep clean – wash hands before and during food preparation and after using the toilet; keep surfaces and utensils clean; protect food from insects and pests
  2. Separate raw and cooked – keep raw meat, poultry and seafood away from other foods; use separate knives and boards; store in separate covered containers
  3. Cook thoroughly – especially meat, poultry, eggs and seafood; bring soups and stews to boiling; reheat cooked food thoroughly
  4. Keep food at safe temperatures – do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours; refrigerate promptly (below 5 °C); keep hot food hot (above 60 °C); do not thaw at room temperature
  5. Use safe water and raw materials – use safe water; choose fresh, wholesome foods; wash fruits and vegetables; do not use food beyond its expiry date

Use: simple messages for teaching food handlers, mothers and the community.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Define food safety. What are food hazards?
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Food safety – the assurance that food will not cause harm to the consumer when it is prepared and/or eaten according to its intended use (Codex Alimentarius)
  • Food hygiene – all conditions and measures necessary to ensure the safety and suitability of food at all stages of the food chain – from farm to fork

Food hazards – agents in food that can cause harm:

  1. Biological – bacteria (Salmonella, Staphylococcus), viruses (hepatitis A), parasites (worms), toxins (aflatoxin)
  2. Chemical – pesticide residues, adulterants, non-permitted colours, heavy metals, cleaning chemicals, natural toxins
  3. Physical – stones, glass, hair, metal pieces, insects

Importance: unsafe food causes diarrhoea, typhoid, hepatitis, poisoning and cancers; food safety is a shared responsibility of producers, sellers, government and consumers. World Food Safety Day – 7 June.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Name the common types of bacterial food poisoning.
answer_html:
Definition Bacterial food poisoning is an acute illness, usually with vomiting and/or diarrhoea, caused by eating food contaminated with bacteria or their toxins.

Types

  1. Toxin type (toxin already formed in food – short incubation, 1–6 hours, vomiting prominent, little fever)
    • Staphylococcus aureus – milk products, sweets, cream; from food handlers with boils or nasal carriage
    • Bacillus cereus – reheated fried rice
    • Clostridium botulinum – improperly canned or preserved foods; causes botulism (double vision, difficulty swallowing, paralysis) after 12–36 hours
  2. Infection type (bacteria multiply in the gut – incubation 12–72 hours, fever, diarrhoea)
    • Salmonella – eggs, poultry, meat
    • Clostridium perfringens – meat dishes cooled slowly and reheated
    • Vibrio parahaemolyticus – seafood; E. coli, Campylobacter

Prevention: personal hygiene, proper cooking, refrigeration, avoiding reheated and stale food.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: What is the temperature danger zone for food?
answer_html:
Definition The temperature danger zone is the range between 5 °C and 60 °C in which bacteria multiply rapidly in food – some can double in number every 20 minutes.

Safe practices

  1. Keep cold food cold – below 5 °C (refrigerator)
  2. Keep hot food hot – above 60 °C until served
  3. Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours (less in hot weather)
  4. Cool leftovers quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate
  5. Thaw frozen food in the refrigerator, not on the kitchen counter
  6. Reheat food to at least 70 °C (steaming hot) before eating – only once

Importance: most outbreaks of food poisoning occur when cooked food is kept in the danger zone for hours, as in parties, hostels and canteens.

subject: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics
question: Describe food-borne diseases – classification, investigation of an outbreak of food poisoning, prevention and the role of the nurse. (3 + 4 + 3)
answer_html:
Introduction Food-borne diseases are diseases of an infectious or toxic nature caused by eating contaminated food or water. WHO estimates about 600 million illnesses and 420,000 deaths every year, with children under five bearing a large share. Outbreaks often follow community meals, weddings, hostels, canteens and mid-day meals.

A. Classification (3 marks)

1. Food-borne infections (organisms multiply in the body)

  • Bacterial – typhoid, cholera, salmonellosis, shigellosis, E. coli, Campylobacter, listeriosis, brucellosis
  • Viral – hepatitis A and E, norovirus, rotavirus
  • Parasitic – amoebiasis, giardiasis, tapeworm (taeniasis, cysticercosis), roundworm, trichinosis

2. Food-borne intoxications (toxins cause illness)

  • Bacterial toxins – Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, botulism
  • Natural toxins – aflatoxin (mouldy groundnuts and maize), poisonous mushrooms, solanine (green potatoes), cyanogenic glycosides (raw cassava), BOAA in khesari dal (lathyrism), ergot, toxic fish and shellfish
  • Chemicals – pesticide residues, heavy metals (lead, arsenic, mercury), adulterants (argemone oil – epidemic dropsy; metanil yellow)

3. Food allergies – peanut, milk, egg, shellfish (not infection or poisoning but food-related reactions)

B. Investigation of an outbreak of food poisoning (4 marks)

  1. Verify the diagnosis and confirm the outbreak – many people with similar symptoms after a common meal
  2. Treat cases immediately – ORS, IV fluids, antiemetics; refer severe cases; arrange antitoxin and ventilation for botulism
  3. Case definition and case finding – prepare a line list (name, age, sex, time of onset, symptoms, foods eaten)
  4. Describe by time, place and person
    • epidemic curve – a sharp rise and fall suggests a point-source outbreak
    • calculate the incubation period – short (1–6 hours) suggests a preformed toxin; longer (12–72 hours) suggests infection
  5. Food history from ill and well persons – calculate food-specific attack rates
    • Attack rate = number ill among those who ate the food ÷ total who ate the food × 100
    • the food with the highest attack rate among eaters and the lowest among non-eaters is the likely source
  6. Collect specimens – vomitus, stool and blood from cases; leftover food samples in sterile containers, kept cold; swabs from food handlers (nose, hands, skin lesions); water samples; send promptly to the laboratory
  7. Environmental investigation – inspect the kitchen, storage, cooking and holding temperatures, water supply and health of food handlers
  8. Laboratory confirmation of the organism or toxin
  9. Control measures – withdraw the suspected food, close or disinfect premises if needed, exclude infected handlers, educate staff
  10. Report to the District Surveillance Unit (IDSP) and the Food Safety Officer; write a report with recommendations

C. Prevention (3 marks)

  1. WHO Five Keys to Safer Food – keep clean; separate raw and cooked; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials
  2. Food handler hygiene – medical examination, training, exclusion when ill
  3. Safe water supply and sanitation
  4. Pasteurisation of milk; proper canning; avoid reheated stale food
  5. Enforcement of food laws – FSS Act, licensing, inspection
  6. Vaccination – typhoid and hepatitis A for high-risk groups and food handlers
  7. Health education of the public; awareness of food labels and adulteration
  8. Surveillance – early reporting of clusters through IDSP

D. Role of the nurse

  • Early recognition of an outbreak; first aid and rehydration
  • Help prepare the line list, collect and send specimens correctly
  • Report promptly to authorities; follow up affected persons
  • Educate food handlers, mid-day meal cooks, hostel staff and families on food safety
  • Participate in hospital infection control and kitchen supervision

E. Clues to the cause from incubation period and symptoms

  • 1–6 hours, mainly vomiting – preformed toxins: Staphylococcus aureus (milk sweets, cream), Bacillus cereus (reheated rice)
  • 8–24 hours, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea – Clostridium perfringens (reheated meat dishes)
  • 12–72 hours, fever and diarrhoea – Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter
  • 12–36 hours, double vision, difficulty swallowing, paralysis – botulism (home-canned foods) – an emergency
  • Minutes to a few hours, tingling, salivation, sweating, small pupils – chemical poisoning (e.g. organophosphate-contaminated food)
  • Weeks – typhoid, hepatitis A and E

F. Groups at higher risk of severe illness – infants and young children, pregnant women (listeriosis can cause abortion), elderly people and immunocompromised patients (HIV, cancer, transplant) – they should avoid raw milk, raw eggs, undercooked meat and stale food.

Conclusion Food-borne diseases include infections, intoxications and chemical poisonings; an outbreak is investigated by confirming cases, studying time, place and person, calculating food-specific attack rates, collecting samples and inspecting the kitchen, while prevention rests on the five keys to safer food, healthy food handlers, safe water and enforcement of food laws.
